World.title: Liberia: Defense Alleges Witness Tampering at AREPT; Taskforce Denies Wrongdoing in Saudi Rice Trial
World.content:
Defense attorney Gbawou Kowou says witnesses who testified for the accused were summoned to AREPT’s headquarters and pressured, while the taskforce says the incident was a misunderstanding and denies attempting to influence the witnesses.

By Jaheim T. Tumu

[email protected]

PAYNESVILLE CITY — A confrontation at the headquarters of the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce (AREPT) has triggered fresh tensions in the ongoing Saudi rice criminal trial, after defense lawyer Gbawou Kowou accused the agency of attempting to intimidate or tamper with witnesses who recently testified for the defense.



AREPT has denied the allegation, saying the individuals at the center of the controversy were not invited for questioning and that its lawyers immediately asked them to leave after discovering that they had recently testified as defense witnesses.

The dispute unfolded Sunday after Kowou went to the AREPT compound and began a livestream in which he alleged that several witnesses who had testified before Criminal Court “C” had been summoned to the agency and were being pressured about their testimony.

Standing outside the facility, Kowou repeatedly demanded access to the compound, claiming that his witnesses were being held inside.

“I’m live at AREPT. Witnesses who testified on our behalf yesterday were brought here and threatened,” Kowou said during the broadcast, describing the alleged conduct as witness tampering.

He later alleged that AREPT officials had locked the facility’s gate to prevent him from entering.

“They have locked the gate. The witnesses are in there,” he said. “If the witnesses are not there, open the gate.”

Kowou specifically accused AREPT Chairman Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin of directing the witnesses to report to the agency after their appearance in court.

The lawyer argued that the witnesses had already completed their testimony and should not have been subjected to further engagement by officials connected to the prosecution.

Kowou Allowed Into Compound

Kowou was later allowed into the AREPT compound, where he confronted officials over the presence of the witnesses.

Speaking to FrontPage Africa afterward, Kowou said the witnesses were members of the Group of 77 and the community of persons living with disabilities who had testified for the defense.

According to Kowou, the witnesses told him they had been threatened or pressured to report to the AREPT office in Paynesville after appearing in court.

He said he subsequently went to the facility to establish why witnesses who had already testified were being summoned by an agency involved in the prosecution.

Kowou was later taken to a police station following the confrontation.

According to the defense lawyer, AREPT subsequently told him that the situation was a misunderstanding.

But Kowou rejected the explanation, maintaining that the circumstances surrounding the witnesses’ presence at AREPT were troubling.

He characterized the move as sinister and argued that attempts to engage or influence witnesses after they had testified could amount to improper interference with the judicial process.

Kowou described the alleged conduct as tantamount to witness tampering, and said the matter should be taken seriously given the ongoing trial.

Heated Exchange at AREPT

Video footage from the scene showed a heated exchange between Kowou, AREPT employees and other individuals gathered outside the facility.

At one point, persons inside the compound instructed Kowou to stop filming and lower his camera. He refused.

“No, I can’t put the camera down so the world will know this kind of criminal act carried on by the prosecution,” Kowou said during the livestream.

As tensions escalated, officers of the Liberia National Police arrived at the scene.

Kowou repeated his allegations to the officers, insisting that a crime was being committed because defense witnesses had allegedly been brought to AREPT after testifying in court.

“A crime is being committed. My witnesses testified before the court yesterday, and they were brought here,” he told the officers.

The livestream ended as Kowou indicated that he would accompany the police inside the compound to further address the matter.

AREPT Rejects Allegation

In a statement issued after the incident, AREPT denied that its officials had threatened, intimidated or attempted to influence any defense witness.

According to AREPT Public Relations Officer Joseph F. Daniels, the controversy arose after a potential witness who had previously provided a statement during the agency’s investigation was asked to appear at AREPT with other individuals familiar with the Saudi rice matter.

AREPT said the potential witness arrived with two people whom he identified as being familiar with the case.

The agency said its lawyers did not initially know that the two individuals had recently appeared before Criminal Court “C” as subpoenaed defense witnesses.

“Upon recognizing them, AREPT lawyers immediately asked the two individuals to leave the premises,” the statement said.

AREPT said the two witnesses were not invited by the agency, were not interviewed and did not provide any additional statements.

The taskforce said it therefore rejects the allegation that its lawyers attempted to influence or intimidate the witnesses.

“If defense counsel has evidence of witness tampering or intimidation, that evidence should be presented to the court, where such allegations can be properly addressed,” AREPT said.

Dispute Comes as Prosecution Prepares Rebuttal

The controversy comes as AREPT prosecutors prepare to present rebuttal witnesses in the high-profile Saudi rice case involving 13 former government officials.

The defendants are facing corruption-related charges stemming from the handling and distribution of Saudi-donated rice during the transition to the Boakai administration.

The trial has attracted public and political attention, with defense lawyers repeatedly challenging aspects of the prosecution’s case and government witnesses providing competing accounts of how the rice was handled.

The latest dispute places the conduct of both the prosecution and defense under renewed scrutiny.

For the defense, the central question is whether witnesses who have already testified were subsequently approached in a manner that could influence their testimony.

For AREPT, the agency maintains that no such engagement occurred and that its lawyers acted to remove the two former defense witnesses from the premises once their status became known.

World.title: SN Brussels Travelers from Liberia, Sierra Leone Face Tougher Scrutiny as Europe Hunts ‘Bolle Jos’
World.content:
MONROVIA – For many Liberian and Sierra Leonean families, the SN Brussels flight is more than a ticket. Brussels Airlines, still called “SN” by most travelers here after the carrier it succeeded in 2007, is the plane that brings a mother home for Christmas, carries a student to a European campus and returns a trader with goods for a Waterside shop.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

It is also, investigators in Monrovia and Brussels now say, a route drug networks have tried to exploit.



Caught at the carousel

On July 31, Belgian customs officers were checking passengers off a Brussels Airlines flight from Freetown when they stopped a 22-year-old woman from Anderlecht, according to the Halle-Vilvoorde prosecutor’s office and Belgian media. Her two suitcases held 51 kilograms of cocaine.

She had not been on the plane. Investigators believe she was sent only to collect the bags and are still trying to establish how she got into the baggage reclaim hall. A judge later moved her from detention to electronic monitoring.

Weeks earlier at Roberts International Airport (RIA), Liberian security officers flagged six cargo boxes labeled as Maggi cubes and lappa. Inside were 198 compressed plates of cocaine. The Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) said at the time the shipment, valued at US$19.2 million, was bound for Brussels Airlines’ Europe-bound operations. A Justice Ministry charge sheet later listed London as the final destination.

This week, those two scenes met in a single policy fight in Europe. And the people likely to feel it first are not the kingpins, but honest passengers queuing at RIA and Lungi.

‘Chubby Jos’ next door

The man at the center of Europe’s anger lives one border away. Jos Leijdekkers, known in the Netherlands as “Bolle Jos” (Chubby Jos), is that country’s most wanted criminal. Dutch media placed him in Sierra Leone in early 2025.

In the Netherlands he was sentenced to 24 years in prison for cocaine trafficking and an attempted assassination. In Belgium, his sentences across several cases total more than 100 years, Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported. In May, a court in Dendermonde, Belgium, sentenced him in absentia to eight years for his role in moving 11 tonnes of cocaine from Sierra Leone to the Port of Antwerp in October 2023, hidden in palm kernel meal. Twenty accomplices were also convicted.

The Economist’s 1843 magazine reported on September 18 that he lived in Sierra Leone under the name “Omar Sheriff,” posed as a wealthy investor and kept bodyguards from Ghana and South Africa.

Dutch media have reported that he has a relationship, and a child, with a daughter of President Julius Maada Bio. FrontPageAfrica has not independently confirmed this.

No treaty, no handover

The Netherlands and Sierra Leone have no extradition treaty. The Dutch formally delivered an extradition request anyway, and Freetown has yet to sign off on it. Van Weel said in June that Sierra Leone keeps telling him the procedures are under way.

That patience has run out. On X on Thursday morning, Van Weel announced that “the EU will no longer provide budget support to the authorities of Sierra Leone this year.” He told the Dutch daily De Telegraaf a day earlier that the suspension, about €18 million for 2026, was because Sierra Leone is not cooperating on the extradition. The Netherlands also wants a planned €22.5 million for next year held back.

The freeze hits money paid straight into the state budget. Development and humanitarian aid are excluded, so Europe is aiming at the government, not at Sierra Leoneans in need. Van Weel has called it bizarre that Europe should support a country sheltering one of the world’s biggest drug criminals.

Speaking to NOS in Luxembourg on Thursday, Van Weel welcomed the Commission’s decision. “It sends a very clear signal from the European Commission that Sierra Leone must stop harboring this criminal,” he said.

Asked whether the measure was too harsh on an impoverished country, Van Weel turned the question back on its government. Leijdekkers, he said, causes “immense destruction, including for the people of Sierra Leone.”

“They could resolve this within 24 hours by arresting and extraditing this man,” he said.

If the aid freeze does not work, Van Weel warned, “we will continue to increase the pressure through other channels.” He added: “We are fully committed to bringing this criminal to the Netherlands.”

The Dutch have also worked through Sierra Leone’s neighbors. Van Weel told De Telegraaf in July that Liberia and Ghana are aware of the risks and frustrated by Freetown’s refusal to act.

Ghana has already moved. In September, its Narcotics Control Commission arrested three men accused of representing Leijdekkers’ network there, after French customs seized nearly 3.9 tonnes of cocaine in Dunkirk. The drugs, valued at about €225 million, were hidden in a container of plastic waste shipped from Ghana.

The Economist estimates about a third of the cocaine reaching Europe now passes through West Africa. Liberia is on its route map.

Liberia’s own test

Liberia’s record this year shows how close the trade has come to home.

Police charged five men and the cargo firm Global Logistics Services (GLS) on July 4 over the June RIA seizure of about 237.6 kilograms. Among them was Michael U.S. Browne, whose release from prison after a 2024 drug charge the Senate has ordered investigated.

Prosecutors allege GLS operations manager Paul Jamaal King organized the shipment and then tried to recover it after it was flagged, including by offering money to airport security. King has pleaded not guilty and is presumed innocent. In July, the Monrovia City Court found probable cause and sent him and six co-defendants to Criminal Court “C” for trial. Days later, the case appeared stalled because certified records had not reached the court.

Investigators followed the airport leads to the VOA community on the RIA Highway. On July 22, joint security forces arrested two foreign nationals and uncovered a suspected cocaine cache officials valued at up to US$50 million.

When the guards are the thieves

On Tuesday, a jury in Kakata convicted two LDEA agents posted at RIA, Special Agent Joe Logan and Agent Lovette Flowers, along with Nigerian national Tony Obi. Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie of the 13th Judicial Circuit sentenced each to 20 years, the maximum.

Prosecutors said the agents took four of 14 seized plates of cocaine and sold them, and that the network paid about US$10,000 in bribes to LDEA officers. The case began in July 2025 with Quita Dolo Kosso, who landed at RIA from Thailand on a Kenya Airways flight with about 3.4 kilograms of cocaine. She pleaded guilty and is serving five years.

The lesson for travelers is uncomfortable. Drugs can be caught at the gate and still leak out the back door. Europe has noticed both.

Brussels takes aim

Van Weel is in Luxembourg, where EU justice and home affairs ministers meet Thursday and Friday. The agenda covers migration, the EU drugs strategic framework and how the geopolitical climate is affecting Europe’s security. He wrote on X that talks would include “the safety of Europe and the EU-sanctions regime for organized crime.”

He is urging ministers to adopt the regime swiftly, Politico Europe’s Playbook reported. He told Playbook the Bolle Jos case calls for measures against all organized criminals Europe cannot immediately detain, “not only against him,” and said he hopes the regime is concluded by year’s end.

An EU diplomat with the Dutch delegation told OCCRP that cross-border networks can be “very effective” when based in a third country whose authorities will not cooperate or extradite. “The standard criminal law approach isn’t achieving the results we want,” the diplomat said. “That is why there is a push to expand that toolkit.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the package in her 2025 State of the Union address, and the EU Council mandated work on it. On July 9, the Commission and the EU’s foreign policy chief proposed a regime covering drug trafficking, migrant smuggling, human and firearms trafficking and money laundering. It would freeze assets, impose trade restrictions and bar listed people from entering or transiting EU states.

It still has to be agreed, and adoption needs the backing of all 27 member states. Earlier efforts stalled because national police feared sanctions could tip off suspects and spoil investigations. Van Weel said support is stronger now.

What it means for SN Brussels passengers

Sanctions target kingpins, their financiers and fixers, not ordinary travelers. But passengers on the Monrovia–Freetown–Brussels line already live with the side effects, and those are likely to grow.

Tighter checks on arrival. The 51-kilogram arrest came during a targeted customs check of passengers off the Freetown flight. Expect more of those, and more bags opened.

Networks recruiting the young. This week, Belgian and French authorities announced 21 arrests in a ring that used Brussels Airport. It recruited “extractors” through social media, bought tickets just to reach baggage halls and paid airport workers to pull drugs from suitcases before they reached the carousel.

Your bag, someone else’s crime.

The RIA cases show cargo and luggage can be tampered with by insiders. Lock and label bags, and refuse parcels from anyone, even relatives, without seeing what is inside.

Travel bans for facilitators. Once adopted, the EU regime could bar listed people from entering or passing through Europe. Anyone working for a front company, freight forwarder or fixer tied to a listed network risks being swept up.

A reputation tax. Every bust adds to the suspicion attached to a Liberian or Sierra Leonean passport at a European counter. Honest travelers pay that bill in delays and questions.

For now, the man Europe most wants sits a short flight from Monrovia, beyond reach. Van Weel insists Freetown could change that in a day. The question for Liberia is whether it is seen as part of the problem or part of the fix. The 20-year sentences handed down in Kakata this week were a start. The next test is the US$19.2 million trial.

World.title: Hungry and Out of Options, More Poor Liberians Turn to Begging as Prices Outrun Income
World.content:
Members of Vamoma group seeking assistance in Monrovia. Photo: Fatu A. Kamara

Summary

As Liberia’s economy shows signs of recovery on paper, soaring food and fuel prices, worsened by a government fuel surcharge and new health care fees imposed after US aid cuts, have outpaced wage growth.

Ten Liberians interviewed in Monrovia say growing unemployment, lost livelihoods and financial hardship in the last two years have pushed them to depend on strangers and charitable support to survive.

Humanitarian organizations and government say they are seeing growing demand for assistance as families struggle with food, school fees, healthcare and other basic needs.

By Fatu Kamara with New Narratives

BROAD STREET, Monrovia – It has been a long day for Joseph. The sun is beginning to set, and the 48-year-old father of three has been trawling the streets of Monrovia since morning, asking for money.



On most days, he begs for money to feed his family. Today, he can’t even raise enough to get home to Brewerville, on the outskirts of the city.

“Since this morning, nobody has given me a dime,” he says.

Joseph lost his job in waste management in 2025 after the death of his boss. A high school graduate who earned L$10,000 (US$55) monthly, he spent about a year looking for another job without success.

He says he now has two options: begging or stealing. “It is not fair for me to be begging people in the streets, but I will not go to steal.”

Joseph is one of 10 people interviewed for this story who said they began begging within the past two years. Most said they had no jobs, had lost sources of income or lacked money to start a business. (FrontPage Africa/New Narratives is withholding the names of people in this story to protect them from stigma.) Liberia’s economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, according to the African Development Bank, a jump from years before, but most families haven’t felt it. Growth came mostly from mining royalties to government, not job creation, and extreme poverty still rose to 35.8 percent.

The crisis deepened when the Trump administration canceled 27 of 29 USAID programs in Liberia in May 2025, cutting nearly US$360 million from health and education. Large cuts by other donors followed too. The government responded by adding a $0.25 per gallon petroleum surcharge and implementing new patient fees for healthcare. For families already struggling to afford food, the surcharge pushed up transport and food costs, and the hospital fees have deterred many from going for treatment or crippled them financially when they face emergencies. Baba Conteh, an economist, says economic recovery has not translated into meaningful jobs and stable incomes for ordinary households. Aid cuts have trickled down throughout the economy. “Job loss is one of the most common pathways into poverty,” Conteh says, particularly when the loss continues long enough for families to exhaust their savings and sell productive assets. In extreme cases, he says, people may become homeless, engage in high-risk survival activities, depend heavily on public charity or even resort to committing crimes.

That is exactly what is happening. At Vamoma house on Tubman Boulevard, in Sinkor, Esther Kamara leads a group of widows, elderly people and people with disabilities who gather to seek assistance. She says the group had about 280 members in 2024 and has since grown by 50.

People living in poverty gather at Vamoma house, on Tubman Boulevard, in Sinkor

“I have even started refusing people because the number just getting plenty and no help is coming,” Kamara says.

After more than a decade of leading the group, Kamara says the past two years have been the toughest. “Many days the women come to me when they or their children are sick and no money to take them to hospital, so we just buy drugs and they take it,” she says. The drugs are usually antibiotics, bought without a prescription and taken with no medical guidance, making the child likely to build antibiotic resistance.

Support groups under pressure from growing demand

The pressure is being felt by organizations that provide assistance. Siakeh Foundation and Kimbo Foundation, two organizations working with vulnerable Liberians, say requests for help have doubled over the last two years.

Four Hunger, a U.S.-registered nonprofit in Liberia, reports an increase in requests from families who previously managed to meet at least some of their basic needs but now struggle with food, school fees, healthcare and other essentials.

“The growing demand has put considerable pressure on our resources. One of the most difficult parts is that we often receive requests we genuinely want to respond to but cannot fully meet,” says co-founder Windell S. King.

At Rescue for Abandoned and Children in Hardship, or REACH, Ne-Suah Livingstone, founder and executive director, says she has also seen families pushed into situations they previously managed to avoid.

“One case that remains with me involved a family whose daughter’s annual school fees were about US$1,000. Her father had previously worked on a USAID-funded project but lost his job after the projects ended.”

She says the fees were far beyond the reach of the small organization.

REACH receives about twice as many requests for assistance as it did two years ago.

“This is one of the hardest tasks I face every day,” says Livingstone. “To say to a person in dire need that neither I nor my organization is able to help you; saying this can be like you have asked me to hurt someone.”

“I won’t steal” but begging comes with humiliation

At Vamoma, Hawa, a 43-year-old widow with two children, says asking for help became a last resort after she lost her husband in 2024. She says her youngest child, 14, is still in school through support from her church. Her older child is at home because she has not found the money to keep him in school.

“People were mocking me in my community because I am poor,” Hawa says. “I felt embarrassed and I could not bear the shame anymore.”

She says Vamoma offers more than the possibility of receiving money or food.

“At least when I am among my friends and we are laughing, the stress goes down,” Hawa says. “I don’t know what I was going to do if I had not joined the group.”

For some members, the hardship goes beyond asking strangers for help. Kamara says some elderly and vulnerable people face stigma in their communities.

“You know when people are like this, you will not find any family member coming around them,” she says. “They can abandon them. Sometimes they call them witches and wizards.”

Larwuo, a member of Vamoma, stands in front of her home. She says she was abandoned by her son.

Last month one elderly member of the group died here. Kamara had to ask government to collect the body.

Government response constrained by limited resources

Officials at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection have observed the growing need but have little money to help.

“The key gap in addressing the issues affecting these vulnerable groups is limited resources, preventing the ministry from reaching them,” says Alex Divine, the ministry’s assistant director of Programs, Partnership and Resource Mobilization.

The government tried to reduce the rapidly growing number of street children, which hit 366,000 according to a survey in 2023, before the cost-of-living crisis escalated. Through its “Support a Child, Save the Future” initiative, launched in 2024 to remove children from the streets through school enrollment, family reunification and support for caregivers. The government has conceded that it did not raise any of the $15 million cost of the project from donors and only budgeted a total of $1.3m itself. The ministry came under public fire this month when an official posted the names of children who were allegedly helped on Facebook. Since then, the ministry has refused to share details. There has been no independent audit of the project.

Women share cooked food donated by the Jetty company.

“While existing programs provide critical support, the support is insufficient because it reaches a limited number of the overall vulnerable population across the country,” Divine says.

At Vamoma, the group has no permanent shelter. Kamara says members once put together sticks and zinc to create a small shelter, but police later dismantled it.

“When the rain is falling, some people cover themselves with plastic,” she says. “Sometimes you see people trembling with the cold. We are disappointed in our leaders because they are sitting down and the people dying.”

The only help comes in food donations from groups like the Indian company Jeety Rubber or Yamah Brown, a dry goods seller in Red Light, who recently donated two bags of rice.

“They are our mothers. They don’t deserve it, but condition made them like this,” Brown says. “We will continue to help as long as we can afford.”

While assistance is important, Kamara says they want something reliable.

“What we really want is jobs for members, especially the widows, people who are able to work,” she says. “Many of them are strong and able to work, but we all come here and sit from morning to night because there’s nothing to do. If we had jobs, we won’t be here.”

Joseph agrees that breaking the cycle of dependency requires opportunities beyond daily charity.

“Even if I can get money to start a business, I would be grateful,” he says. “And a man is only respected when he provides for his family.”

For now, as the sun sets, Joseph gives up finding enough money to get transport home. He sets out on foot for a walk that may take hours and will end with the faces of disappointed and hungry children. He will wake up tomorrow and try again.

This report is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency which had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Landmark Rape Trial, Defendant Jallah Accuses Police of Planting His Saliva on Survivor’s Clothing
World.content:
Monrovia – Peter Bon Jallah, on trial for alleged gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping involving a 16-year-old boy, took the witness stand Thursday and accused investigators of deliberately placing his DNA on the teenager’s clothing to implicate him in the case. Jallah denied the charges, said he was elsewhere when the alleged assaults occurred, and insisted he did not know the teenager.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Jallah told Criminal Court “E” that police had obtained his saliva sample during the investigation and used it to connect him to clothing recovered from the alleged survivor.



“Why is my saliva DNA profile on the white T-shirt and boxer?” Jallah asked the court, directing attention to the Liberia National Police, which he said had custody of his DNA sample.

He went further, alleging that investigators intentionally placed his saliva on the clothing.

“They intentionally placed my saliva DNA on the white T-shirt and the boxer. Obviously, it was a means to an end,” he testified.

Jallah did not present evidence during his testimony to substantiate the allegation, and the court has made no finding that police manipulated or planted the DNA evidence.

What the Forensic Report Says

The DNA evidence is a significant component of the prosecution’s case.

Clothing recovered during the investigation was submitted to the Rwanda Forensic Institute for examination. According to the forensic report, a male DNA profile recovered from a white T-shirt, black T-shirt, shorts and boxer shorts matched Jallah’s DNA profile.

The Judiciary has confirmed that Rwandan forensic examiner Bavugirije Pascal was summoned to testify regarding the findings.

Jallah has not simply disputed the laboratory’s conclusion. His defense is that his DNA could have been placed on the clothing after investigators obtained his saliva sample.

That allegation now puts the handling and chain of custody of the DNA evidence at issue before the court.

Jallah: ‘I Was Somewhere Else’

Jallah also denied being present during any of the alleged assaults.

The teenager has testified that he was assaulted on three occasions—twice at Jallah’s residence in November and December 2025, and again in January 2026 at a building on Camp Johnson Road after he was allegedly taken from the Airfield area and held for several days.

Jallah rejected that account.

He testified that he was in the Mikey Gray Community on Du-Port Road with his partner and her family on the relevant date. He also denied being at his home on November 29 and December 24, 2025, when two of the alleged assaults were said to have occurred.

Jallah questioned the teenager’s description of his residence, telling the court that the boy could not accurately describe the bedroom where the alleged assaults were said to have occurred.

He further pointed to phone records from January 1 to 3, 2026, and around Christmas 2025, which he said could establish his whereabouts.

‘I Never Knew Him’

Jallah also rejected the prosecution’s account of his relationship with the teenager.

Prosecutors have alleged that the boy was familiar with Jallah’s residence and performed chores there, including washing his vehicle.

Jallah denied knowing the teenager.

He told the court that he has an assigned vehicle and a driver who, according to him, washes the vehicle twice daily.

He also denied giving the teenager LD$1,500 to dispose of garbage, describing the allegation as untrue.

Jallah Challenges Medical Evidence

Jallah also challenged the interpretation of the medical evidence presented in the case.

He argued that the medical findings, at most, indicated signs consistent with penetration and ejaculation but did not independently establish that rape occurred.

He similarly questioned the ability of the Rwandan forensic examiner to determine whether a sexual assault had occurred, maintaining that the expert’s role was limited to the scientific examination of evidence.

The statutory rape charge, however, is based on the alleged victim’s age and the applicable provisions of Liberian law.

Testimony Comes After Failed Acquittal Bid

Jallah’s testimony came a day after Criminal Court “E” Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. denied his motion for a judgment of acquittal.

In his September 30 ruling, Judge Wesseh found that the prosecution had presented sufficient evidence for the trial to continue.

The defense had asked the court to dismiss the charges after the prosecution rested its case, arguing, among other things, that the teenager’s descriptions of the alleged crime scenes did not correspond with observations made during the court’s visit to the locations.

With the motion denied, Jallah took the stand to present his defense and directly challenge the evidence and testimony presented by the prosecution.

DNA Evidence Now Central to Defense

The prosecution has presented testimony from the alleged survivor, police investigators and medical personnel and has relied, in part, on the forensic findings linking Jallah’s DNA to clothing examined by the Rwanda Forensic Institute.

Jallah disputes the prosecution’s account and maintains that investigators manipulated the DNA evidence.

Whether the DNA evidence was properly collected, handled and preserved—and whether the forensic findings establish the connection alleged by the prosecution—are matters for the court to determine based on the evidence presented at trial.

Jallah faces charges of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. He has pleaded not guilty and remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Two other men allegedly linked to the January incident have not been arrested and were charged in absentia.

World.title: Coming Home to Heal: Liberian American Surgeon Bringing Global Team to Treat Patients and Train Health Workers
World.content:
Monrovia – Dr. Carolyn Baindu Moore built her career in the United States as a robotic thoracic surgeon, operating on the chest with some of medicine’s most advanced tools. In December, she is bringing a team home to Liberia, where some counties have no specialist surgeon at all.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Moore is CEO and founder of the Liberia Global Health & Surgery Consortium (LGHSC), which officially launches in the country from December 1 to 15. Over two weeks, the group plans to operate on patients, train 250 people in emergency care, screen 100 market women for cancer and hold its first fundraising dinner in Monrovia.



She says she doesn’t want this to be a one-time trip.

“Our goal is to leave a lasting impact through compassionate care, practical training, and partnership with Liberian healthcare teams,” she said.

The gap

Liberians who have had to travel to Monrovia for an operation, or wait weeks for one, know the problem well. The civil war emptied hospitals and drove doctors and nurses abroad. Ebola came a decade later and killed health workers the country could not afford to lose. Liberia has been rebuilding ever since.

The most recent nationwide count of surgical staff, published in the World Journal of Surgery, found 286 surgical providers in Liberia in 2018. Only 67 were accredited specialists. That is 1.6 specialist surgeons, anaesthetists and obstetricians for every 100,000 people. The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery says a country needs at least 20. At the time, Liberia had three specialist anaesthesiologists for the whole country.

Most of those specialists work in Montserrado. In the poorest counties, the study counted 0.7 per 100,000 people.

Women pay much of the price. A UNFPA policy brief drawn from the 2022 national census puts Liberia’s maternal mortality ratio at 854 deaths per 100,000 live births, roughly one mother lost for every 117 babies born alive. The sub-Saharan African average is 536. The global target is under 70.

Then there is cervical cancer. The ICO/IARC Information Centre on HPV and Cancer estimates that 656 Liberian women are diagnosed with it each year and 469 die, about nine women every week. Most of those deaths can be prevented, because screening can catch the disease before it turns deadly. But many women are never screened, and by the time they reach a doctor, little can be done.

Who is coming

The visiting team is made up of five surgeons, six nurses, four global health partners and two medical students. On the ground, they will join five Liberian surgeons, 15 nurse volunteers and 17 Consortium volunteers. The Consortium says it works in partnership with the Ministry of Health, and that its plans were drawn up with Liberian hospital leaders, county health teams and community representatives.

In the operating room

From December 7 to 11, visiting and Liberian surgeons will operate side by side. Where equipment and facilities allow, that will include laparoscopic surgery, sometimes called “keyhole” surgery. Instead of one long cut, the surgeon works through a few small openings with a camera. Patients generally hurt less, heal faster and go home sooner. Few Liberian hospitals offer it now, and teaching it is one of the main reasons for the mission.

The hospital where the operations will take place, and how many patients will be treated, have not yet been confirmed. Local clinical teams will screen patients.

Learning to save a life

The same week, at the Liberian Learning Center at Paynesville Town Hall, the Consortium plans to train 250 people in Basic Life Support and Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support. The courses teach CPR and what to do when a heart stops, the kind of emergency where a few minutes decide whether someone lives.

Not all the trainees are medical workers. Doctors, nurses, residents and emergency medical staff will sit alongside ordinary citizens. Some will be trained to teach the course themselves, so the skills keep spreading after the visitors leave. The team is also donating automated external defibrillators, or AEDs, the portable machines that can shock a stopped heart back into rhythm. They are still hard to find in Liberia.

For the women who feed the city

On December 14 and 15, a mobile clinic will set up in the Rock Church community in Duazon for 100 market women. They will get health education, consultations, breast and reproductive health checks, and screening for cervical cancer and high-risk HPV. The Consortium’s pathology team will process the samples, and its OB/GYN workgroup will work with local health authorities to make sure women who need further care are referred.

The choice of market women is deliberate. They keep homes running and children in school, often on what they earn in a single day. Taking a day off to sit in a clinic queue means losing that money, so many simply don’t go. This time, the clinic is coming to them.

A dinner and a longer plan

On December 12, the Consortium will host its founding fundraiser banquet at Afro Beach, Thinker Village, from 6:00 to 10:30 p.m. Dr. Deddeh E. P. Supuwood will give the keynote address, and Mr. Leo Lekpele Nupolu-Johnson will be master of ceremonies. Money raised will go to patient care, training, equipment, and community outreach.

Medical missions to Africa have a mixed reputation. Too often, a team flies in, operates, takes pictures and flies out, leaving behind patients with no follow-up and local staff no better prepared than before. LGHSC, which now counts more than 120 members in more than 16 workgroups on four continents, says it is trying to do the opposite. It wants to work through Liberian teams, keep mentoring them, and keep checking on patients long after December.

Whether that works will only be clear after the visitors fly home. It will show in the nurse in Paynesville who can now run a resuscitation, the surgeon who can do a keyhole operation without help, and the market woman in Duazon whose results come back in time.

“Our measure of success,” Moore said, “is the quality of care we provide and the knowledge, confidence, and capacity that remain long after we leave.”

Those wishing to volunteer, partner, or support the launch can contact [email protected] or visit www.libghsc.org. Donations can be made at https://givebutter.com/XYetak.

World.title: Liberia: House Honors Fallen Former Bong County Lawmaker Ranney Jackson
World.content:
Monrovia – The leadership and members of the House of Representatives on Thursday paid their final respects to the late Dr. Ranney B. Jackson Sr., a former Bong County lawmaker and veteran public servant, during a State Funeral held at the Capitol Building in Monrovia.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The ceremony brought together members of the Legislature, government officials, family members, friends, former colleagues, and well-wishers who gathered to honor Jackson’s decades of service to Liberia.



Speaker of the House Richard Nagbe Koon, speaking on behalf of the leadership and members of the House, extended condolences to the bereaved family and recognized Jackson’s contributions to the Legislature and the Liberian state.

Speaker Koon said the presence of the House leadership and members at the funeral reflected the institution’s respect for those who have served the Liberian people under its mandate.

Members of the House joined the Speaker in a moment of solemn reflection and paid their final respects to their former colleague.

Dr. Jackson’s public service career spanned local government, the Legislature, national administration and public policy.

He served as a member of the National Transitional Legislative Assembly (NTLA) from 2003 to 2005, representing Bong County during a critical period in Liberia’s post-war transition.

During his two-year tenure, Jackson chaired the NTLA’s Post and Telecommunications Committee. His work on the committee included efforts that contributed to reducing the cost of SIM cards from US$65 to US$15 in 2005.

Following his service in the transitional legislature, Jackson remained active in national politics and public administration. He made three unsuccessful bids for the Bong County senatorial seat, contesting the elections in 2005, 2011 and 2014.

He later served as Superintendent of Bong County during the first administration of former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. During Sirleaf’s second term, he was appointed Deputy Minister for Operations at the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Jackson’s public service continued under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who in 2024 appointed him Co-Chairman of the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Core Team, where he served alongside Chairman Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin.

At the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force, Jackson was recognized for his experience in governance, public administration, finance and public policy as the government intensified efforts to trace, recover and safeguard public assets.

Before his death, Jackson had also recently earned a Ph.D. in Public Policy and Administration, specializing in Local Government Management and Sustainable Communities, from Walden University in the United States.

His career reflected a progression through several levels of public service—from county administration and the transitional Legislature to senior positions within the national government and public policy.

Dr. Jackson died at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Hospital in Monrovia on August 22, 2024, at age 74, following a brief illness.

According to the obituary, the body will be taken to Bong County on Friday, October 2, for a night of wake-keeping, followed by the funeral service and burial on Saturday.

World.title: “Healing Must Start With Us Leaders”: Silumbe Calls for National Indaba and Urges Hichilema To Embrace Dialogue
World.content:
Leadership Movement (LM) president Dr Richard Silumbe has called for a national indaba on reconciliation, saying Zambia’s healing must begin with its leaders and cannot be put off.

Dr Silumbe said the country has lost its identity as One Zambia One Nation because of the issues surrounding the outcome of the August 13 general election. He said Zambians are living through politics of hate and division, which should not be allowed in a Christian nation.

“We need to heal this nation and we must do it now, not any other day,” he said. “And this healing must start with us leaders. Let us open our hearts to the current situation in the country.”

He warned that delay carries a price. “We need a genuine national indaba for reconciliation because if we don’t do it now, we are building a fertile land for a national crisis,” Dr Silumbe said.

The LM, he said, is ready to push for genuine and earnest reconciliation, but the country cannot move forward while it stays bitter and vengeful. “We cannot move forward if we are still bitter, if we are still a nation of vengeance, if we are vindictive, if we cannot forgive and forget,” he said. The only ground on which healing can take place, he added, is respect for the rule of law.

The LM leader then turned to party cadres, and to the leaders who have kept quiet about them. He said supporters are insulting one another and promoting hatred while those in leadership say nothing.

“We need to call for order; we need to call out these cadres to stop, while we promote unity, national reconciliation, forgiveness and national healing,” he said. “This is very important for this nation.”

His appeal to President Hakainde Hichilema was tied to the Government’s own targets. Dr Silumbe urged the Head of State to look beyond the election and face reality if he wants the Grow Zambia Agenda to yield results and benefit the nation.

He said he has seen Mr Hichilema working towards that agenda, but it cannot be achieved while the nation is polarised. “We cannot achieve the three million metric tonnes of copper production; we shall not achieve the 10 million metric tonnes of maize; we shall not grow the economy,” he said. “We will achieve nothing in that Grow Zambia Agenda in the current state of the nation.”

Dr Silumbe’s request to the President was direct: embrace dialogue and call for reconciliation towards national healing.

He also said the United Party for National Development (UPND) government has exposed itself to many battlefronts against its own citizens, and he pointed first to its relationship with the Church. “We have a government that is not in good books with the Church. For me, this is dangerous,” he said.

He went on to say that the Government is in power while people are still challenging its legitimacy, which he called an eye-opener for reconciliation. He said he accepts that Mr Hichilema is President, but the Head of State should extend an olive branch to a grieving society.

“Let him extend a hand to the Church and talk,” Dr Silumbe said. “Let him do that to civil society and political stakeholders.”

The healing he is asking for, he stressed, is not about a few individuals but the entire nation. The opposition still claims it won the election.

The LM says it is ready to lead the push for reconciliation once the call for an indaba is taken up.

World.title: Hichilema Tells Chiefs To Keep Enough Maize for Homes as Drought Warning Stands
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged traditional leaders to tell their subjects to keep enough maize for their own families, warning that an El Niño-induced drought is coming and that no one should say they were not told.

The Head of State spoke at the 2026 Samu Lya Moomba traditional ceremony in Bweengwa, Monze, his first traditional ceremony since his re-election. He assured the nation that the Government will ensure that no one dies of hunger, but said households must also take responsibility by preserving adequate food stocks.

Mr Hichilema put the request to the chiefs directly. He said traditional leaders could “inform our people to retain as much maize as possible for your own family consumption because we have a drought and don’t say we were not told”.

“Please keep as much maize so that we can protect our children from going hungry,” the President said.

He warned that the drought alert should not be taken lightly. He asked traditional leaders to make sure communities, particularly children and vulnerable people, are protected from hunger.

The President also advised farmers to store their maize in granaries rather than in sacks. Households are more likely to sell grain kept in sacks when they need money, he said.

The Government is already preparing programmes with traditional leaders and other partners to support vulnerable communities. It is also working with the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) to rehabilitate existing storage sheds in communities, a step Mr Hichilema said will cut the cost of moving maize from production areas to storage facilities and back to consuming centres.

He invited private individuals to invest in storage that the FRA can later rent.

“A 30×20 storage shed under the FRA specifications is only costing K1.8 million. You can invest back in your village. K1.8 million and FRA will rent your shed. But it will preserve the crop right at the local communities,” Mr Hichilema said.

The President urged Zambians to increase production and become producers rather than merely consumers. A hungry country cannot be a happy country, he said.

Farmers in Chief Choongo‘s area were encouraged to venture into wheat and soya beans, two crops the Government has marked for higher output under the Grow Zambia Agenda. Mr Hichilema said he has shown what wheat can do by cultivating 400 hectares in the area, with the crop sold to a customer at US$550 per tonne.

On water, he said the Government will allocate substantial resources to drought-prone areas to protect communities and support economic activity. Funds have already been allocated, and additional funding is expected in the 2027 national budget.

He asked Members of Parliament and other elected leaders to direct a large share of Constituency Development Fund resources to water harvesting.

Livestock was also on his list. Mr Hichilema called for stronger disease control to protect the country’s target of earning US$1 billion from livestock exports, and said the Government will support communities with additional dip tanks in areas targeted for increased livestock production.

On payments to farmers, he said the Government remains committed to making sure the FRA pays them. The agency has performed better this year than last year, he added.

Mr Hichilema urged Zambians to preserve their cultural heritage, noting that the Samu Lya Moomba site is historically important because it was used to mobilise resources during the struggle for independence.

Chief Choongo pledged to support the Government’s efforts to reduce the effects of El Niño. The chief congratulated the President on his re-election, thanked him for declaring the Samu Lya Moomba ceremonial site a national heritage site, and said the country was in safe hands.

Mr Hichilema, for his part, pledged to donate a pontoon to the chiefdom to improve connectivity and support community needs.

Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Gift Monde said the province is preparing to limit the effects of the expected weather on people, livestock and crops. He urged farmers not to sell their entire harvest and to make sure household food needs are adequately covered.

Mr Monde also asked traditional leaders and communities to safeguard food security and protect livestock from foot-and-mouth disease. He encouraged partnerships in sustainable forest management and carbon trading as an alternative source of income for communities.

Programmes for vulnerable communities are already being prepared, and additional funding for water provision in drought-prone areas is expected in the 2027 national budget.

World.title: Sympathy Abroad, Deafening Silence Home: Why Sishuwa Sishuwa is Not Getting Support from Zambian Academics
World.content:
Sympathy Abroad, Deafening Silence Home: Why Sishuwa Sishuwa is Not Getting Support from Zambian Academics

There have been several statements of solidarity with Sishuwa Sishuwa by foreign academics following the cancellation of his passport by the Zambian government. The most recent of these is a short statement by Jeremy Seeking claiming that the decision by the government is in response to Sishuwa’s trenchant criticism of HH and his government and, therefore, undermines Sishuwa’s academic freedom.

Surprisingly, however, there has been a deafening silence from the Zambian academia on Sishuwa’s predicament. There is no string of statements of solidarity. No outpouring of sympathy. No grieving over his fate. No defence of his academic freedom. Silence. What could be the reason for this dichotomy? I argue that the people who live in the context in which his “activism” has a bearing have a better understanding of Sishuwa’s “activism” and are better placed to judge his actions.

The local academics have a better understanding that Sishuwa had gone rogue and acted in a territory beyond academic freedom as many of his commentaries cannot be defended on the basis of academic freedom. He had crossed the line of academic integrity into the world of conspiracy and alternative reality, personalised attack, fake news, misinformation, disinformation and hate speech, and possibly cyber bullying and cyber harassment.

This is not to argue that the action by government to revoke is passport is justified. I don’t have sufficient information of the basis on which the government acted and would not like to make assumptions for or against.

Let us start with academic freedom and responsibilities of academics. Principle 1 of the Human Rights Council’s Principles for Implementing the Right to Academic Freedom (2024) defines academic freedom as “the human right to acquire, develop, transmit, apply, and engage with a diversity of knowledge and ideas through research, teaching, learning, and discourse.” Similarly, the Dar es Salaam Declaration on Academic Freedom and Social Responsibilities (1990) defines academic freedom as “the freedom of members of the academic community, individually or collectively, in the pursuit, development and transmission of knowledge, through research, study, discussion, documentation, production, creation, teaching, lecturing and writing.”

Academic freedom, like any other right, is not an open cheque to abuse others, to denigrate those with divergent views, to fabricate lies, spread misinformation, defame others and engage in conspiracy theories and belittle others. Academic freedom comes with responsibilities and academic ethics. As the Dar es Salaam Declaration noted, these include the need for academics to “perform their academic functions in accordance with ethical and highest scientific standards,” perform their role “without prejudice to the rights of others and the needs of our society,” and to engage in academics with “spirit of tolerance towards differing views and positions and enhance democratic debate and discussion.” Academic freedom is not unlimited. As Judge Oliver Wendell Holmes famously stated, “The right to swing my fist ends where the other man’s nose begins.”

Sishuwa’s social and political commentaries have not always respected the responsibilities that come with academic freedom. He often fabricates facts, demeans those with contrary views, makes wild and unsubstantiated claims and often makes claims that border on hate speech, purveys false/fake documents. He has often called academics who have exposed some of his falsehoods or hold different views from his as simply driven by their stomachs and not principle. He has made unsubstantiated claims and personalised attacks against some diplomats, such as the British High Commissioner and the UN Country Coordinator for simply holding views that do not align with his.

If reality does not fit into his political views, he manufactures his own set of facts and tries to fit reality into his manufactured facts using conspiracy theories. For example, in the lead to the 2026 election, Sishuwa came up with totally fake outline of what he called a government strategy for re-election, that the government planned to burn markets and then offer support to affected individuals as a campaign strategy (https://x.com/ssishuwa/status/1986112642763923764 ). In shock at such a baseless claim, for example, Tarcisius Mukuka, a respected senior retired academic posted: “I must have missed the memo in which Sishuwa Sishuwa mutated from government critic to conspiracy theorist evident in his tweeter feed.

Should he not provide evidence of UPND market burning campaign strategy.” Even where Sishuwa has the right like anyone to comment on public affairs, he had crossed the academic line of dispassionate and objective commentary and moved into the realm of toxic emotional, personalised venom and toxic vitriol. For example, when making his prediction for the 2026 election outcome, Sishuwa posted: “Hichilema will lose the election on 13 August. The only thing that can save him from defeat is pre-ballot death or industrial scale vote-rigging. Never again should Zambia elect a lying, tribal, corrupt, unpatriotic, vindictive, hypocritical, lawless, and undemocratic scumbag.”

By the time his passport was revoked, many media houses had long stopped entertaining or publishing his commentaries or giving him space to engage with the public as they were seen as not enlightening but deleterious. In his own post in June 2026, Sishuwa indicated that News Diggers, Radio Phoenix, Lusaka Times and the Mail and Guardian of South African had blacklisted him, but speculated that these media houses had colluded with the government to block him. No evidence of this collusion was furnished.

An impression should not be created that academic freedom is unlimited or that whatever proceeds from an academic, no matter how unethical or unprofessional, should be entertained as academic freedom. History is full of academics who crossed the line and committed atrocious crimes for which they were held accountable. For example, Bilijana Plavsic, a biology professor, was convicted by the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) based on her hate speech and propaganda that led to atrocities and killings of innocent people, while Augustin Ngirabatware, an economics professor and government official, was convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) for his propaganda that incited violence and genocide.

Given this context, it is not surprising that there is hardly any public discourse among local academics about the Sishuwa fate. Claims of a clamp down on academics do not resonate with what is on the ground in Zambia. It seems there is a nuance the foreign academics have missed, demonstrating their costly naivety and ignorance of the context. Sishuwa is not one thing and his academic life must be separated from his social or political commentaries where he often goes rogue and makes claims that are not driven by any evidence or are simply fake.

Sishuwa himself has personally acknowledged this. When asked why he was spreading fake or unsubstantiated news, Sishuwa responded in a post on X in September 2025: “There is a difference between Sishuwa the public intellectual or political commentator, and Sishuwa the scholar.

The former draws inspiration from the world of public debate, the latter from that of scholarship. The former can proudly take a partisan position in the service of a social cause, the latter almost always claims objectivity as an observer.” It is this dichotomy in Sishuwa that the international scholars have not appreciated as they are removed from the context and have given flesh to the ugly stereotype of a concubine who mourns louder than the bereaved wife.

By O’Brien Kaaba

World.title: Sisters of the Child Jesus celebrate 100 years of existence in Kasama
World.content:
Apostolic Nuncio to Zambia and Malawi, Gian Luca Perici, has described the 100 years of existence of the Sisters of the Child Jesus (SCJ), as a testimony of God’s faithfulness and unwavering dedication to serving humanity.

Most Reverend Perici says the congregation’s journey from a humble beginning a century ago to its current position is a story of courage, sacrifice and total trust in God.

The Vatican Ambassador to Zambia and Malawi said this during the centenary celebration of the Sisters of the Child Jesus at Chilubula Mission in Kasama yesterday.

“We are here to celebrate a great milestone. 100 years ago, this congregation began from a humble beginning. Throughout this period, the Lord has guided your journey which has not been easy,” Archbishop Perici said.

The Nuncio disclosed that despite numerous challenges over the decades, the Sisters have remained steadfast and have continued to be a visible sign of God’s love, especially to the most vulnerable people in society.

“Despite numerous challenges, you have continued to show God’s love,” he said.

The Nuncio, who is the Pope’s representative, paid special tribute to the founding members of the congregation, describing them as brave women whose vision and faith laid a strong foundation for the works being seen today.

“We thank God for the brave women who started this mission. We thank the women who have stood firm for this organisation. Your work in health and education is commendable, you have always remembered the poor, giving them comfort,” he said.

He added that the centenary celebration is not only a moment to look back at the past with gratitude, but also an opportunity to look at the present with joy and to the future with hope.

“As we celebrate the present, we see how God continues to bless your congregation. God has sustained you and He is still doing great things through you. I encourage you to stay united. Continue to live out your calling with love, serve the people with total dedication, do not be afraid of what lies ahead,” he said.

Meanwhile, Archbishop of Kasama Archdiocese, Ignatius Chama, called on members of the Sisters of the Child Jesus to continue supporting and appreciating one another as they fulfill God’s work.

Archbishop Chama urged the Sisters to rediscover their vocation of love and to remain true to their identity.

“To find your vocation of love, look, it is who you are,” Archbishop Chama said.

He said the Sisters should remain rooted in love, unity and service which defines their congregation.

Archbishop Chama also thanked the Apostolic Nuncio for accepting to celebrate the milestone with the Sisters of the Child Jesus.

The Sisters of the Child Jesus are a diocesan congregation founded in Chilubula, in the Archdiocese of Kasama in 1926 by Bishop Étienne Larue, a Missionary of Africa.

World.title: President Hichilema reiterates call to preserve culture
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has reaffirmed the government’s recognition of the importance of traditional ceremonies in preserving Zambia’s cultural heritage, national identity, unity and social cohesion.

President Hichilema said traditional ceremonies such as the Lukwakwa, provide an important platform for communities to preserve and showcase their culture and heritage.

He said this in a speech read on his behalf by Northwestern Province Permanent Secretary, Grandson Katambi at the 2026 Lukwakwa traditional ceremony of the Mbunda- people of Manyinga and Kabompo Districts.

President Hichilema said the government will continue supporting the hosting of traditional ceremonies and working with traditional leaders to preserve cultural heritage.

He said the government will also continue working with traditional leadership to accelerate development in their chiefdoms.

“Government has supported various developmental projects in the chiefdom, including the drilling of boreholes, construction of health facilities, classroom blocks and science laboratories, provision of desks and construction of a local court,” he said.

He explained the projects were aimed at improving service delivery to the people of Manyinga district.

He has since called on traditional leaders, Members of Parliament and Ward Development Committees to work together in identifying and planning developmental projects which should be financed through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

The Head of State has meanwhile cautioned Ward Development Committees against frustrating government’s development efforts, saying successful implementation of projects required cooperation among stakeholders.

President Hichilema said Ward Development Committees should be scrutinised and strengthened to ensure that projects are successfully implemented.

He said partnerships among traditional leaders, local authorities, government and communities were important in advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President has therefore appealed to traditional and local leaders to encourage young people to participate in skills training, particularly entrepreneurship programmes.

He said the responsibility of empowering young people required all stakeholders to come on board.

The Head of State has further encouraged young people to be proud of their identity, tribes and origins and advised them not to be ashamed of speaking their traditional languages.

And speaking at the same event, Lukwakwa Traditional Ceremony Organising Committee National Chairperson, Ndandula Livingi, has called for the protection and promotion of Mbunda cultural heritage.

Mr Livingi said culture should not be reduced to dancing but must instead encompass the broader values, traditions, language, history and practices of the Mbunda people.

He has since called on organisers and participants to reduce dances that were not part of Mbunda heritage in order to give prominence to authentic Mbunda cultural practices.

Mr Livingi also urged the people to support efforts aimed at transforming the Lukwakwa traditional ceremony into a major cultural and tourism event.

He said the ceremony had great potential to attract tourists and contribute to the promotion of the Mbunda culture.

“Lukwakwa is a big ceremony which, unfortunately, has been a sleeping lion, but eventually we will start seeing tourists coming to the ceremony,” Mr Livingi said.

He said the people belonging to the Mbunda tribe should take ownership of their culture and ensure that cultural materials and practices showcased during Lukwakwa reflected their heritage.

Mr Livingi said the transformation of the ceremony required collective support from traditional leaders, government, local communities and other stakeholders.

He further urged the people to embrace and promote the Mbunda culture so that it could be preserved for future generations.

The Lukwakwa traditional ceremony is an annual gathering of the Mbunda people of Manyinga and Kabompo districts aimed at showcasing and preserving their cultural heritage.

World.title: Heads of departments urged to prioritise Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Brian Sichande, has urged provincial heads of government departments under head 88 in Muchinga to plan and budget deliberately to support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Sichande noted that it is imperative for the Heads of Departments to identify practical interventions within their respective mandates that will enable them to contribute to national aspirations of the Grow Zambia production targets.

He further advised them to ensure that they also align the identified targets to National Development Plan and provincial priorities.

Mr Sichande said this when he addressed Heads of Department during the planning and budgeting meeting to prepare for the 2027-2029 medium term budget plan held in Chinsali district.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary disclosed that the Muchinga Province Administration Head 88 has been given an indicative budget ceiling of K124 million for the 2027 budget.

He added that with the constrained fiscal requirements given, the ceiling requires discipline in prioritisation in order to obtain maximum value from every Kwacha allocated.

Mr Sichande further said departmental submissions should prioritise statutory and legal obligations, realistic costing of tasks and operations, and provision for operational costs of key programmes.

World.title: ECZ trains DVEC, VEFs in Kanchibiya ahead of by-election
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has commenced training for the District Voter Education Committee (DVEC) and Voter Education Facilitators (VEFs) in Kanchibiya district ahead of a by-election in Lubaleshi Ward.

The by-election was caused by the death of United Party for National Development (UPND) aspiring Councilor for Lubaleshi Ward in the August 2026 general election, Evans Chileshe, who passed away immediately after filing his nominations.

The training workshop for DVEC and VEFs is being held at Kanchibiya Town Council’s new Civic Centre.

Kanchibiya District Electoral Officer, Julius Katuka, urged participants not to be complacent but proactive in their approach to voter education ahead of the by-election.

Mr. Katuka acknowledged that the district’s vast terrain often proves to be a challenge for Voter Education Facilitators hence the need for them to devise effective strategies for undertaking the voter education exercise.

“A lot of things happen in the field and we must strive to ensure we are professional as we carry out activities that will help facilitate the coming by-election,” Mr Katuka said.

He said every member of the committee has a part to play and must play it well.

Meanwhile, DVEC Coordinator, Chrispin Chishimba urged members to participate fully in the workshop so as to be well equipped for the coming by-election.

Mr Chishimba thanked members for attending the meeting promptly and urged them to demonstrate the same zeal towards the by-election that they have shown in previous electoral exercises.

And DVEC member, Ernest Kambindi, said the committee stands ready to carry out activities for the by-election.

Mr Kambindi said the by-election is of great importance to Kanchibiya district as Lubaleshi Ward is the district’s largest ward.

World.title: President Hichilema asks Zambians to unite to achieve Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called on Zambians to embrace unity, discipline and hard work to drive the newly unveiled Grow Zambia Agenda.

Speaking when he graced the Samu Lya Moomba Traditional Ceremony of Chief Choongo in Monze District, President Hichilema said the values demonstrated by freedom fighters and traditional leaders during the struggle for independence remained critical to Zambia’s development.

He said Zambians should emulate the spirit of unity and hard work as the country pursues economic development.

“Freedom fighters and traditional leaders of old demonstrated unity and hard work that earned the country its independence,” President Hichilema said.

And President Hichilema reaffirmed the government’s commitment to increasing power generation, saying a thermal power plant would be established in Chief Choongo and Chief Hamusonde’s chiefdoms as part of the target to generate 10,000 megawatts.

“We will continue investing in power generation, including establishing a thermal power plant in Chief Choongo and Chief Hamusonde’s chiefdoms as part of our 10,000 megawatt target,” he said.

President Hichilema also challenged traditional leaders to support the government’s one-billion dollar beef export target by promoting livestock disease control and increased production.

“We need our traditional leaders to support the one-billion-dollar beef export target by ensuring that livestock disease control is strengthened and production is increased through effective management of grazing areas,” President Hichilema said.

The President also called for the preservation of historical sites to ensure that young Zambians understand the country’s liberation struggle.

“We must preserve our historical sites like Samu Lya Moomba and many other sites across the country so that our young people can understand and appreciate the struggles that brought us our freedom,” he said.

The President further called for concerted efforts to curb bush burning in the plains and other parts of the country.

The President has meanwhile urged councils to prioritise water-related programmes in preparation for the projected 2026/2027 El Niño weather conditions to ensure communities continue accessing water during dry periods.

“Councils must prioritise water-related programmes so that our communities can continue accessing water during the dry periods that may arise from the anticipated El Niño conditions,” President Hichilema said.

And President Hichilema has assured farmers who supplied grain to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) that the government was making progress towards settling all outstanding payments.

“Government is making progress towards ensuring that all outstanding payments to farmers who supplied their crops to the FRA are settled,” President Hichilema said.

He also urged farmers to retain sufficient maize for household consumption and not to sell all their produce.

The President said the government was rehabilitating and constructing maize storage sheds, while encouraging cooperatives to invest in their own storage facilities, which could also generate income.

Meanwhile, Minister of Green Economy and Environment Gilbert Siame said the government was working to ensure communities likely to be affected by the projected El Niño conditions were adequately prepared.

And Acting Southern Province Permanent Secretary, Gift Monde, said the province was well prepared and had adequate information on the anticipated weather conditions.

“Government and stakeholders in the province are working to ensure that communities are adequately prepared to mitigate the possible effects of the weather phenomenon,” Mr Monde said.

The ceremony was also attended by 71 traditional leaders from across the country, government officials, 40 United Party for National Development (UPND) Members of Parliament and hundreds of people from the local community.
