World.title: Zimbabwe: Chivayo and Wife's Remains to Be Laid to Rest Without Heads Following Horror Helicopter Crash
World.content:
The bodies of controversial tycoon Wicknell Chivayo and his wife, Lucy Muteke, will be laid to rest this Thursday at Glen Forest Cemetery in Harare without their heads, a family spokesperson has said.

The couple died last Wednesday when the Bell 430 helicopter they were flying in crashed in the middle of Kudenga Farm in Marondera.

Chivayo and his wife were travelling from their rural home in Gandami, Chikomba East, when the crash happened.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The couple died along with three other people. On impact their bodies were shred into pieces and scattered across the fields. Fire also consumed some of the remains, making it even harder to identify and gather them. Their heads have still not been found.

Speaking to the media this afternoon, family spokesperson Hebert Chivayo said the burial is planned for Thursday at Glen Forest. Some body parts, including the skulls, are still missing.

"There has been speculation on social media saying that there were four head skulls that were found. That is not true. We did not find any head. There were some pieces of bones that were suspected to be head skulls but they were not. The last things that we found were Sir Wicknell's wristwatch and my daughter-in-law's watch," he said.

In many cultures, a person is buried whole so that the body is treated with dignity and the soul can rest. That comfort has been taken from them. The family has also said there will be no body viewing, so friends and relatives cannot even see the coffin open one last time.

The last memory will be the crash, not the person.

The family representative said the couple will be buried side-by-side, but not in one grave, contrary to some claims on social media.

"They will be buried side-by-side not in one grave. We cannot bury two people in one grave. We have never done that, we have never seen that," he added.

The family also refuted that Chivayo's funeral was a private event. They invited anyone who wishes to join them in mourning at the home of the late mogul in Gletwin Park, Harare.

"We have never had a private funeral in our family. Everyone is welcome to this funeral. Wicknell was a man for everyone both the poor and the rich. He was not selective. So stopping people from coming will be contrary to his values. Those who are free to join us at the burial at Glen Forest, you are welcome. Those who want to come and be with us at home you are also welcome," he said.

Chivayo was declared a provincial hero.

World.title: Sudan: 'Sudan's Children Face Recruitment, Sexual Violence, and Lasting Trauma' - Amnesty Researcher
World.content:
Amsterdam / El Fasher — Children in North Darfur have been recruited by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), subjected to sexual violence and left facing the effects of starvation and years without education, according to Amnesty International researcher Janine Morna.

Children in Sudan are not only being caught up in the violence of war but are also being deliberately targeted, according to researcher Janine Morna of international human rights advocacy organisation Amnesty International.

Janine Morna is an Amnesty International human-rights researcher specialising in children affected by armed conflict. Her current role is Thematics Researcher - Children, within Amnesty International's Crisis Response Programme. She has researched conflicts in Niger, north-east Syria, Ukraine, Haiti, and Sudan.

In an exclusive interview at Radio Dabanga studios in Amsterdam (scroll down for full transcript), Morna describes to Radio Dabanga's English Editor, Andrew Bergman how the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have recruited boys in North Darfur to fight, herd livestock used by the force, and gather intelligence about opposing forces.



She says the investigation found that recruitment happened in different ways. Groups allied with the RSF sometimes worked with community leaders and others to mobilise young people, including older boys and, in some cases, younger children, to fight alongside the force. In other cases, young men and older boys were abducted during attacks on villages and forced or compelled to fight.

Morna says one RSF leader whose unit numbered about 90 told researchers that around 40 per cent of its members were young people.

Girls have faced a different pattern of abuse, she says, with rape and other forms of sexual violence documented in the investigation. When young women were rounded up, there was not necessarily any consideration of whether they were under 18.

The youngest case describes by Morna involved a 13-year-old girl who was abducted and gang-raped repeatedly over several days.

"Children are caught up in the killing, bombardment and displacement, and suffer the same violations as adults," she says. "But they are also deliberately targeted for a range of other violations."

Starvation and the impact on young children

The investigation, which included interviews with 39 children, also examined the effects of the siege of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, where children struggled to find enough food.

Morna says children and babies were particularly vulnerable because they could not survive prolonged food shortages in the same way as adults. Researchers documented cases in which children were not eating regularly and found that four children had died because food was unavailable. She says the actual number was believed to be much higher.

The researchers also heard of babies who could not breastfeed and were surviving on mixtures of water and sugar.

Amnesty spoke to two malnutrition health experts to understand the consequences of going for a prolonged period without adequate nutrition. Morna says children who survive for months eating animal feed can still suffer devastating long-term effects.

Malnutrition can affect children's health, growth, and development, including those under five and older children. Its consequences can extend into the next generation, she says. If girls experience stunted growth, for example, their ability to carry children may be compromised.

Morna says the impact on children could be missed if an investigation relied only on adult survivors, satellite imagery, or video footage. Children's accounts helped researchers understand what life under siege meant from day to day, including the difficulty of finding food and the particular risks faced by babies and young children.

How researchers verified children's accounts

Morna says Amnesty approached interviews with children carefully, both to protect them from further harm and to test the reliability of the information gathered.

Researchers often spoke to older children first. With younger children, they might not have access to the referral services and psychosocial support needed when recounting traumatic experiences.

Morna says testimony from older children could be as credible as testimony from adults. As with any interviewee, researchers sought to verify what they heard by comparing accounts from different people and looking for corroborating evidence.

That could include digital material relating to an incident, interviews with family members and, where relevant, health documentation. In a case involving the rape of a child, for example, researchers might also speak to the child's mother about what she understood had happened.

"We don't rely on one person's testimony," Morna says, describing the process of cross-checking accounts. "We speak to multiple people and look for corroborating evidence."

Years without education and the risk of further violence

The effects of the conflict are not limited to immediate physical harm. Morna says none of the children Amnesty interviewed had had access to education for several years.

Many were keen to continue their studies and had ambitions for the future, but their education had effectively stopped in El Fasher when the conflict broke out in 2023. Displacement had prevented them from returning to learning in any meaningful way.

Morna warned that the loss of education could have long-term consequences for Sudan's ability to rebuild its professional workforce and economy.

She also highlighted the psychological effects of violence and displacement. Without support to address trauma, she says, there was a risk that cycles of violence could continue.

When researchers asked older boys how they imagined their futures, some saw a choice between continuing their education where they had been displaced and returning to seek revenge on those who had destroyed their families.

Morna says families were often dealing with several forms of trauma at once: relatives killed, fathers missing after detention and sisters who had been raped. When families reached a displacement site or a relatively safer place, access to services was often limited, and their basic needs were not always met.

That left few opportunities for children and adults to recover from what they had experienced.

Many children had spent much of their lives in displacement around El Fasher. Some had been born in camps and barely knew their villages or where their families came from. They had grown up without the safety and stability needed to develop and contribute to society.

Morna says Sudan would be dealing with the consequences for many years.

Evidence of coordinated abuses

The report also examined whether the violations documented in North Darfur were isolated acts by individual fighters or part of a wider campaign.

Morna says Amnesty had identified two commanders in the report. Interviews with people who had been detained helped researchers understand the degree of control exercised by senior figures, she says, because detainees had repeated contact with particular commanders and a clearer understanding of the RSF network operating in the area.

One commander named in the report was [Major General Gedo Hamdan Ahmed Mohamed (popularly known by his alias 'Abu Shouk']. Morna says researchers understood him to be responsible for much of the detention and oversight of detention in El Fasher.

She describes the wider campaign as "widespread, systematic, and coordinated", saying the pattern of violence was not made up of sporadic or one-off incidents. Researchers documented repeated cases of rape and sexual violence, killings, and detentions in particular towns, as well as the targeting of particular areas and ethnic groups.

Morna says the consistency of the patterns across locations and individuals suggested that the abuses could not be explained simply as the actions of a few rogue fighters.

"To me, that suggests a high degree of command responsibility," she says. Senior leaders, she added, needed to be investigated both for what they had done and for what they had failed to do to control their forces.

Amnesty calls for protection and accountability

Morna says the international community should take more concrete action to protect civilians and make it more costly for those waging war to continue in this way.

She called for greater scrutiny of the economic factors enabling the conflict, and says the United Arab Emirates had an important role in backing the RSF with resources, weapons, and other support. Cutting off some of those enablers, she argued, could change the course of the conflict.

Amnesty also believes an independent, neutral protection force is needed on the ground, particularly in areas where violence is concentrated and civilians are repeatedly displaced in search of safety.

Morna says the organisation was using the report to lobby for the international community to move towards authorising some form of protection presence. She describes this as a meaningful way to protect civilians.

Accountability was another priority. Morna pointed to commanders such as Abu Lulu, who she says had filmed themselves committing atrocities and appeared to act with impunity. She argued that investigative mechanisms examining abuses in Sudan needed adequate resources and funding, and that international cases brought against alleged perpetrators should be supported.

The aim, she says, should be to prevent the patterns of violence documented in North Darfur from being repeated elsewhere in Sudan, including in areas that have become new hotspots.

'A window of opportunity'

Despite the scale of the abuses, Morna says she was hopeful that international attention on Sudan was changing.

Since the launch of Amnesty's report City Under Siege, Children Under Fire, the organisation had been engaged in advocacy. Morna says the response from media, international audiences, stakeholders, and states suggested that the conversation about Sudan was different from what it had been a year or two earlier.

She describes the events in El Fasher as an important turning point in recognising the severity of the harm suffered by civilians.

"There is an international community here that cares about what is happening in Sudan," she says, adding that people were mobilising to try to act before the violence spread further.

Morna says the increased global attention created a "unique window and opportunity" to press for meaningful and bold action. She had seen civil servants and humanitarian workers making efforts to engage, she says, and added that Sudan would remain a priority for Amnesty International.

The long-term challenge, however, would extend well beyond the end of the fighting. Children who have endured sexual violence, hunger, displacement, and years without schooling will need sustained support if they are to recover and rebuild their lives.

For Morna, documenting what has happened is only one part of the response. Protecting civilians, supporting investigations, and ensuring that senior figures are held accountable are also essential if the abuses describes in the report are not to be repeated.

Transcript of interview:

Radio Dabanga: Janine Morna, welcome to Radio Dabanga. To introduce you to our listeners, Janine is an Amnesty International human rights researcher specialising in children affected by armed conflict. Her current role at Amnesty is thematic researcher on children within Amnesty International's Crisis Response Programme. She has researched conflicts in Niger, north-east Syria, Ukraine, Haiti, and Sudan.

Last night, 1 October 2026, you spoke to an audience at De Balie, the venue in Amsterdam, about your report, which you partly initiated and co-authored, called City Under Siege, Children Under Fire. I want to focus on children, because what is happening to them is difficult to get your head around. You initiated this investigation, and much of your work at Amnesty focuses on children affected by armed conflict. What did you discover in North Darfur that made you conclude that children were not simply victims caught up in the violence, but were in some cases being deliberately targeted?

Janine Morna: There are a couple of different violations specifically affecting children. I'm thinking in particular of the way boys are being targeted by the Rapid Support Forces to fight, herd livestock they use, and collect intelligence and information about potential opposing forces.

We found this happened in two main ways. Groups allied with the Rapid Support Forces would often work with community leaders and others to mobilise young people--older boys, and sometimes younger boys as well--to fight alongside the RSF. In other cases, when the RSF attacked a particular village, young men and older boys would be abducted and forced or compelled to fight.

We spoke to one RSF leader whose unit numbered about 90. He said that around 40 per cent of the unit was made up of young people. So, we're looking at a very young population of men, younger boys and older boys helping to wage this violent campaign.

Girls, in particular, are also being targeted for rape and sexual violence. When young women are rounded up, there is not necessarily any real consideration of their age or whether they are under 18. We documented a number of cases of rape and sexual violence. The youngest case, I think, involved a 13-year-old girl who was abducted and gang-raped repeatedly over several days.

Time and again, we see that children are caught up in the killing, bombardment, and displacement, and suffer the same violations as adults. But they are also deliberately targeted for a range of other violations.

Radio Dabanga: You interviewed 39 children as part of this investigation. What can children tell us about what happened in and around Darfur, and El Fasher specifically, that might otherwise be missed in an investigation based on adult survivors, satellite imagery, and videos? And how did you establish the credibility of their testimony while protecting them from further harm?

Janine Morna: That's a really important question. One reason we wanted to shed light on children, particularly in El Fasher, was the starvation that was happening at the time.

One important distinction is that when an adult is unable to secure food, they may be able to survive in a way that children--and babies in particular--cannot. We tried to flesh this out in the report, because when a city is under siege, it can be difficult to understand what that means on the ground, day to day.

We documented not only that children were not eating regularly, but also that four children had died because of the lack of available food. We believe the actual number was much higher.

We looked at babies who were unable to breastfeed and were consequently surviving on mixtures of water and sugar.

We spoke to two malnutrition health experts, I think, to understand the implications of going for a prolonged period without appropriate nutrition. Even if you survive several months eating animal feed, the long-term consequences can be devastating, particularly for children under five, but also for older children. Their health, growth and development can be affected, with consequences that can even pass from one generation to the next.

For example, if young women and girls experience stunted growth, their ability to carry children can be compromised, affecting the next generation as well.

It is really important for people to understand the disproportionate impact of the conflict. That can be difficult to capture if you speak only to adults or look at satellite imagery and other material.

As for the credibility of the testimony, we often speak to older children first, for a number of reasons. We want to work ethically, and when children are younger, we may not have the appropriate referral services and psychosocial support to help them as they relive the trauma of describing their experiences.

I find that the credibility of testimony from older children is almost the same as that of adults. We verify it in the same way: first, by triangulating information. If we document a particular attack, we don't rely on one person's testimony. We speak to multiple people and look for corroborating evidence.

In our case, that can include digital evidence relating to the incident. In some cases, we speak to family members. For example, if a child has been raped, we might also interview her mother, who can provide her account of what she understands her child to have experienced, and review any health documentation.

It is the same kind of triangulation that we would use for any interviewee.

Radio Dabanga: That's very clear. From our experience reporting for Radio Dabanga, and looking at the figures in your report, it seems this is only the tip of the iceberg: these are the cases you have managed to verify. The numbers are mind-blowing, almost difficult to take in.

What have you observed among the children in Sudan you have spoken to? They have seen a great deal for their age, but are they precocious, or do you see a lack of development?

Janine Morna: There are a couple of things I would note. None of the children we spoke to had had access to education for several years.

You're looking at really bright people with lots of aspirations. They want to engage and continue their education, which effectively stopped in El Fasher when the conflict broke out in 2023. They have not been able to continue it in any meaningful way while displaced.

That has devastating intergenerational effects when it comes to developing a professional workforce that can return, help Sudan grow and rebuild its economy.

Another major concern is that, unless the trauma and psychological pain caused by these experiences are addressed, cycles of violence will continue. When you speak to older boys about where they see their lives going, the choice can be: 'Either I continue my education here, or I go back and get revenge on the people who have devastated and destroyed our families.' That is why psychosocial support will be really important.

People are experiencing unprecedented levels of trauma. Within a single family, there may be multiple deaths, a father missing because he was detained, and sisters who have been raped. Any one of those incidents is hard to process, but people are experiencing all these traumas compounded.

When people reach a displacement site or somewhere relatively safer, they have very limited access to services. Some are not even in formal refugee camps, and their basic needs are not being met. The opportunities to heal, recover and process what has happened are already very limited.

It is also important to note that El Fasher is surrounded by major camps for internally displaced people. Many children were born in displacement. They have barely known their villages or where they came from, because they have lived with conflict for almost their entire lives.

These are people who have never experienced safety--the conditions people need in order to develop meaningfully and contribute to the economy. I think Sudan will be dealing with those long-term effects for many years to come.

Radio Dabanga: What you say about people growing up without an environment of safety holds true for anyone in Sudan under 40, simply because there have been civil wars, especially in Darfur, and now there is conflict across the country.

Amnesty says that some of the conduct documented in North Darfur amounts to crimes against humanity, and you mentioned that eight of the 11 crimes against humanity have been documented. What is the strongest evidence you have of a pattern of command responsibility, rather than simply individual acts of violence by fighters on the ground, as both sides say?

Janine Morna: In the report, we name two commanders. We have been able to identify the level of control some senior commanders exercise partly through interviews with people who have been detained. Those individuals have repeated exposure to particular commanders and a much better understanding of the RSF network involved in the conflict in this context.

One commander named in the report is quite senior and has been sanctioned by others: [Major General] Gedo Hamdan Ahmed Mohamed [popularly known by his alias/nom de guerre] 'Abu Shouk'. We understand him to be responsible for much of the detention and oversight of detention in El Fasher, which we identify as one of the major violations.

More broadly, if you look at the way this campaign of violence was waged, it was widespread, systematic, and coordinated. These were not sporadic events or one-off incidents; the patterns of violence were part and parcel of the way the Rapid Support Forces took over the area.

Close 

These were not isolated acts, and I think that speaks to a degree of coordination within the RSF. The patterns are too consistent across locations and individuals to be explained as one-off acts by 'bad actors' or 'bad apples'.

There are multiple instances of rape and sexual violence in particular towns, multiple killings, and multiple detentions. Particular areas and ethnic groups are targeted. You can't help but conclude that this comes from somewhere at the top, and that at a minimum these practices are accepted in the way the campaign of violence is being waged. To me, that suggests a high degree of command responsibility. Senior leaders need to be investigated for what they did, and what they failed to do, to control their forces.

Radio Dabanga: Amnesty says some of the conduct documented in North Darfur relates to genocide, as you said. Having documented what happened to civilians, particularly children in El Fasher, what do you believe the international community needs to do differently now to prevent these patterns of violence from being repeated elsewhere in Sudan? We mentioned, for instance, El Obeid, which is now the latest hotspot, and the violence moves. So, what does the international community need to do tangibly, rather than just talk from the podium of the Security Council? What can it do concretely to end this war?

Janine Morna: Well, certainly, from Amnesty International's perspective, there are a number of actions it should be taking. First, you need to make the cost of waging war in this manner much higher. I think that includes the international community being much more engaged and outspoken about the economic enablers of the conflict. The United Arab Emirates has a really important role in backing the Rapid Support Forces with resources, weapons, and other support. Cutting off some of those economic enablers could really change the tide of the conflict. I think that's really important.

There must also be much bolder action in terms of what is happening on the ground. We certainly believe that a protection presence is necessary to secure the safety of civilians, particularly in those hotspot areas. We saw time and again people being continually displaced, looking for a safe place to be and not being able to find one. To secure safe places, we need an independent, neutral protection force on the ground.

With this report, we are trying to lobby and advocate for the international community to move towards authorising some kind of protection presence. We believe it is the only really meaningful way to protect civilians. Then there is the need to pursue accountability. In El Fasher, you have commanders such as Abu Lulu filming themselves committing some of the worst atrocities on camera and acting with impunity. That gives you a sense of how much people perceive the international community cares about what is happening in Sudan.

Pursuing accountability is so important. We need to make sure the investigative mechanisms established to investigate what is happening in Sudan are well resourced and well-funded, and have the opportunity to document these violations meaningfully. International cases brought against some of these perpetrators must also be supported.

Radio Dabanga: That's very clear. Thank you very much. To conclude, what message do you want to send to the listeners of Radio Dabanga? The bulk of our listeners are in Sudan. Our shortwave broadcasts can also be received in Chad, in the displacement camps and in all the places where there is no internet or telephone communication. Very often, we are the only source of information for people. Do you have a message of hope to send out?

Janine Morna: Yes. The one thing I would say is that we have been doing a lot of advocacy since the launch of this report, and I am hopeful that the tide in Sudan is changing. If we look at the response from the media and international audiences that Amnesty International engages with, and even at stakeholders and states, the conversation about Sudan now is quite different from what might have happened a year or two ago.

El Fasher really feels like an important turning point, a real recognition of the severity of the harm people are suffering. I want to say that there is an international community that cares about what is happening in Sudan and is mobilised to try to do something before the violence continues to spread.

I think there is a unique window of opportunity to capitalise on increasing global attention on what is happening in Sudan and to motivate meaningful, bold action. I have seen many committed civil servants and humanitarian actors really trying to engage on this. Sudan will continue to be a priority country for Amnesty International. We want to see meaningful action by states, and we are mobilising our resources and remain committed to trying to make that happen.

Radio Dabanga: Thank you very much, Janine, for talking to Radio Dabanga. We wish you every success with your research. And keep the facts and figures flowing, because they are really important to us as well, as we report the news on the ground. We hope to speak to you again soon.

Janine Morna: Thank you. Thank you for having me.

World.title: Somalia: Somaliland Rejects Somalia's Claims Over Israel, Berbera
World.content:
Hargeisa, Somaliland — Somaliland has rejected claims by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud over its relations with Israel and the strategic port city of Berbera, saying Somalia has no authority over Somaliland's foreign relations.

The Somaliland Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that comments made by Mohamud during a recent interview with Al Jazeera were "misleading", reaffirming Somaliland's sovereignty and what it described as its continuity as an independent state.

"The Somalian Government has no authority to determine Somaliland's foreign relations or speak on behalf of its people," the ministry said.

The statement came after Mohamud discussed Somaliland's relations with Israel, Berbera and Ethiopia's access to the sea during the interview.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Somaliland said its diplomatic relations with Israel reflected the sovereign decisions of the two countries and were intended to advance cooperation, development and regional stability.

"Claims that Berbera would serve as a platform for aggression against other countries are unfounded and misrepresent Somaliland's commitment to peaceful relations," the ministry said.

It also rejected what it described as attempts by the Somalia president to speak on behalf of Somaliland's population.

The ministry said Somaliland attained independence on June 26, 1960, before Somalia became independent on July 1, and said the restoration of Somaliland's sovereignty on May 18, 1991 reaffirmed the continuity of its statehood.

"For more than three decades, Somaliland has built functioning institutions, held competitive elections, ensured peaceful transfers of power, and contributed to regional stability," the statement said.

The government also challenged Somalia's position on Ethiopia's efforts to secure access to the sea.

Somaliland said it had consistently supported negotiated arrangements allowing Ethiopia to obtain sea access through mutually beneficial cooperation. It accused Somalia of taking a contradictory position by opposing the memorandum of understanding signed between Somaliland and Ethiopia in January 2024.

"The Somalian Government's campaign against the 2024 Ethiopia-Somaliland Memorandum of Understanding directly contradicts its professed support for such access," the ministry said.

Somaliland and Israel established diplomatic relations after Israel formally recognised Somaliland in December 2025.

Close 

The ministry condemned what it described as threats of force and interference in Somaliland's internal affairs and called on Somalia's leadership to exercise restraint.

"Somaliland will continue to safeguard its sovereignty, pursue peaceful diplomacy, and strengthen partnerships that promote stability across the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea," it said.

(Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk)

World.title: Rwanda: Rwandan Genocide Hunter Dafroza Gauthier Dies After Long Battle for Justice
World.content:
Dafroza Gauthier, who spent spent decades tracking down Rwandans in France accused of involvement in the 1994 genocide, has died from cancer at the age of 72. By filing a string of civil lawsuits against suspected fugitives, she and her husband Alain pushed the French legal system to hold them to account.

Dafroza Gauthier died on Saturday in Reims, the French city where the couple had lived since the 1980s. She is survived by her husband and three children.

The Gauthiers were often compared in France to Serge and Beate Klarsfeld, the Nazi hunters who tracked down war criminals after the Holocaust.

They founded the Collective of Civil Plaintiffs for Rwanda (CPCR), an association that filed civil suits against dozens of genocide suspects in France. In several cases, these led to criminal trials under the principal of universal jurisdiction, which allows suspects residing in France to be tried for serious crimes regardless of where they were committed.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Seven have received a final conviction and prison sentences ranging from 14 years to life.

Witness to horror

Dafroza Mukarumongi was born on 4 August 1954 in Butare, in southern Rwanda, into a Tutsi farming family.

She experienced ethnic violence from a young age, seeing her family's house burned and property looted. In 1973, her mother sent both her daughters to Burundi for safety. From there, Dafroza moved to Belgium and studied chemistry.

She had met French-born Alain Gauthier while he was working as a teacher in Rwanda, and later visited him in France. The couple married in 1977.

In February 1994, Dafroza - by then a chemical engineer - returned to Rwanda to visit family. She saw militia on the streets of Kigali and heard Hutu extremists broadcasting hate speech against Tutsis.

Her mother pushed her to leave. "I still feel an indescribable sense of guilt for having left her behind," Dafroza Gauthier told Le Monde newspaper decades later.

On 8 April 1994, two days after Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane was shot down and the killings began, Dafroza's mother was shot dead in a Kigali church.

Back in France, "we were glued to the telephone all day", Dafroza Gauthier told the New York Times in 2014. "People would tell us, 'At X's home, they're all dead. They've been killed this morning.' It didn't mean anything anymore. I can't express it with words."

In total, she said, around 70 to 80 of her relatives died - her mother's entire family.

'Speaking helps us heal' says Rwandan survivor on genocide anniversary

A life's work

In 2001, the Gauthiers attended the trial in Belgium of four people accused of taking part in the genocide. All were convicted.

Later that year, they set up the CPCR. Their investigations unmasked several suspects living comfortably in France - including Dominique Ntawukuriryayo, who played in a role in the killing of as many of 25,000 Tutsi refugees and was subsequently convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

They secured their first criminal case in France in 2014, when former chief of intelligence Pascal Simbikangwa was tried in Paris for genocide and crimes against humanity. He was found guilty and sentenced to 25 years in prison.

Close 

France and Rwanda unite to honour genocide victims with Paris monument

Thinking about the 1994 atrocities "makes your head spin", Dafroza Gauthier told France Culture radio around the 30th anniversary of the killings. "But we can't just think - we have to act, do something about this slaughter."

She often said she was seeking not revenge, but justice.

"She was a remarkable person," Christophe Renzaho, president of the Rwandan Community in France expat group, told RFI. "The justice system has lost someone very important, a person who knew no bounds when it came to bringing those who committed genocide against the Tutsis to justice.

"It was her life's work and she carried it out until her very last breath."

World.title: Sudan: WFP Strongly Condemns Attack on Trucks in South Kordofan, Killing One Driver
World.content:
Abyei and Southern Kordofan are key areas in the dispute between north and south Sudan.

Khartoum — The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) strongly condemns an aerial attack that hit two contracted trucks carrying WFP food commodities in South Kordofan in the early hours of Saturday, 3 October 2026.

One driver was killed in the air strike. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends and colleagues.

The contracted trucks were en route from Dilling to Kadugli and clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles. Additional details regarding the circumstances of the incident, including the extent of the damage to the food cargo, are still being collected.

WFP calls for a prompt and impartial investigation into this incident and for those responsible for any violations to be held accountable.



This latest attack comes only one day after a WFP truck struck an explosive device in Dilling, South Kordofan, after delivering lifesaving food assistance.

WFP urges all those involved in the hostilities to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure the safe and unimpeded movement of humanitarian personnel and cargo.

These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need. WFP remains committed to safely delivering life-saving assistance to millions of women, men, and children who depend on humanitarian support across Sudan.

# # #

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

World.title: Dramatic footage shows alleged narco boat erupt in fireball during US military strike
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The U.S. military on Sunday announced a lethal strike on another vessel in the Caribbean carrying alleged narco-traffickers, killing four people on board.

The U.S. Southern Command said the vessel was traveling along "established narco-trafficking routes" in the Caribbean. The military shared a video that showed what appeared to be an explosion destroying a moving boat it described as a go-fast vessel.

"Under the direction of U.S. Southern Command, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean," the military said in a statement.

US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3

Southern Command claimed that intelligence revealed the vessel's "active involvement in narco-trafficking." The military did not provide evidence to back up this allegation.

"The operation killed four narco-terrorists," the statement added.

World.title: Shark bites fisherman twice during kayaking encounter along California beach
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A kayaker fishing off a Malibu beach was rushed to a local hospital Sunday morning after a shark encounter reportedly left him with two bite wounds.

The incident occurred near Paradise Cove in Los Angeles County, according to KTLA.

Witnesses told the outlet that the fisherman had reeled in what was believed to be a mako shark and was attempting to release it when the animal bit him, causing him to fall into the water.

The shark then bit him a second time before swimming away, according to reports. The Los Angeles County Fire Department initially described the incident as a shark attack but later characterized it as a "fishing accident," ABC 7 reported.

SWIMMER RUSHED TO HOSPITAL AFTER SUSPECTED SHARK ATTACK AT MARTHA’S VINEYARD

A manager at the nearby Paradise Cove Beach Cafe said he saw the victim's injuries near his legs.

"He was bitten in two places," the manager told KTLA. "I saw there were some teeth marks on his lower leg and above the knee."

AUSTRALIAN SURFER RISKED HIS LIFE TO SAVE FELLOW SURFER WHO HAD BEEN ATTACKED BY A SHARK

Video captured a lifeguard rushing toward the fisherman moments after the attack, while a small fishing boat floated nearby.

A fisherman reportedly rushed to the victim’s aid, pulled him from the water onto his boat, and brought the fisherman back to shore, KTLA said.

The victim reportedly called his girlfriend, a retired lifeguard, who helped him from the boat, assisted him onshore and called for emergency responders.

Los Angeles County Fire Department crews responded to the scene and took the victim to a local hospital, the outlet said.

Recalling the incident, the cafe manager reportedly said, "We’ve had a lot of crazy stuff happen here, but we’ve never had a shark attack like that."

The beach remained open following the incident, ABC 7 reported.

Chances of encountering a shark in Southern California are higher in October, when warmer coastal waters attract both prey and juvenile sharks. Female sharks often use shallow, warmer waters as nursery grounds, where young sharks can feed and grow with relative protection.

World.title: Mass shooting at Georgia block party leaves 2 dead, 35 injured
World.content:

A mass shooting at a neighborhood block party in South Georgia left two people dead and dozens wounded early Sunday morning, according to officials.

More than 1,000 people were gathered as more than 50 shots were fired in at least two locations about a block apart in Vienna, Georgia, according to Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy.

Deputies were on patrol at a neighborhood block party around 1:25 a.m. when shots were fired on the 900 block of Pine Street, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said in a statement. The sheriff's office had requested the assistance of the GBI.

Two people were pronounced dead at the scene from gunshot wounds. Most of the 35 injured victims suffered gunshot wounds, while several others were hit by cars or suffered other injuries as people fled the scene. The 35 injured victims were transported to hospitals for treatment.

LEXINGTON, KENTUCKY PARK SHOOTING KILLS 1, INJURES 4 DURING LIVE BAND PERFORMANCE

Peavy said people were "going every direction" and, even as officers were on the scene, more gunfire erupted about a block away.

"We don’t know if it’s coming at us or someone else," he said at a press conference on Sunday. "You just have to keep doing what you’re doing and hope you don’t get hit by gunfire."

The GBI said the ages of the injured victims range from 14 to 51 and their conditions range from stable to critical.

The victims killed in the shooting were identified as Jaquevion Jackson, 21, of Cordele, and Macaleb Jackson, 23, of Hawkinsville, the agency said.

The incident happened over homecoming weekend for Dooly County High School.

SHOOTING NEAR BALTIMORE YOUTH FOOTBALL EVENT LEAVES 12-YEAR-OLD GIRL DEAD, 3 ADULTS WOUNDED

The superintendent of the Dooly County School System, Sherrod Willaford, said the shooting was not at a school-sponsored event.

"We recognize that its impact may reach many of our students, families, and staff," he said in a statement.

Schools will open on Monday but additional safety measures have been implemented.

Vienna Mayor Eddie Daniels said the city had not issued any kind of permit for the block party and he did not know if it was a homecoming party.

Authorities have not arrested any suspects, identified a potential motive or said how many shooters may have been involved.

"Please turn yourself in, because we're doing everything we can to find out who you are," Peavy said.

The incident remains under investigation.

Vienna is about 130 miles south of Atlanta and about a 50-mile drive south on the Interstate 75 corridor from Macon, where 12 teenagers were wounded by gunfire during a confrontation at a birthday party last week at a city park.

World.title: Attorney for accused Cornell student calls on Letitia James to step aside over prior comments
World.content:

New York Attorney General Letitia James is facing a call to step aside from the investigation into the alleged Cornell sexual assault after an attorney for one of the accused students questioned whether she had publicly accepted the allegations before taking over the case.

Andrew Miltenberg, who represents one of seven former fraternity members accused in a civil lawsuit, said James’ earlier statements supporting the accuser created an "avoidable question about the appearance of impartiality."

"The concern is whether the public can have confidence that the investigation begins without any predetermined view of the facts," Miltenberg said in a statement to Fox News.

AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS

Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the attorney general’s office as special prosecutor Thursday, replacing Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten in the investigation into an alleged October 2024 sexual assault at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house.

The woman, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, alleges seven former fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.

DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’

Miltenberg’s objection centers on comments James made before her office was appointed to lead the criminal investigation. She publicly described what the woman had "been forced to endure" as "horrific and unacceptable" and told her, together with "all survivors," that "we stand with you."

When asked at Friday’s news conference about her objectivity in light of the Facebook post, James said, "I will not comment on a Facebook post."

Criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno also questioned James’ role during an appearance on Fox News’ "The Big Weekend Show."

"But it should be fair. It should be impartial. And it should not be from someone who’s already made a public statement on Facebook about it," Rotunno said of reopening the investigation.

James has said the investigation will be guided by "the facts and the law."

Miltenberg said his concerns were not political and did not diminish the seriousness of sexual assault allegations.

TRUMP LAWYERS TARGET WHAT LETITIA JAMES WON’T SAY ABOUT EVIDENCE IN $450M CASE

"There is nothing improper about expressing compassion for someone who reports a sexual assault," he said. "But there is an important difference between supporting a person who makes an allegation and appearing to accept the factual premise of that allegation before conducting an investigation."

He urged James to personally recuse herself while allowing senior prosecutors in her office who have not publicly commented on the merits of the allegations to handle the investigation.

"That would not weaken the investigation. It would strengthen it," Miltenberg said.

He argued that the same concerns about independence and public confidence that prompted the appointment of a special prosecutor should apply to the person leading the replacement investigation.

LETITIA JAMES’ RE-ELECTION CUSHION SHRINKS AS LITTLE-KNOWN CHALLENGER STARTS TURNING HEADS

"I am not suggesting that Attorney General James does not believe she can be fair," he said.

The case drew renewed scrutiny after Doe filed a civil lawsuit Sept. 16, nearly two years after the alleged assault. The complaint also names Cornell, fraternity entities, Doe’s sorority and a local bar, among others, alleging failures to protect her.

BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE HANDS LETITIA JAMES SETBACK IN LATEST TRUMP LEGAL CLASH

Van Houten initially declined to pursue criminal charges, saying the signed statement his office received from Cornell University Police did not establish a crime under New York law. He said prosecutors assumed Doe’s account was true and that her credibility was "never in question."

He later reopened the investigation after the lawsuit surfaced.

CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS

Questions about the original investigation intensified when CBS News presented Van Houten with a fuller transcript of Doe’s police interviews that he said his office had never received.

"That wasn’t information that I had," Van Houten said, adding that its existence "changes the landscape for me."

Rotunno also questioned why prosecutors had not sought the complete investigative record before deciding against charges.

"The real question is, why didn’t the DA ask for every piece of information that the campus police gathered?" she said on "The Big Weekend Show."

She warned against allowing public reaction to drive the case.

"We are watching the court of public opinion take over here when we don’t know the facts," Rotunno said.

Cornell has separately agreed to an independent review of its handling of the allegations. University President Michael Kotlikoff said its disciplinary process resulted in two expulsions and two suspensions of at least two semesters. One student graduated before discipline could be imposed, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct.

Those proceedings are separate from the criminal investigation.

Cornell previously told Fox News it "fully support[s] the appointment of a special prosecutor" and is committed to "an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case."

Miltenberg said any decision about criminal charges should come from prosecutors whose impartiality the public can trust.

"The simplest way to remove that question is for her personally to recuse herself and allow an uncommitted prosecutor within her office to lead the investigation," he said.

Fox News' Michelle Langer and Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.

World.title: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas
World.content:
Pushing back

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo woke before dawn on a hot Houston morning on July 7, as he did most days. He had lived in the U.S. for decades without legal status but was in the process of getting a work permit. He had no criminal record.

He picked up workers in his white van and was driving to a jobsite when he was pursued by immigration agents in unmarked vehicles. An officer shot him, according to authorities, after they say he used his vehicle to ram them. It’s a story contradicted by witnesses in the van, but it’s one immigration authorities have told before in explaining how a traffic pursuit turned deadly.

This time, though, the family wasn’t having it. Salgado Araujo’s eldest son stood before cameras and delivered an emotional testimonial to his father that went viral.

“He was a hardworking family man who never wanted his name to be known by anyone outside of his family,” Ronaldo Salgado said at a news conference days after his father’s shooting, as his brother held up a photo of their father.

Ronaldo Salgado stressed that the story of his dad ramming government vehicles could not be true. Their father had always taught his kids that if law enforcement attempted to pull them over, they were to pull off the road, hand over their license and registration and act respectfully.

In the end, authorities admitted Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation.

In an interview with NBC News, Ronaldo Salgado said as immigration arrests became more prevalent in 2025, they talked to their father about the procedure if he had an encounter, including calling his family, and that they’d contact their attorneys.

“Just remember, don’t sign anything. Call us,” Ronaldo Salgado said he told his father.

Sitting at Las Perras Cafe in Houston, where a makeshift altar to his father sits in the corner, Ronaldo Salgado recited the names of those who had been killed by immigration officers, including Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Ruben Ray Martinez, saying the country is not now safe because of their deaths.

“These are lives that are lost, and they need to be investigated, just like any other life lost. It needs to be investigated with the full cooperation of the agents involved and the agencies involved,” the son said.

Ronaldo Salgado at a makeshift altar to his father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, at Las Perras Cafe in Houston. Natasha Korecki / NBC News

“All of this isn’t making us any safer. How is going after my dad going to work making the city safer?” Ronaldo Salgado said. “Criminals don’t wake up at 5 in the morning to pick up their crew and go to do a day of backbreaking labor. You don’t.”

In an unusual move, federal officials made public an FBI search warrant to get inside Salgado Araujo’s van after his death. Then, federal officials released a stinging detail: The bureau sought entry to look at baggies with crystals that they said resembled meth.

When he heard that, Ronaldo Salgado said he couldn’t help but break into a little smile: “Ohhh, they messed up.”

He knew what it was. And it would only make things worse for federal authorities. It was a homemade electrolyte mixture, mainly of salt, that his father later mixed into Gatorade for himself and workers to combat the triple-digit Houston summer heat outside.

The U.S. attorney’s office later confirmed that the mix was in fact not methamphetamine, surprising few who knew Salgado Araujo.

Ronaldo Salgado felt it was an effort to sully his father’s reputation and dampen public outrage.

The implication just added to community anger, viewed as a thinly veiled attempt at smearing the man immigration authorities killed.

“It really shook the community,” said Jasmine Khadem González, an immigrant rights organizer with the Houston Democratic Socialists of America. “A lot of us who are Latino, we have somebody in our family: If it’s not our father then it’s our uncle who has a very similar job. … To see somebody like that be targeted for just being on his way to work or for the color of his skin or for the kind of truck that he’s driving — because it’s associated with Latino men — to see somebody like that be targeted for doing a very everyday thing. For just existing.”

In the NBC News/Telemundo poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Amy Zachmeyer, the executive director of New Economy for Working Houston, a group that helped organize community vigils and demanded accountability and transparency in the probe, said the Salgado family’s high-profile pushback kept authorities in check.

“They’ve shown incredible strength to be able to really defend their father,” she said.

Zachmeyer grew emotional as she spoke about the sons. “They never let a narrative set in that he was anything but a loving father, a Houstonian, a Texan, a hard worker.”

Anger reshapes local politics

Adrian Garcia, a Harris County commissioner, said Latinos are “feeling a lot of attack and disrespect.” Over the last year, he’s worked to reach out to those who don’t vote often. From his view, people now are willing to walk across broken glass to send a message to the Trump administration.

“The low-propensity voters that I’ve been speaking to absolutely have a great intensity to vote in this election, and they specifically speak to ICE enforcement. A lot of young kids: ‘I’m voting for my mom. I’m voting for my dad.’ I hear that a lot,” Garcia said.

More Latino registered voters than ever — 72% — rated their interest in the upcoming election as 10 out of 10 in the NBC News/Telemundo poll.

Garcia described the greater impact that fear of immigration enforcement has had across the Texas economy.

“This is not what our community deserves, and it is also what is impacting the things that we care about the most, the business, the economy. They’re hurting the industry,” he said. “They’re hurting those who work hard and play by the rules.”

Jareli Barrera, who works as a server at the popular Cielito Cafe in Houston, said she has never been so tuned into an election. Today, she said she’s helping others, including co-workers, to register to vote.

She cannot stand seeing the level of fear in her community, including among those who are citizens but fear being separated from family or an aggressive encounter.

“Republicans are probably going to lose. It’s not going to be the greatest thing for them at the end of the day,” Barrera said. “Most of these immigrants are the ones that are making the U.S. successful. They’re doing the hard work. … If everyone’s deported, who’s gonna do the hard labor? Who’s gonna construct? Who’s going to do all this cleaning that they don’t want to do?”

Since 2025, local activist groups have tried to work with the city of Houston to better protect Latinos as they watched intense enforcement operations in cities like Minneapolis, Los Angeles and Chicago upend life for residents and lead to encounters with immigration authorities that turned violent or deadly.

Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, a Houston-based senior policy attorney and strategist with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said Salgado Araujo’s death was a “culmination of years of Texas entrenching itself, entangling itself with ICE” and “illustrated to them the fear, the levels of persecution of justice that immigrant communities have been living with in Texas for a very long time.”

Before Salgado Araujo’s death, Canales-Pelaez was among those who worked to deter cooperation between Houston police and federal police agencies and pushed for greater transparency into immigration operations. Abbott, the three-term governor and a staunch Trump ally who is up for re-election in November, threatened to block $200 million in grants to Houston and other major cities if they didn’t change local rules that directed police forces not to hold individuals they encounter for longer time periods to assist ICE. The cities, including Houston, reworded their ordinances.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a centrist Democrat, told The New York Times last October that he kept his head down as other city and state leaders in the country grew combative with the White House over immigration operations. Whitmire said his city had avoided “turmoil” that others faced.

Whitmire initially declared his hands were tied after the shooting; the Houston Police Department had no jurisdiction to conduct an independent investigation. After community uproar, the city changed course. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare has now launched a probe, with the county government approving the $2.5 million request to fund it.

“It ignited this flame and really showed other people that aren’t necessarily living this experience or working in this line of work, ‘Oh, this got to us,’” Canales-Pelaez said. “When the mayor told us that we weren’t going to be another Minneapolis, we weren’t going to be a Los Angeles, well, now we are. Someone’s dead. That really has sparked this rage, this collective, righteous anger.”

World.title: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
World.content:
There are clear signs his party is paying the price.

A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.

Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%.

That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election.

Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference.

The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country.

The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections.

Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.”

“What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.”

But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012.

“Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said.

Trump struggles

Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling.

His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy.

Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference.

Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it.

Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue.

Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters.

A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024.

Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues.

“It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.”

“I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added.

Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family.

While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies.

Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough.

While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S.

Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans.

“There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added.

In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.

Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics.

She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.”

“They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added.

Midterms fallout

The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

“In a lot of the heavily Hispanic and Latino districts across the country that Trump and Republicans did well, and better than ever in, in 2024, you’re going to see that reversal,” said Roberts, the Republican pollster, noting Trump’s tough numbers on immigration and the cost of living.

“This entire poll is full of very clear directional signals that Latinos have turned from 2024 and are ready to make a different choice with regard to who’s in control of Congress,” Roberts said.

Democrats’ 24-point lead on the generic congressional ballot is twice as large as their margin in the 2024 version of the poll. But it’s not nearly as wide as the 43-point lead the party enjoyed at this point in the 2018 midterms.

Latino voters also now say Democrats would better handle the cost of living and the economy by significant margins, erasing the advantages Trump and Republicans have enjoyed in past elections.

Latino voters favor Democrats to handle other issues, and they break even on which party would better handle border security. More voters also say Democrats are more likely than Republicans to share their values and address the concerns of the Hispanic community.

Amid the economic frustrations, voters are also more motivated to head to the polls in November. A sizable majority (72%) rank themselves a 10 out of 10 in terms of interest in November’s elections, compared with 54% at this time in 2024. Meanwhile, 62% say they are more motivated to vote this year than in midterms past.

And a majority (54%) say their midterm vote is meant to send a signal of opposition to Trump, while 21% say they want to signal their support for Trump and 23% say their vote is not about sending a signal to the president either way.

While the poll results offer plenty of short-term upside for Democrats, they also outline longer-term changes trending against the party.

While Latino voters’ negative views of the GOP have jumped since 2024, views of the Democratic Party have not improved. Now, 62% of Latino voters have negative views of the Republican Party, a 16-point increase from two years ago, while 42% have a negative view of the Democratic Party, a 4-point increase from 2024.

“I’m still wary about the Democratic Party because I don’t really know that much other than what I was fed,” said Maria, the Florida voter in her 20s, before adding that she’s still leaning toward voting for Democrats: “I feel like I have to put my faith in them now to fix things.”

She said she voted for Trump in 2024 in large part because her family instilled a fear of socialism and Democrats in her.

The poll found that socialism remains underwater with Latino voters — 13% feel positively about it and 41% view socialism negatively, with 38% feeling neutral about socialism.

Cardona-Arroyo, the Democratic pollster, noted that the party has work to do after the midterms to develop a broader message.

“What do Democrats do to move beyond this place where they’re running on opposition to the Republican Party, which I think will work in ’26?” Cardona-Arroyo said. “It’s sort of an open question of whether that will work in ’28.”

The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters Sept. 21-28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20% of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

World.title: U.S. bombers scrambled out of U.K. airbase after threats
World.content: The Pentagon is withdrawing all of its B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the U.K. The move, categorized by two officials as quick or rushed, comes just days after five men were arrested for a suspected terror plot involving vans containing explosives parked near the perimeter of the base.
