World.title: Who’s the best team in the NFC East? Through four weeks, it’s anyone’s guess
World.content:
Nearly one-quarter of the way through the NFL regular season, a hierarchy of contenders and pretenders is beginning to become defined in some divisions.

Just not in the NFC East.

A rash of down-to-the-wire results Sunday has left the division as up for grabs as any in the league, with no clear favorite to run away with the division title and the playoff spot that comes with it.

The New York Giants are 3-1 (1-0 in division play), but how long can their backup quarterbacks keep up a winning streak?

The Philadelphia Eagles are 2-2 and 1-0 in the division but have been outscored by 18 points overall, and neither star running back Saquon Barkley nor quarterback Jalen Hurts has done much to quiet offseason concern about their offense.

The Dallas Cowboys are 2-2, including 1-1 in the division, and remain one of the league’s biggest threats to score — just as their defense is still one of the least trustworthy to get stops. Only the Washington Commanders (1-3, 0-2) look like a nonfactor one month in after a lopsided 30-13 loss Sunday in London to Indianapolis.

Parity has historically been the norm in the NFC East, which had different teams win the division every year from 2003-04 to 2024-25. Not much separates them this fall, either. The Cowboys (plus 10) have the best scoring differential among the group, but the Giants (plus 3), the Eagles (minus 18) and the Commanders (minus 34) aren’t far behind.

The Giants’ playoff hopes appeared damaged two weeks ago after starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the season, leaving the team in the hands of the turnover-prone backup Jameis Winston.

And yet, the Giants have won two straight games to improve to 3-1. Sunday’s latest win, 36-24 against Arizona, was sealed only when defensive back Deonte Banks returned an interception 98 yards for a touchdown in the final seconds. It followed a nail-biting, 12-7 win last week against Tennessee that showed the limits of Winston, only for the 32-year-old former No. 1 overall pick to throw three touchdown passes against the Cardinals. The Giants also were the beneficiaries of three interceptions to win their first three home games of the season for the first time since 2008.

How sustainable is this? In addition to Dart’s season-ending injury, the Giants are without outside linebacker Brian Burns for the year, as well. It also was the first time since 2021-22 that Winston had won back-to-back games as a starter.

“We’re in a good position four games in, but it’s only four games in,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said. “We can play so much better.”

As that game was ending, so were two others that kept the division in flux.

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts during the second quarter against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday. Emilee Chinn / Getty

In Philadelphia, the Eagles had an opportunity to boost their uneven early-season results with a win against the prohibitive preseason favorite to win the Super Bowl, the Los Angeles Rams. Leading 20-10 with 7:31 to play in the fourth quarter, the Eagles were 2 yards from the Rams’ end zone when coach Nick Sirianni opted against kicking a short field goal to try for what might have been a game-sealing touchdown.

When Hurts’ pass fell incomplete, though, the Rams answered with a 98-yard scoring drive, then added a second touchdown less than three minutes later to win, 24-20. If the game’s outcome shifted in the final minutes, there were warnings all afternoon for the Eagles, who were 0-for-12 on third down, the worst performance in franchise history.

“I know when we’re 0-for whatever we were today, everybody has a hand in that,” Sirianni said.

He called the fourth-down decision his own fault.

“We have to look at ourselves in the mirror,” Sirianni said. “We have to be accountable. I’ve got to do a better job. All of us have things to improve on.”

Barkley also continues to look little like the player who rushed for 2,000 yards in Philadelphia’s Super Bowl-winning season two years ago. He entered Sunday with 174 yards in three games. After two rushes for just 8 yards, Barkley left the game with an injury — ominously, making him the 10th Eagles starter to be hurt this season.

Dallas Cowboys receiver Ceedee Lamb celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Houston Texans on Sunday. Alex Slitz / Getty

In the same 10-minute span in which Philadelphia saw a victory slip out of its grip while the Giants secured their own in the final minutes of the fourth quarter, Dallas had its own late drama to avoid a 1-3 start that would have been its worst through four games since 2020.

Trailing 30-26 with a little more than two minutes left, the Cowboys produced an 11-play drive that traveled 74 yards for the go-ahead score to beat Houston, 34-30. Dak Prescott’s game-winning touchdown pass went to CeeDee Lamb with 40 seconds left — because who else could it have been? Against a Houston defense that was one of the NFL’s best last season, Lamb was unstoppable, catching a career-high 17 passes for 189 yards. (Lamb came into Week 4 with 20 catches all season.)

Lamb joined Brandon Marshall (2009) and Terrell Owens (2000) as the only players since 2000 with at least 17 catches, 180 receiving yards and a touchdown.

The win could be seen as a response to earlier, dispiriting results. Last week, the Cowboys lost on a last-second field goal to Baltimore thanks to questionable decisions by coach Brian Schottenheimer, calls that he acknowledged to the team were his fault, according to a report. It wasn’t entirely on the offense, however. The Cowboys’ defense entered Sunday allowing opponents to convert 58.8% of third downs, the NFL’s worst mark. The Texans managed just 3-for-10.

“I just want Schotty to know that I got his back,” Lamb told reporters Sunday. “I’m with him. I’m one of his strongest soldiers. It’s just going to battle with each other.”

World.title: NFL reviewing referee’s interaction with Arizona Cardinals player during game
World.content:
The NFL said Sunday that it is reviewing an interaction between an official and Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.

During the Cardinals’ loss at the New York Giants, McBride was coming off the field during the fourth quarter when a sideline camera showed line judge Jeff Seeman appearing to use profanity to McBride.

An NFL spokesman told NBC News the league was reviewing the matter.

“This kind of behavior from an official towards a player is unacceptable,” JC Tretter, the executive director of the NFL Players Association, wrote on X. “Players are consistently held accountable when the roles are reversed. We expect the NFL to hold officials to the same standard.”

Seeman has been an NFL official since 2002.

An NFL spokesperson did not reply to a request for comment about whether the league has specific rules governing officials’ conduct toward players. Under league rules, it is considered unsportsmanlike conduct if players use “abusive, threatening, or insulting language or gestures to opponents, teammates, officials, or representatives of the League.”

World.title: Brazil presidential election heads to runoff after no majority vote
World.content:
Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, and Brazil's veteran President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff on Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America's powerhouse economy.

The country's electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the more than 50% of the total vote needed for an outright win.

Brazil's electoral court in Brasilia had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula's 53.7 million, with 99.8% of the vote reported.

Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house.

"Brazil wants change, that's the reading of what happened today," Bolsonaro said. "It's the end of the Workers' Party era," he added, in a reference to Lula's party.

Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was "unexpected" as he had thought he could win in the first round.

"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," Lula said. "I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan."

Trump allies have fared well in recent elections in Latin America, including in Argentina, Colombia, Honduras and Peru. Lula has accused the U.S. administration of trying to sway his country's election to Bolsonaro by imposing tariffs, revoking the visa of the country's ambassador to Washington, and imposing sanctions on government officials and one Supreme Court justice.

The Trump administration did not respond to a request for comment on whether it is seeking to interfere in the vote.

The next presidential term begins on Jan. 5, 2027. The winner will be in charge of Latin America's biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China.

Lula faces a tough battle

Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who found moderate support in Sunday's election, have previously said they will not endorse either bidder in the runoff.

With another 21 days of campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival's many legal woes.

While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians' lives.

But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.

Sen. Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals.

He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.

"Brazil needs change. Brazil can't stand so much suffering," he told reporters at the Rio de Janeiro voting center, where he cast his vote Sunday.

Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil's population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula's Workers Party, according to multiple polls.

Four years ago, Lula beat the then-incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.

Voters choose between incumbent or return to right

"I'm feeling calm but very sad with the result," said Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro who watched the count with friends at a bar. "I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win."

Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro's eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father's footsteps.

"I voted for his father, and I don't regret it," she said.

The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father's presidency, "people felt more at ease to discriminate," she said.

"I'm an LGBTQ+ woman, I can't think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected," she added.

Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula's social policies that help the "less fortunate" and how he stands up to Mr. Trump.

"That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there," she said at a voting center in Brasilia. "He won't succeed if Lula wins."

Confidence in Brazil's electronic voting system

No significant fraud has ever been detected since Brazil adopted its electronic voting system in the 1990s.

The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission reported Sunday that "the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions." Electoral authorities have assured that electronic votes are secure and verifiable.

"We are almost three hours away from the end of the voting and everything is proceeding normally and with the greatest possible transparency," the president of the Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said Sunday afternoon, adding that there was "no concrete indication of international interference."

Voters appeared largely confident that the country's voting system can't be tampered with.

Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, said that the rapid availability of results helped combat fraud and uncertainty.

"When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there's been a problem," he said.

World.title: Experts are training AI on how to do their jobs
World.content:
Music producer Robbie Hiser is confident there will always be a place for creatives like him even though he taught artificial intelligence some of the tricks of his trade.

Hiser trained AI for Mercor, a company that works to make AI models like ChatGPT or Claude better in a wide variety of subjects from finance to poetry. The multibillion-dollar company has assembled more than 100,000 freelancers in a wide range of industries, available to teach AI what they know about their fields.

But Hiser and other trainers said they don't believe they're training themselves out of a job. Hiser thinks creative work like great songwriting, for example, will always require a human touch.

"AI doesn't have any life experience to pull from," he said. "An AI never had a girlfriend break up with it."

Still, nearly three-fourths of Americans now fear AI is coming for our jobs, according to a Pew Research study. And a September report from McKinsey Global Institute found AI could force 11 million U.S. workers into new careers by 2035.

Robbie Hiser. CBS News

A natural evolution?

Mercor CEO Brendan Foody sees the changes prompted by AI as a natural evolution. He believes with the use of AI, people will be freed from the dull, repetitive parts of their job, leaving them with more time to do other more meaningful and engaging work.

The evolution is happening across the country. Columbus, Ohio, law firm Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease, for instance, worked with Stanford University's Liftlab to build AI personas trained on the experience and philosophy of some of its senior lawyers. These AI personas can offer feedback from the unique perspective of individual Vorys partners on documents, trial lawyer and partner Kim Herlihy said.

"AI is never going to walk into the courtroom and give an opening statement to the jury," she said. "But it helps us have additional tools to use as we prepare that opening statement."

Kim Herlihy. CBS News

The AI may have Herlihy's expertise, but she said it's designed for optimization, not replacement.

"AI cannot take the place of what's a fundamentally human business," she said. "You call your lawyer because you want to look in their eye and say, 'What should I do about this issue?'"

AI training is currently America's fourth-fastest-growing job category on LinkedIn. At the moment, the gig work training AI at Mercor can pay $20 or even $200 an hour. To Foody, it's the career of the future.

What a top economist says

Foody's sunny picture is at odds with what Nobel Prize-winning economist Daron Acemoglu fears could be coming for American workers. On its current trajectory, many areas are set to become more automated, leading to worker displacement.

"What we are living through with AI is unprecedented," said Acemoglu. "The first phase of the Industrial Revolution took 80 years. Today it's taking place in one or two years and it's taking place across many different sectors at the same time."

In a worst-case scenario, unemployment could triple in the next decade, if nothing is done and the U.S. continues on its current course, Acemoglu said.

And while Acemoglu acknowledged there will be employment for people training AI, he said, "The number of people they're employing in these positions is small relative to the number of people who will be replaced."

"I mean, that's the whole point of automation," Acemoglu said.

Who will be impacted as AI advances?

While unemployment is generally steady at the moment, research from Stanford shows hiring is down for young people in the most AI-exposed jobs — like software developers. Research from the U.S. Census, found hiring and wages among recent college grads in AI-exposed majors have declined due to AI.

Clara Shih, who oversaw major AI divisions at Salesforce and then Meta, said at her workplace there used to be dozens of people involved in conceiving a product, creating a prototype and ultimately delivering it to customers. Now, she said, the same task can be done with just a few people using AI agents.

Clara Shih. CBS News

Shih was so alarmed by what this meant for the future of work that she quit her tech job in January and started a nonprofit helping young workers, who've been among the hardest hit, navigate the new economy.

"Traditionally, the tasks that you might assign to a young person, maybe doing some market research or creating the first draft of a memo, AI is just really good at doing those now," Shih said.

Shih believes AI could ultimately affect workers across every profession, impacting more than just workers' livelihoods.

"It's never just about the jobs. It's people's sense of self-worth. It's the fracturing of communities," Shih said.

What can be done?

Shih witnessed the decline of factory work when her family moved from Hong Kong to Ohio. She sees clear parallels between the impacts of globalization and automation and what AI could mean for the white-collar workforce

"I think what we can learn is that first we have to be honest with people about what the risks are," Shih said. "I think, you know, sugarcoating that this AI utopia, maybe we'll get there, but there's a lot of hurt that could happen between now and there."

For Acemoglu, it's not about saying no to technology.

"Absolutely not. But in every technological revolution there is pushback, and that pushback takes many different forms," he said.

Acemoglu said there is a lot that can be done to ensure AI doesn't lead to mass unemployment — companies could intentionally design AI to make humans better, not expendable, or the government could implement a tax code that incentivizes companies to hire real people.

But the window to act is closing.

"It should move us into thinking about what we can do because there is a lot we can do," Acemoglu said. "Because the future is so uncertain, because the future is so much subject to our choice and agency, it is all the more important that we have this discussion."

Read the full transcript of the segment.

World.title: Florida GOP governor candidate Byron Donalds courts skeptical Black voters
World.content:
MIAMI — For most of his nine years in Congress and Florida's state House, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, of Florida, rarely made his race part of his political pitch. This past weekend, in a string of Black voter outreach events across the Miami area, he did — carefully, and on his own terms.

In an interview with CBS News, the Republican nominee for Florida governor said he's now targeting "north of 20%" of the Black vote.

"I think there's a lot of Black voters who are looking at my campaign because they're just trying to figure out who's going to be the best person to lead Florida into the future," Donalds said. "I think the other thing with Black voters: they're starting to not be as monolithically tied to the Democrat Party."

For comparison, around 13% of Black voters backed Gov. Ron DeSantis's reelection bid in 2022, according to CBS News exit polls. President Trump won around 15% of Black votes in Florida during his 2024 presidential bid.

In 2024, Donalds was one of Mr. Trump's most visible surrogates to Black voters nationally, co-headlining a multi-city tour with Rep. Wesley Hunt of Texas billed as "Congress, Cigars & Cognac" — informal, sit-down conversations meant to make the case for Mr. Trump in rooms that weren't always receptive. Now he's running that same playbook for himself, as the principal rather than the surrogate.

A potential win for Donalds would put him in an exclusive club of Black state executives. Only three elected governors have been Black in U.S. history. Donalds is among three nominees this year who would be the first Black Republican governors ever elected.

Asked what it would mean to him to make history, Donalds paused, smiled to himself, and let his guard down for a moment. "It's wild, honestly," he told CBS News — a rare admission from a candidate who has spent his campaign avoiding identity-based appeals.

"I don't talk about my race in this campaign," Donalds told a crowd at the Black Professionals Summit's Legacy Con on Saturday, one of several stops targeting the key voting bloc. "Florida is a meritocracy. Here in Florida, we have people who have come from so many different parts of the country. What they really care about now is: Can you get the job done?"

Republican Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds speaks at the Black Professionals Summit's Legacy Con on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Seiji Yamashita/CBS News

Legacy Con's organizers told CBS News they also invited Democratic nominee David Jolly to address the summit, but he didn't attend, citing a scheduling conflict.

With less than a month of campaigning left, Donalds also pushed back on criticism that his minority outreach was new or narrow. "We're actually targeting every voter," he said, pointing to his team's door-knocking aimed at Black voters in North Miami and Broward County, Hispanic voters in Doral and Hialeah, and more.

But some voters he met during his South Florida swing say his loyalty to the president is clouding their opinion of him. At a retail stop at the Black-owned Lorna's Caribbean Restaurant in Miami Gardens, Jermaine Woodside, 54, said he came in skeptical but left more open to the congressman after an hour-long dinner conversation, even as he said bluntly that Donalds should not associate himself with Mr. Trump. "That's going to hurt him, and that's the reason why I was reluctant to be a part of his campaign," Woodside told CBS News.

Donalds told CBS News voters shouldn't judge him solely on his history with Mr. Trump.

"Look at the issues I'm pushing forward. Look at the ideas that I talk about. Yes, the president's endorsed me. Yes, a couple years ago I endorsed him to be president. But I'm running to be governor of Florida," he said.

Not everyone was swayed. Miami resident Kalyn James came alone to a meet-and-greet Donalds hosted at an outdoor event space in the predominantly Black Overtown neighborhood. James quietly protested the event by holding a sign that read "Vote Blue" with Donalds' name crossed out while he worked the room, talking to other attendees.

"I just don't think that he has a buy-in that he thinks he has," James told CBS News. "And honestly, [his win] would make history, but I think he'd be on the wrong side of history."

Jasmine Burney-Clark, founder of the nonpartisan voting rights group Equal Ground, had sharper criticism. She noted Donalds declined to sign her organization's candidate pledge, affirming an intent to sign into law a Democratic-backed state voting rights bill — which Jolly did sign — and argued his weekend events were not genuine.

"Byron Donalds has been Black at the start of this election, and he will be Black at the end of this election," Burney-Clark told CBS News. "Black voters are not going to be fooled by his targeting and his manipulation tactics to pander to get their vote."

The outreach comes as recent polling shows a surprisingly tight race for an office a Democrat hasn't won since the 1990s. For Donalds, the math is clear even if the politics are complicated: close the gap with Black voters, and Democrats' path back to the governor's mansion gets much harder.

World.title: Beavers brought to London to help solve a flooding problem: "They make people smile!"
World.content: Beavers help future-proof the city of London London is now home to some wild beavers, the first to live there in 400 years. The critters were brought in to help solve a flooding problem, but now they are a thriving part of the city. Leigh Kiniry has the story.

World.title: New expedition tries to solve Amelia Earhart mystery: "We owe it to Amelia's legacy"
World.content: Expedition tries to solve Amelia Earhart mystery A new expedition is underway, hoping to solve the mystery of Amelia Earhart's disappearance. Lana Zak reports on the latest clues and details.

World.title: CBS News poll finds 66% disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy
World.content: Trump tries to bolster GOP support in Ohio Pressure is building on President Trump to address the cost of living, with Americans frustrated with his handling of the economy and rising prices. A new CBS News poll found that 70% say the president's policies are raising the cost of food and groceries, and 64% said the war in Iran is driving oil and gas prices much higher. Taurean Small has more.

World.title: 2 dead, dozens injured in Georgia block party shooting
World.content:
Two people are dead and another 35 were injured after a shooting broke out at a neighborhood block party in southern Georgia, authorities said. Twenty-five of those injured were hospitalized, officials told local media.

Shots were fired in the early hours of Sunday morning in the city of Vienna, with sheriff's deputies hearing them ring out at around 1:25 a.m. local time while patrolling the area, according to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI).

Deputies discovered multiple people had been hit by gunfire when they arrived at the site of the shooting on Pine Street, according to investigators. Victims were taken to several different hospitals in the area, they said.

The two individuals who were fatally wounded had been found several blocks away from the location on Pine Street where investigators said the shooting originated.

Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told CBS affiliate WMAZ that more than 1,000 people had gathered along Pine Street for the block party, which was held to celebrate homecoming. Peavy said at least 50 shots were fired in total, at two different locations about one block apart. He said some people were hit by cars as drivers scrambled to leave the area, WMAZ reported.

The GBI Medical Examiner's Office will conduct autopsies on both of the deceased, each of whom was pronounced dead at the scene.

Authorities haven't released information about a possible suspect or potential motive behind the shooting. Neither the dead nor the injured individuals have been publicly identified, either.

Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told CBS News the two killed were both men, ages 20 and 23.

The GBI said it joined the probe at the request of the Dooly County Sheriff's Office, which initially responded to the incident. The investigation was "active and ongoing" later on Sunday, investigators said.

Dooly County includes the city of Vienna, which is about 50 miles south of Macon.

World.title: Brazil's presidential race heads to Lula–Bolsonaro run-off as right gains ground
World.content:
Brazil's presidential race heads to Lula–Bolsonaro run-off as right gains ground

toggle caption i Mauro Pimentel, Sergio Lima/

AFP via Getty Images





RIO DE JANEIRO —Brazil's presidential race is heading to a runoff between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after neither candidate secured the more than 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.

The race was tight, with Flávio Bolsonaro finishing ahead of Lula in Sunday's first-round election. With more than 99% of the vote counted, Bolsonaro secured roughly 47% of the vote, while Lula came in second place with 45%.

If that sounds like déjà -vú, it's because in many ways, this election is a rerun: Lula narrowly defeated Bolsonaro's father, former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest after being convicted of plotting to overturn that election and prevent Lula from taking office.

Sponsor Message

Flávio has pledged to carry on his father's legacy. Speaking to journalists and supporters outside his home in Brasília after the results came in, he said the vote showed Brazilians were ready for a political change.

"Brazil wants change, that's the reading of what happened today," Bolsonaro said. "It's the end of the Workers' Party era," he added, referring to Lula's political party.

Sunday's results also pointed to a broader rightward shift in Brazilian politics, with the Bolsonaro camp performing strongly across the country.

Lula sought to rally his supporters in São Paulo, framing the next stage of the campaign as a fresh contest.

"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," Lula said. "I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan."

Lula also took aim at his opponent, warning voters about Bolsonaro's political background. "On the other side we have an uncertainty with a biography of a dark past," he said.

The presidential candidates who came in third, fourth, and fifth place are all right-wing, suggesting that Bolsonaro could have a natural pool of voters to draw from in the runoff. That could set the stage for another extremely tight contest on October 25.

Sponsor Message

Brazilians also chose governors and state and federal lawmakers Sunday, with early results showing that the right also made significant gains in Congress, particularly in the Senate. That could give Bolsonaro a stronger political base if he wins the presidency.

Lula, 80, is aiming for his fourth nonconsecutive term and has pledged to continue broad social spending and to stand up to Trump's aggressive policies toward Latin America.

Bolsonaro, 45, pledges to slash the deficit and realign the country's foreign policy with Washington. The result suggests Lula will now have to do more than defend his record: he will need to rebuild the broad coalition that returned him to power in 2022, including among younger voters who have shown less enthusiasm for his campaign.

This year's presidential campaign featured smaller rallies compared to past years, perhaps because both of the candidates felt like known quantities to voters.

"I think the campaign feels more muted because people are tired of fighting," said 38-year-old nutritionist Raysa Tavares after she voted Sunday afternoon in the Rio de Janeiro favela of Vidigal.

Businessman Caio Farias, 37, who voted in Rio's upscale neighborhood of Leblon, said that he preferred other right-wing candidates to Bolsonaro, but voted for Bolsonaro in an effort to try to get the election over in one round.

Now, Brazilians are gearing up for another three weeks of campaigning. In the 2022 election, the second round of the election saw a sharp uptick in political violence, with dozens of people physically attacking each other for political reasons, Brazilian news site Pública reported.

Beyond the fact that this year's contest features a younger Bolsonaro, there's something else setting it apart from the last one: Trump is in the White House, with big ambitions for drawing politics in Latin America to the right. Lula has accused the United States of trying to meddle in Brazil's election, which the U.S. State Department has denied.

Sponsor Message

Bolsonaro rallies have featured American flags and a giant inflatable doll of Trump holding a jailed Lula, while Lula has campaigned on the idea of protecting Brazilian sovereignty from foreign interference—a rarely-heard watchword in 2022. In Rio on election day, voters could be seen on the streets both with Trump T-shirts and "out with Trump" stickers.

The topic of Brazil's relationship with the United States is sure to feature in second-round campaigning, as are domestic themes of security policy, corruption, and the economy, which polls say are top of voters' minds.

But the first-round results have added another defining issue to the runoff: whether Brazil wants to continue with Lula or embrace the broader rightward shift that emerged from Sunday's vote.

World.title: Brazil votes, with Lula facing Bolsonaro's son
World.content:
Brazil votes, with Lula facing Bolsonaro's son

In Brazil, President Lula da Silva faces Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former president, in a tight race. If neither wins more than half the votes they'll face each other again on Oct. 25.

Transcript

ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST:

This is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED from NPR News. I'm Elissa Nadworny. It's election day in Brazil, where voters have been choosing between two very different visions for the country and for Brazil's role in the world. President Lula da Silva is seeking another term against right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president, who was convicted of plotting a coup to overturn the results of the 2022 election. The stakes go well beyond Brazil's borders, and the outcome could test President Trump's efforts to expand U.S. influence across the hemisphere. Our South America correspondent Carrie Kahn is on the line from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Hi, Carrie.

CARRIE KAHN, BYLINE: Hi, Elissa.

NADWORNY: So you've been out all day talking to voters. What have you heard?

KAHN: Well, first off, unlike yesterday when we were talking, the sun finally came out today.

NADWORNY: (Laughter).

KAHN: The rain finally stopped. And the lines at the polling places were very long across the city. I went to the famous beaches of Copacabana and Ipanema and all the way to the northern reaches of Rio and the Tijuca neighborhood. It's a middle- and working-class neighborhood, and people there, like most voters, were very set on who they will vote for in polarized Brazil. Few voters are going to be deciding this race.

NADWORNY: What was foremost on their minds?

KAHN: I heard it a lot today. It was about crime and insecurity, especially in the Tijuca voting place I visited. Robbery and theft is prevalent there. People want more solution. Most people at those sites were Lula supporters. Mariano Hizenje (ph) is 78 and says he always votes for Lula because he takes care of Brazil's Black people, like himself. And Hizenje worries if Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil would abandon the poor.

MARIANO HIZENJE: (Speaking Portuguese).

KAHN: He says, "we are the most in need, and so we had to come out and vote today."

I also spoke with a Bolsonaro voter, 55-year-old psychologist, Ana Barbosa (ph). She says she wants a new government that will look out for everyone and not just one social class. She's worried about crime too and says Bolsonaro and the conservatives are better equipped to tackle those problems.

ANA BARBOSA: (Speaking Portuguese).

KAHN: She's saying that the people of the lower class don't take enough care about crime and violence, and she says Bolsonaro will crack down on criminals who she said she feels like are closing in on her family.

NADWORNY: President Trump has exerted more influence and military action in Latin America during his term. He says it's needed to fight drug traffickers and organized crime. Has U.S.-Brazil relations been a big issue with voters?

KAHN: Somewhat. Lula campaigned on stopping any U.S. interference in Brazil. Bolsonaro has said he welcomes Trump's heavier influence in the region. Trump has trumpeted a recent shift to the right throughout the region lately. Lula losing to Trump ally, Bolsonaro, would be greatly welcomed by the U.S. But Gustavo Ribeiro - he's a cofounder of The Brazilian Report, an English-language news and analysis site. I talked to him, and he says he really doesn't believe Trump was much of an influence in this first round of voting.

GUSTAVO RIBEIRO: The Trump White House prefers Flavio Bolsonaro, but I wouldn't overstate the importance of Donald Trump's support because this election, in the end, has not been about sovereignty, which was what Lula wanted. This election has been almost exclusively about domestic issues.

KAHN: He says he's worried what the U.S. and Trump will do if Lula wins, especially by a small margin. And polls do show a tight race ahead, and a runoff is most probable. And like Gustavo Ribeiro said, bread-and-butter issues are going to continue to be most important to voters.
