Who Is Who

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL): senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, leading the count on the right.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT): the sitting president, on the left, seeking another term.

Superior Electoral Court (TSE): the body that runs the election and publishes the official count.

Why It Matters for the US

Most American money in Brazil sits in a few places. An ADR (American depositary receipt) is a US-listed certificate for a foreign share. PBR and VALE are the best-known Brazilian ones. EWZ is an exchange-traded fund that holds a basket of Brazilian stocks. All three trade in dollars but follow Brazilian prices and the real.

That makes the real a second variable. A US holder of EWZ gains when Brazilian shares rise, and also when the real strengthens against the dollar. Both depend on how investors read the next three weeks of campaigning.

What to Watch This Week

Brazilian trading on B3 opens at 10:00 Brasília time on Monday, which is 9:00 a.m. Eastern. That is before the New York open at 9:30 a.m., so the Ibovespa and the real give the first clue. PBR, VALE and EWZ then trade from 9:30 a.m. Eastern.

The data calendar is also busy. The S&P Global Brazil composite PMI for September is due at 10:00 a.m. Brasília time Monday, after 49.1 in August. A reading below 50 signals a shrinking private sector. The September trade balance follows on Tuesday 6 October, and the IPCA consumer price index on Friday 9 October.

What Is Not Known

How markets react on Monday. Whether Friday’s gains were tied to the vote or to wider moves in emerging markets. The final TSE count, since one section was still outstanding. And how the 33.5 million registered voters who did not vote on 4 October will behave on 25 October.

Who is in Brazil’s presidential runoff?

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) and President Lula (PT). The TSE count at 99.99% of sections gives Flávio 47.03% and Lula 45.16% of valid votes. The runoff is on Sunday 25 October 2026.

How did Brazilian assets close before the vote?

On Friday 2 October the Ibovespa rose 2.63% to 192,114.55. The real closed at R$5.2133 per US$1. EWZ closed at US$38.19, the Petrobras ADR at US$21.65 and the Vale ADR at US$13.76.

What is an ADR?

An American depositary receipt is a certificate traded in the United States that represents shares of a foreign company. Petrobras and Vale both have ADRs listed in New York.

When can US investors react to the result?

Brazil’s B3 exchange opens at 10:00 a.m. Brasília time on Monday 5 October, or 9:00 a.m. Eastern. The New York market opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern.

World.title: Peru Likely Heads to 14 Regional Runoffs on 29 November
World.content:
Peru’s regional elections are far from settled. An exit poll sees 14 governor races heading to a second round, while Lima’s mayor race stays open as counting continues.

Download the PDF checklist Key Facts The picture An exit poll by Datum points to governor runoffs in 14 of Peru’s regions on 29 November 2026. Official counts were partial on Monday.

Lima In the partial official count, the Renovación Popular list led. A legal question over re-election remains. No runoff exists for mayors.

The 30% rule A governor ticket must win at least 30% of valid votes to avoid a runoff (ONPE).

What it means for you Some regional governments will stay undecided for weeks. Plan local permits and paperwork with that in mind.

Still open Final counts, contested tally sheets and which regions really go to a second round.

What the Exit Poll Shows

Peru voted on Sunday 4 October 2026 for regional governors, mayors and councils for the 2027 to 2030 term. More than 26 million citizens were registered to vote, according to ONPE figures cited by Infobae Perú.

The firm Datum published an exit poll (a survey of voters leaving polling places). It points to 14 regions where no governor ticket reaches 30% of valid votes: Amazonas, Áncash, Arequipa, Huancavelica, Ica, La Libertad, Lambayeque, Lima Provincias, Loreto, Moquegua, Piura, Puno, Tumbes and Ucayali. Several races look tight. In Huancavelica, the poll had Juan Común at 29.5% and Samuel Morán at 29.3%. In Arequipa, it had Alfredo Zegarra at 27.0% and Jenry Huisa at 15.3%. ONPE had asked the court to keep 6 December for any runoff, but the court set 29 November.

File photo: Lima’s coast. (The Rio Times archive)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Exit Polls Are Not Results

An exit poll estimates; it does not count. The official count by ONPE was still partial on Monday, and early counts often come from urban areas first. Rural results arrive later and can change the order. Treat the list of 14 regions as a first picture, not a final one.

The rule is simple. A governor ticket wins in the first round with at least 30% of valid votes, which exclude blank and null ballots. If no ticket does, the top two meet in a Second Regional Election. The electoral court (JNE) set Sunday 29 November 2026 for that vote.

Lima’s Mayor Race

Lima’s mayor is decided in one round. At 23.566% of tally sheets counted, the Renovación Popular list headed by Rafael López Aliaga had 28.927% of valid votes, or 382,429 votes, according to Infobae Perú. Francis Allison of Avanza País was second, and the gap moved as the count advanced.

The Datum exit poll gave López Aliaga 31.2% and Allison 25.2%. A legal question hangs over the result. López Aliaga was mayor from 2023 to 2026, and Peru’s constitution bars immediate re-election of mayors. He ran as first councillor (regidor) on the list, and he would become mayor if the list wins. He argues the ban does not apply. The Lima Centro electoral jury will proclaim results, and the national court (JNE) can rule on appeals, according to Infobae Perú. Daniel Urresti of Podemos Perú has questioned a proclamation. The final winner is not confirmed.

What This Means for Expats

Local paperwork. A region without a confirmed governor may keep its current officials in place for a few weeks. Ask your municipality or regional office about timing before relying on a particular decision.

Travel. The vote does not change entry rules or tourist sites. Check regional notices for any second-round restrictions, such as alcohol sales limits, if a runoff is confirmed.

The other direction. A clear leader in a region can settle matters within days. A split field means a campaign until late November. In both cases, the local effect on daily life is usually slower than the headlines suggest.

What Is Not Yet Known

We do not know the final shares, which regions will really go to a second round, or how many tally sheets will be contested. The JNE’s deadline for delivering contested sheets is Sunday 11 October. Recount hearings may run until Wednesday 28 October.

Which Peruvian regions may have governor runoffs? An exit poll by the firm Datum points to 14: Amazonas, Áncash, Arequipa, Huancavelica, Ica, La Libertad, Lambayeque, Lima Provincias, Loreto, Moquegua, Piura, Puno, Tumbes and Ucayali. Exit polls are estimates. The official count by ONPE, the electoral office, decides, and it was still partial on Monday morning. Does Lima’s mayor face a runoff? No. Mayors in Peru are decided in a single round, and the candidate with the most votes wins. In the partial ONPE count, the Renovación Popular list led, ahead of Francis Allison of Avanza País, according to Infobae Perú. Whether its leader, Rafael López Aliaga, can take office is a separate question for the electoral court. When would the regional runoffs take place? Sunday 29 November 2026, the date set by the electoral court (JNE), and only in regions where no governor ticket wins at least 30% of valid votes. The JNE asked ONPE to hand contested tally sheets to local election juries by Sunday 11 October. Recount hearings may run until Wednesday 28 October.

World.title: What Brazil’s 25 October Runoff Means for Expats
World.content:
Brazil’s first round ended with Flávio Bolsonaro narrowly ahead of Lula. The runoff on 25 October will decide who governs from January 2027.

The runoff The two meet again on Sunday 25 October 2026, according to the TSE (Brazil’s electoral court).

The count About 56 million votes for Bolsonaro and about 54 million for Lula (Rádio Senado). At 99.95% counted, Reuters had 47.04% and 45.15% of valid votes.

What it means for you Foreign residents cannot vote and no residency rule changes. Currency and market swings may affect prices and transfers.

Still open Where the first-round voters of eliminated candidates go, and how markets price a three-week campaign.

What Happened on Sunday

Brazil voted on Sunday 4 October 2026. About 158 million citizens were registered to vote. Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) came first, and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party (PT) came second.

Rádio Senado reports about 56 million votes for Bolsonaro and about 54 million for Lula. Reuters, with 99.95% of polling sections counted, gave 47.04% and 45.15% of valid votes, a gap of about 2.3 million votes. Valid votes exclude blank and null ballots. Other outlets show slightly different shares, so the TSE’s final tally is the reference.

Augusto Cury, Renan Santos, Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu Zema finished third to sixth, according to Rádio Senado. More than 33 million registered voters did not vote.

File photo: bank offices in São Paulo. (The Rio Times archive)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Brazil election Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why This Was a Surprise

Major pollsters, including Quaest and Datafolha, had Lula ahead before the vote, according to Reuters. The result therefore moved opinion about who is favoured. Some analysts now see Bolsonaro as the favourite for 25 October.

That is one view, not a forecast we share. Polls missed the first round, and a runoff is a different contest: voters of the eliminated candidates choose between two names. Campaigning restarts on Monday. Bolsonaro called the result the end of the PT era, according to Reuters.

How Markets Reacted

Brazil’s own markets were closed on Sunday. In US after-hours trading, the EWZ fund, which tracks Brazilian stocks, rose between 7% and 10% depending on the moment, according to InfoMoney and Exame. Petrobras and Vale shares listed in the US rose about 5%. Brazilian markets react on Monday, and we do not yet know how far the first move holds.

For context, the central bank’s PTAX reference rate (the official dollar rate) was 5.2238 reais per dollar on Friday 2 October. R$1,000 is about US$191 at that rate. Currencies often overshoot on a political surprise and then settle. The next Copom meeting, which sets the Selic rate (Brazil’s benchmark interest rate), is on 3 and 4 November, after the runoff.

What This Means for Foreign Residents

Residency and visas. Only citizens vote, so foreigners have no ballot. The vote itself changes no visa rule. Any later policy change would need new decisions after the January 2027 inauguration.

Money. If you move money into or out of Brazil in the next three weeks, expect larger daily swings in the real. Splitting a large transfer into steps is a common way to reduce timing risk, but that is a personal choice.

Daily life. Expect more campaign events and media noise until 25 October. On that Sunday, polling places in schools can bring traffic and noise nearby.

The other direction. A calm campaign and a clear result on 25 October would end the uncertainty quickly. A very close result could keep it going for days.

What Is Not Yet Known

We do not know how the voters of the four eliminated candidates will split, or how the real and Brazilian stocks trade once local markets open. The TSE’s final first-round tally also still has to be published in full.

When is Brazil’s presidential runoff? Sunday 25 October 2026, three weeks after the first round on Sunday 4 October, according to the electoral court (TSE). Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula are the two candidates. A runoff is needed because neither won more than half of the valid votes. Can foreign residents vote in the runoff? No. Only Brazilian citizens vote in presidential elections. Voting is compulsory for most citizens aged 18 to 69. Foreign residents are not required to do anything, and no visa or residency rule changes because of the vote. What time will runoff results appear? If the TSE keeps the first-round schedule, polls close at 5 p.m. Brasília time. On 25 October that is 20:00 UTC, 4 p.m. US Eastern time and 8 p.m. in Lisbon and London, because Europe returns to winter time that day. Confirm the hours with the TSE nearer the date.

World.title: Uruguay Economy 2026, Who Runs It and How
World.content:
URUGUAY · ECONOMIC POWER

Key Facts — What it is A mixed economy where state utilities, foreign banks and multinational pulp producers share control with a small number of Uruguayan business families.

— Why it matters The state controls electricity, water, telecoms, ports and the largest bank, while foreign groups dominate pulp, private banking and digital payments.

— The numbers Pulp was Uruguay’s second-largest goods export in 2025 at approximately US$2.31 billion, according to reported figures.

— Who is who

— The catch Uruguay’s relatively strong peso has created competitiveness concerns for exporters, a tension the Central Bank manages as of 2026.

— What it means for you Foreigners can bank, invest and do business in Uruguay, but must understand that the state remains a major economic actor in daily life.

The Uruguay economy is not run by a single tycoon or corporation. It is a carefully balanced system where the state owns the utilities and the largest bank, while foreign multinationals dominate pulp, private banking and digital payments.

Uruguay is a small South American country of 3.4 million people, but its economy punches above its weight in agriculture, forestry, logistics and financial services. This guide explains who actually controls the levers of the Uruguay economy in 2026, from the presidential palace to the boardrooms of Finnish pulp companies.

The ANCAP refinery at La Teja on Montevideo's bay, a state-owned institution central to Uruguay's energy sector and fuel prices.

The Political Command Centre

The Uruguay economy is steered from Montevideo by a small group of elected officials and technocrats. President Yamandú Ramón Orsi Martínez, of the centre-left Frente Amplio coalition, has held office since 1 March 2025. His administration sets the strategic direction for public enterprises, energy policy, infrastructure, taxation, labour rules and investment promotion.

The day-to-day management of fiscal policy falls to Gabriel Oddone París, minister of Economy and Finance since 1 March 2025. Oddone oversees the national budget, taxation, public debt and coordination with the financial sector. His deputy is Martín Vallcorba Urrutia, and the ministry’s senior team includes Director of Economic Policy Bibiana Eloísa Lanzilotta Mernies, Director of Public Finance Juan Benítez Parga, and head of the Debt Management Unit Herman Kamil, according to the ministry’s official authorities page as of October 2026.

Monetary policy belongs to the Banco Central del Uruguay, the central bank, led by Guillermo Tolosa since 24 March 2025. The BCU controls banking regulation, payment systems, foreign-exchange oversight and financial stability.

Other ministries shape the economy too. The Ministry of Industry, Energy and Mining, led by Fernanda Cardona since 1 March 2025, oversees energy, mining and industrial policy, including the state fuel company ANCAP. The Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries regulates the country’s core export industries. Uruguay XXI, the official investment and export-promotion agency, works to attract foreign capital and promote Uruguayan products abroad.

The UPM 2 pulp mill in central Uruguay, symbol of the forestry and pulp industry that earned US$2.31 billion in exports in 2025. Photo: Astromessier, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons.

State-Owned Companies That Control Infrastructure

Uruguay’s public enterprises are legally owned by society through the state. They are central to infrastructure, employment and national investment, and they give the government direct influence over the cost of doing business.

UTE: Electricity for Everything

UTE, the Administración Nacional de Usinas y Trasmisiones Eléctricas, controls electricity generation, transmission and distribution. The Ministry of Industry describes UTE as central to the expansion and consolidation of the national electricity system. Its investment decisions shape Uruguay’s renewable-energy system, grid capacity and the country’s ability to attract energy-intensive industries such as data centres.

ANCAP: Fuel, Refining and Offshore Ambitions

ANCAP, the Administración Nacional de Combustibles, Alcohol y Portland, is the state energy and fuels company. It handles fuel imports, refining, distribution and cement. In 2026, ANCAP also sits at the centre of Uruguay’s offshore exploration strategy. Exploration work involving Chevron in the OFF-6 block was expected to begin during the year, including seismic activity and preparations for a deepwater exploration well. ANCAP’s president was identified in the available official public-sector directory as Alejandro Stipanicic, with Diego Martín Durand Arrambide as vice president. Public-company boards can change through government appointments, so these names should be checked against ANCAP’s latest official board notice.

ANTEL: The Digital Backbone

ANTEL, the Administración Nacional de Telecomunicaciones, is Uruguay’s state-owned telecommunications company. It controls a major share of fixed-line, mobile, broadband and data infrastructure. The government describes ANTEL as developing digital services for industry, agriculture and logistics, including solutions intended to add value to production chains. ANTEL is strategically important for broadband connectivity, government digital services, data centres and Uruguay’s positioning as a regional digital-services hub.

OSE, ANP and AFE: Water, Ports and Rail

OSE, Obras Sanitarias del Estado, controls public drinking-water and sewerage services. It is a state monopoly in an essential sector, particularly important for industrial users and agriculture. The ANP, Administración Nacional de Puertos, controls Uruguay’s public-port system. The Port of Montevideo is central to the country’s role as a logistics platform for Paraguay, southern Brazil and the wider Río de la Plata region. AFE, the Administración de Ferrocarriles del Estado, is the state railway entity. Its role has become more significant because the forestry and pulp industries require reliable inland logistics to move timber and pulp toward export terminals.

The State-Owned Financial Institutions

The state does not just run utilities. It also operates the country’s largest bank and important insurance and mortgage institutions.

BROU, the Banco de la República Oriental del Uruguay, is Uruguay’s largest and most politically important public bank. It provides retail, corporate and agricultural finance and acts as a major channel for state-directed credit. BROU is especially important for farmers, small and medium-sized enterprises, public-sector entities, deposits and payments, and rural banking. The public directory available in the search results listed Salvador Ferrer as president and Alejandro Lafluf as vice president, with Max Sapolinski, Pablo Sitjar and Leandro Francolino as directors. Those names require final verification against BROU’s current official authorities page because the directory result was last updated in 2025.

The Banco de Seguros del Estado, or BSE, is the state insurance company, an important participant in worker-accident insurance and agricultural insurance. The Banco Hipotecario del Uruguay, or BHU, is the state mortgage bank, still relevant to housing finance and government housing policy.

Montevideo's skyline, with the iconic Palacio Salvo tower. The capital holds about 1.3 million of Uruguay's 3.5 million people. Photo: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Private Banks: Foreign Groups Dominate Credit

Uruguay’s private banking system is concentrated among a mixture of foreign-owned institutions and large regional banking groups. The largest private banks are not generally controlled by Uruguayan families. They are subsidiaries of Spanish, Brazilian and Canadian banking groups, while BROU provides the principal domestic public counterweight.

Bank Controlling group Economic role Santander Uruguay Spanish Santander group Retail, corporate, payments, consumer credit BBVA Uruguay Spanish BBVA group Corporate, retail, wealth banking Itaú Uruguay Brazilian Itaú Unibanco group Corporate, institutional, affluent, retail Scotiabank Uruguay Canadian Scotiabank group Retail, corporate, consumer finance HSBC Uruguay HSBC group, subject to local corporate changes Corporate and international banking Banco Heritage Private Uruguayan banking group Wealth management, private banking BROU Uruguayan state Public and agricultural banking

In 2026, the banking sector’s most important structural issues include peso interest rates, dollar lending, corporate credit, agricultural exposure, payment-system competition and digital banking. The Central Bank’s regulatory role means its decisions influence credit conditions throughout the economy.

The Largest Corporate Actors

Beyond the state and the banks, a small number of foreign multinationals and regional technology companies shape the Uruguay economy’s export profile and digital landscape.

UPM: The Finnish Pulp Giant

Finland’s UPM is one of the most powerful foreign corporate actors in Uruguay. Its Fray Bentos and Paso de los Toros operations have made pulp one of the country’s largest export industries. UPM’s influence includes forestry plantations, pulp production, rail and road logistics, port infrastructure, energy generation from biomass, and large-scale regional employment and supplier networks. Pulp was Uruguay’s second-largest goods-export category in 2025 at approximately US$2.31 billionUPM is not a listed Uruguayan company; it is a foreign multinational whose strategic decisions are made outside Uruguay.

Montes del Plata: The Other Pulp Power

Montes del Plata is a major pulp producer operating in Uruguay. It is associated with Arauco, the Chilean forestry group, and Stora Enso, the Finnish-Swedish forestry company. Together with UPM, Montes del Plata means that a small number of foreign forestry groups control a large share of Uruguay’s pulp production, plantations and logistics chains.

Mercado Libre and dLocal: The Digital Challengers

Argentina-based MercadoLibre, listed on Nasdaq, is a major technology and payments actor in Uruguay. Its marketplace, logistics and Mercado Pago services affect e-commerce and digital payments. It is not an Uruguayan-controlled company, but its regional scale makes it an important competitor to banks and traditional payment providers. Uruguay-founded dLocal, also listed on Nasdaq, is one of the country’s most internationally visible technology companies. It provides cross-border payment infrastructure for global companies operating in emerging markets.

Food and Beverage Multinationals

International food companies, including Arcor and PepsiCo, have a significant presence in Uruguay’s processed-food sector. They operate within a wider market that includes domestic dairy, beverage, meat and food-processing companies. The Coca-Cola system operates through local bottling and distribution arrangements, commercially important but fragmented across brands, bottlers and distributors rather than controlled by a single listed Uruguayan company.

The Current State in 2026 and Open Questions

The Uruguay economy entered 2026 with moderate growth, low inflation and a stable institutional framework. The National Institute of Statistics reported 12-month CPI inflation of 4.55% in August 2026, within the Central Bank’s target range. Unemployment stood at 7.1% for June–August 2026, with a labour-force participation rate of 64.0% and an employment rate of 59.5%, according to the INE household employment survey published on 1 October 2026.

The Central Bank’s policy challenge in 2026 has been balancing low inflation against concerns about Uruguay’s relatively strong peso and the competitiveness of exporters. The average wage index rose 5.71% year-on-year in July 2026, while the housing construction-cost index rose 4.94% in August 2026, according to the INE.

The Orsi administration is implementing its first full budget and working to preserve Uruguay’s reputation for institutional stability while addressing competitiveness, the exchange rate and moderate growth. The government’s economic team, led by Oddone and Tolosa, faces the task of keeping inflation low without letting the peso become so strong that exporters suffer.

Open questions for the rest of 2026 and beyond include whether offshore oil exploration with Chevron yields commercial discoveries, how the pulp sector’s expansion affects logistics and land use, and whether the digital payments sector continues to erode traditional banking margins.

What This Means for Foreigners, Investors and Expats

For a foreigner considering Uruguay, the structure of the Uruguay economy has practical consequences. You will deal with state companies for electricity, water, internet and possibly banking. You will find familiar foreign banks such as Santander, BBVA, Itaú and Scotiabank. You will encounter Finnish and Chilean pulp companies if you do business in forestry, logistics or regional exports.

Uruguay’s institutional stability is a genuine asset. The country has a long tradition of respecting contracts, maintaining an independent central bank and avoiding the extreme political swings that affect some neighbours. The presence of major foreign banks and multinationals reflects that confidence.

However, Uruguay is not a low-cost country. The relatively strong peso, high wages in dollar terms and state-dominated utilities mean that operating costs can be higher than in other Latin American markets. Foreigners who succeed in Uruguay typically focus on value-added sectors such as technology, financial services, specialised agriculture or logistics, rather than competing on price alone.

What to Watch

Several dated events and trends will shape the Uruguay economy in the coming months. The Central Bank’s official publication calendar lists the monetary balance on 8 October 2026, minutes of the October 2026 Monetary Policy Committee meeting on 9 October 2026, the Monetary Policy Report for the second quarter of 2026 on 13 October 2026, and the October 2026 inflation-expectations survey on 14 October 2026.

Beyond those dates, watch for any announcements from ANCAP about offshore exploration results, any changes to the Central Bank’s policy rate, and any signals from the Orsi administration about tax or labour reforms. The pulp sector’s export performance and the evolution of the peso will also be key indicators of where the Uruguay economy is heading.

Related reading: Uruguay Neighbours Explained, the Southern Cone in 2026; Uruguay Explained: The Country, Its Stability, Its Economy and What to Watch; Cost of Living Punta del Este 2026: Half Again Above Montevideo; more from Uruguay.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the president of Uruguay in 2026?

Yamandú Ramón Orsi Martínez leads the Frente Amplio coalition. His constitutional term runs from 2025 to 2030.

Who is Uruguay’s economy minister in 2026?

Gabriel Oddone París is minister of Economy and Finance. He oversees fiscal policy, the national budget, taxation and public debt.

Who controls Uruguay’s central bank?

Guillermo Tolosa is president of the Banco Central del Uruguay. The central bank controls monetary policy, banking regulation and financial stability.

What are Uruguay’s biggest exports?

Pulp was Uruguay’s second-largest goods-export category in 2025 at approximately US$2.31 billion, according to reported figures. Agriculture, meat, dairy and forestry products are also core export industries.

Which foreign companies operate in Uruguay?

Major foreign companies include Finland’s UPM in pulp, Chile’s Arauco and Finland-Sweden’s Stora Enso through Montes del Plata, Spain’s Santander and BBVA in banking, Brazil’s Itaú, Canada’s Scotiabank, and Argentina-based MercadoLibre in e-commerce and payments.

Is Uruguay a good place for foreign investment?

Uruguay offers institutional stability, an independent central bank and a long tradition of respecting contracts. However, operating costs can be higher than in other Latin American markets due to the relatively strong peso and state-dominated utilities.

World.title: Chile Culture, the Key Figures to Know in 2026
World.content:
CHILE · CULTURE

Key Facts — What it is Chile culture is a dense network of music, literature, cinema, visual art, sport and festivals rooted in folk memory and political history.

— Why it matters Culture is how Chile processes dictatorship, exile, inequality and regional identity, and how it exports creative work to the world.

— The numbers In 2024, 75.4% of people participated in at least one cultural activity, and 9,013 books were registered with ISBN, according to INE.

— Who is who Violeta Parra and Víctor Jara anchor memory; Ana Tijoux, Mon Laferte and Pablo Chill-E lead contemporary music; Isabel Allende and Alejandro Zambra carry literature.

— The catch Cultural prestige is increasingly examined alongside personal conduct, as debates around Pablo Neruda show, and public funding remains contested.

— What it means for you For foreigners, expats and investors, Chile culture offers a practical lens on political memory, creative exports and everyday social life.

Chile culture is not a backdrop: it is a living argument about memory, identity and power. Knowing its key figures helps you read the country beyond the headlines.

Chile is a long, narrow country where geography shapes identity, and where music, literature and film have carried political memory through dictatorship, exile and return. This guide explains the people, genres, institutions and festivals that define Chile culture in 2026, and what they reveal about the country today.

The Andes, Chile's natural spine, running the length of the country. (File photo)

The institutional map: who shapes Chile culture

The central public institution is the Ministry of the Cultures, the Arts and Heritage, which funds programmes, protects heritage and coordinates national cultural policy. It was created under Law No. 21.045, which provided for the ministry to begin its functions on 1 March 2018.

As of September and October 2026, the ministry’s website identifies Francisco Undurraga Cantuarias as Minister of the Cultures, Arts and Heritage. The ministry’s music structure is led operationally by the Council for the Promotion of National Music.

Television is regulated by the Consejo Nacional de Televisión, linked to the Presidency through the General Secretariat of Government. The audiovisual sector is organised under the Council of Art and the Audiovisual Industry.

The National Council of Cultures, Arts and Heritage advises the ministry on policies, plans and programmes. Its membership is designed to include representatives of the arts, traditional cultures, heritage, Indigenous peoples, migrants, academia and National Prize winners. This institutional layer matters because Chile culture is not only produced by artists; it is shaped by public funding, heritage protection and broadcast regulation.

Valparaíso, the port city on Chile's Pacific coast, known for its colourful hillside neighbourhoods. Photo: Till Niermann, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Music: memory, identity and export potential

Violeta Parra, the foundational figure

Violeta Parra remains the single most important reference point for Chilean popular culture. A singer, composer, visual artist, researcher and collector of folk traditions, she transformed rural and Indigenous-rooted materials into modern national art. Her influence extends across music, literature, visual art and political memory.

Her work continues to structure official programming in 2026. The Violeta Parra Museum is also presenting anniversary programming extending her legacy into contemporary music and performance.

For international readers, Parra is best understood not simply as a folk singer but as a national cultural institution in human form. Her work connects class, rural life, women’s authorship, political violence and the preservation of oral traditions.

Víctor Jara and nueva canción

Víctor Jara remains central to Chile’s political and cultural identity. His songs combine folk forms, social criticism and an explicitly democratic and popular outlook. Alongside Quilapayún, Inti-Illimani, Illapu and Los Jaivas, he helped establish the international image of Chilean nueva canción.

The genre became globally associated with the Popular Unity period, the 1973 coup and exile. In 2026, this memory remains active rather than archival. The first Festival of Music, Human Rights, Democracy and Art at the National Stadium brought together musicians, writers and journalists around memory and democracy.

Music in Chile therefore often functions as testimony, commemoration and political education.

Contemporary popular music

Chile’s current music ecosystem is more diverse than the traditional folk versus nueva canción narrative suggests. It includes Ana Tijoux, whose hip-hop combines feminism, migration, inequality and political critique; Gepe, who blends pop with Andean and Latin American references; and Mon Laferte, whose career links Chilean songwriting, rock, bolero, cabaret and the Mexican market.

Francisca Valenzuela is a singer-songwriter and cultural entrepreneur associated with women’s visibility and gender equality. Los Bunkers are a major rock band whose reunion demonstrated the depth of Chile’s guitar-based popular music audience. Alex Anwandter’s pop and electronic work addresses sexuality, memory and social change.

Paloma Mami is a prominent Chilean-American voice in Latin urban music. Pablo Chill-E and the wider Chilean trap scene reflect youth culture, urban inequality and digital distribution. Tiro de Gracia, Chancho en Piedra, Congreso, Jorge González and Los Prisioneros still shape Chilean rock and pop.

The state’s music policy remains important because Chile has a relatively small domestic market and high concentration in cultural distribution. The Ministry describes Law No. 19,928 as a framework to promote, protect and disseminate Chilean music. The ministry also highlights Rockódromo, a public festival and professionalisation platform with an internationalisation focus.

Chilean Music Day

The government launched the 2026 edition of Día de la Música Chilena on 2 October at Santiago’s Plaza de la Constitución. The ministry stated that the event is held annually on 4 October, in connection with Violeta Parra’s birth date, and that the 2026 featured honouree was Cecilia, La Incomparable. The programme extends across all 16 regions.

The importance of the day is larger than its concerts. It turns national music into a public-policy category and gives emerging artists access to regional stages, public audiences and institutional visibility.

Literature: from Nobel prestige to uncomfortable memory

Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda

Her poetry, essays and educational work remain foundational to Chilean identity. She is associated with childhood, rural landscapes, grief, motherhood and education, but her international importance also lies in the tension between national symbolism and the complexity of her personal, sexual and political histories.

Pablo Neruda, Nobel laureate in 1971, remains Chile’s most globally recognised poet, with an enormous international publishing and tourism footprint. His houses in Isla Negra, La Sebastiana and La Chascona are among the country’s best-known literary heritage sites.

Neruda’s status is also contested. Allegations concerning sexual violence and the treatment of women have changed how institutions, readers and younger writers discuss him. His place in Chile culture therefore illustrates a wider national debate: cultural prestige is increasingly examined alongside personal conduct and political responsibility.

Roberto Bolaño and contemporary writers

Roberto Bolaño is the most influential Chilean novelist for many international contemporary readers. Although he spent much of his adult life outside Chile, novels such as The Savage Detectives and 2666 made Chilean literary references part of a global, post-dictatorship literary conversation. His work resists tourist images of Chile, presenting exile, literary subcultures, violence, political disillusionment and Latin American mobility.

Important living or recently active literary figures include Diamela Eltit, a major novelist and essayist whose work examines dictatorship, gender, marginality and institutional power. Isabel Allende’s novels remain among Chile’s most successful literary exports, despite a substantial US-based career. Alejandro Zambra explores memory, family and the post-dictatorship generation. Lina Meruane addresses illness, the body, migration and power. Nona Fernández links theatre, fiction, memory and the representation of dictatorship. Raúl Zurita’s poetry and performance-based work remain central to Chile’s post-traumatic cultural landscape.

Alberto Fuguet is an important voice in debates about globalisation, urban identity and the so-called McOndo generation. Pía Barros, Leonardo Sanhueza, María José Ferrada and Paulina Flores represent the continuing vitality of Chilean fiction, poetry and children’s literature. In 2026, literary culture is increasingly connected to archives, human-rights sites, book fairs, libraries and public education rather than only to commercial publishing.

A Copec service station in Santiago, symbol of Chile's energy sector. Photo: Warko (Marco Correa), CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Cinema and television: memory and international recognition

Patricio Guzmán, Sebastián Lelio and Pablo Larraín

Patricio Guzmán is Chile’s defining documentary filmmaker. His trilogy The Battle of Chile established an international visual record of the Popular Unity government and the 1973 coup. Later films, including Nostalgia for the Light and The Pearl Button, connect political violence to landscape, astronomy, Indigenous history and the country’s geography.

Sebastián Lelio brought Chilean cinema to a global audience with films including Gloria and A Fantastic Woman. The latter, starring Daniela Vega, won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film and made transgender representation a central topic in international discussion of Chilean cinema.

Pablo Larraín has built an internationally recognised filmography around political power, trauma and iconic women. His Chilean films include Tony Manero, No, Neruda and Spencer. His production company, Fabula, has also been a major force in Chilean and international screen production.

Other filmmakers and public institutions

Other important filmmakers include Alicia Scherson, associated with literary adaptation, urban narratives and women’s perspectives. Maite Alberdi’s documentaries achieved major international distribution and Academy Award recognition. Dominga Ortúzar, Christopher Murray, Alejandro Fernández Almendras and Marialy Rivas represent the diversity of contemporary Chilean filmmaking.

The Ministry of Cultures oversees the Council of Art and the Audiovisual Industry, whose mandate includes the development, financing, dissemination, protection and preservation of national audiovisual works and industry. This public structure helps explain why Chilean documentary and fiction film have achieved unusual international authority despite a small domestic market.

Visual artists, sport icons and media figures

Chile culture extends beyond music, literature and film into visual art, sport and media. Violeta Parra herself was a visual artist, and her work connects folk traditions to modern art. The Centro Cultural Gabriela Mistral is a major public cultural space in Santiago. The Centro Cultural Palacio La Moneda is also a central institution.

Sport is a powerful cultural force in Chile. Football and tennis have produced national icons whose fame crosses borders. The National Stadium, beyond its political history, remains a key venue for sport and mass events. Sport icons are not only athletes; they are cultural figures who shape national pride, media narratives and international perceptions of Chile.

Influential media figures include National Prize winners who shape public debate. These figures connect journalism, literature, human rights and cultural memory, showing how Chile culture is inseparable from public argument.

Festivals and the cultural economy in 2026

Chile’s festival calendar is dense and politically meaningful. The first Festival of Music, Human Rights, Democracy and Art at the National Stadium in 2026 brought together musicians, writers and journalists around memory and democracy. Chilean Music Day on 4 October extends across all 16 regions. Rockódromo remains a public festival and professionalisation platform with an internationalisation focus.

The cultural economy is substantial. In 2024, according to the National Statistics Institute, 75.4% of people participated in at least one cultural activity during the previous 12 months. The same year saw 9,013 ISBN-registered books.

The 2026 Fondos Cultura call awarded CLP 43,755 million to 2,615 cultural, artistic and heritage projects. Of this, CLP 27,063 million went to 1,726 projects outside the Metropolitan Region, representing 66.0% of funding and 61.9% of selected projects. In the Valparaíso Region alone, the Ministry of Cultures announced 401 projects receiving CLP 6,008,286,599 in total funding.

The cultural-sector sales index for artistic, entertainment and recreational activities increased 12.5% year-on-year in February 2026, with a cumulative increase of 13.1% through that month, according to INE. Tourism accommodation data for August 2026 recorded 1,696,082 overnight stays.

Chile’s participation in the Frankfurt Book Fair makes the responsible minister and the ministry’s cultural-diplomacy officials relevant to an October 2026 culture profile. This international presence matters because Chile culture is increasingly an export sector, not only a domestic conversation.

What Chile culture means for foreigners, expats and investors

For foreigners and expats, Chile culture is a practical lens on everyday life. Knowing Violeta Parra and Víctor Jara helps you understand why certain songs, places and dates carry weight. Knowing the debate around Pablo Neruda helps you read how Chile negotiates prestige and accountability. Knowing the festival calendar helps you plan participation, not just observation.

For investors, the cultural sector is measurable. The 2026 Fondos Cultura allocation of CLP 43,755 million shows public commitment to decentralised funding. The cultural-sector sales index rising 12.5% year-on-year in February 2026 suggests a recovering creative economy. The development of a Cultural Satellite Account, using Central Bank supply and use tables, signals that culture is being treated as an economic sector, not a subsidy.

There are open questions. Public funding for culture remains contested, and the available official record shows inconsistencies in identifying the presidency and Central Bank governorship as of October 2026. Cultural prestige is increasingly examined alongside personal conduct. For anyone engaging with Chile culture, the task is not to memorise names but to understand the arguments those names carry.

What to watch in Chile culture

Watch the festival calendar. Chilean Music Day on 4 October, the MUDA festival at the National Stadium, and Rockódromo are recurring platforms where memory, music and public policy meet. Watch the Frankfurt Book Fair presence, which signals how Chile positions its literary exports.

Watch the institutional layer. The Ministry of Cultures, the Council for the Promotion of National Music, and the Council of Art and the Audiovisual Industry shape who gets funded and what gets preserved. Watch the cultural economy data from INE, especially the cultural-sector sales index and the Cultural Satellite Account, to see whether culture is treated as a growth sector or a cost.

Watch the debates. The contested legacy of Pablo Neruda, the political memory carried by nueva canción, and the rise of urban music all show that Chile culture is not settled. It is a living argument about who Chileans are, what they remember, and what they want to become.

Related reading: Chile Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026; Chile Geopolitics Explained 2026; Chile and Its Neighbours Explained for 2026; more from Chile.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the most important figures in Chile culture?

Violeta Parra and Víctor Jara anchor musical and political memory. Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda are the Nobel laureates of literature. Roberto Bolaño, Isabel Allende and Alejandro Zambra lead contemporary writing. In film, Patricio Guzmán, Sebastián Lelio and Pablo Larraín define international recognition. In music, Ana Tijoux, Mon Laferte and Pablo Chill-E represent the current scene.

What is nueva canción and why does it matter?

Nueva canción is a Chilean musical movement that combines folk forms, social criticism and democratic politics. It became globally associated with the Popular Unity period, the 1973 coup and exile. Figures like Víctor Jara, Quilapayún and Inti-Illimani made it an international symbol of Chilean resistance and memory.

How big is the cultural sector in Chile?

In 2024, 75.4% of people participated in at least one cultural activity, and 9,013 books were registered with ISBN, according to INE. The 2026 Fondos Cultura call awarded CLP 43,755 million to 2,615 projects. The cultural-sector sales index rose 12.5% year-on-year in February 2026.

Why is Pablo Neruda controversial?

Pablo Neruda is Chile’s most globally recognised poet, but allegations concerning sexual violence and the treatment of women have changed how institutions, readers and younger writers discuss him. His case illustrates a wider Chilean debate about cultural prestige and personal conduct.

What are the main cultural festivals in Chile?

Chilean Music Day on 4 October extends across all 16 regions. The Festival of Music, Human Rights, Democracy and Art at the National Stadium brings together musicians, writers and journalists. Rockódromo is a public festival and professionalisation platform with an internationalisation focus.

How does Chile fund culture?

The Ministry of the Cultures, the Arts and Heritage runs the Fondos Cultura programme. In 2026, it awarded CLP 43,755 million to 2,615 projects, with 66.0% of funding going outside the Metropolitan Region. The ministry also supports music through Law No. 19,928 and the Council for the Promotion of National Music.

What should foreigners know about Chilean cinema?

Patricio Guzmán’s documentaries established Chile’s international authority in political film. Sebastián Lelio’s A Fantastic Woman won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Pablo Larraín’s films about power and trauma, produced through Fabula, have made Chilean cinema globally recognised.

World.title: Argentina Foreign Powers and Investors in 2026
World.content:
ARGENTINA · FOREIGN CAPITAL

Key Facts — What it is The web of lenders, companies and governments that supply most of Argentina’s external capital and shape its economic policy.

— Why it matters Foreign money funds energy, mining and infrastructure, but it also carries conditions on exchange rates, tariffs and reform.

— The numbers The IMF approved a US$20 billion facility in April 2025.

— The catch Capital controls still limit repatriation for some investors, and the timing of full liberalisation depends on economic conditions.

— Who is who China leads in lithium and infrastructure; the IMF and World Bank anchor stabilisation.

— What it means for you A foreigner can invest, work or trade here, but must first understand who controls the money and what they demand in return.

Argentina foreign capital in 2026 is a three-way contest between Washington, Beijing and multilateral lenders, each offering money in exchange for reform, resources or strategic alignment. Understanding who brings what, and what they want back, is the key to reading the country’s economy.

Argentina is South America’s second-largest economy and a major exporter of grains, beef, lithium and, increasingly, shale gas. This guide explains the foreign powers and investors that finance its stabilisation and its long-term bets.

The Andes divide Argentina from Chile, forming the backbone of South America's western edge. (File photo)

The IMF and World Bank: Stabilisation in Exchange for Reform

The International Monetary Fund is Argentina’s most important external anchor. Its main instrument is a 48-month Extended Fund Facility approved in April 2025 for US$20 billion.

This is not project finance. The IMF provides balance-of-payments support and reserves while requiring fiscal, monetary and structural commitments. Argentina receives foreign currency and improved access to private capital. The IMF seeks fiscal consolidation, monetary discipline, reserve accumulation and progress toward a normal foreign-exchange regime.

The United States’ 2026 investment-climate assessment states that the IMF completed a second review in May 2026, allowing a US$1 billion disbursement. The programme was moving to semiannual reviews through 2029, with approximately US$700 million associated with each of the remaining seven reviews.

A runoff follows if no one tops 50%” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The World Bank plays a complementary role. It says Argentina’s economy is driven by macroeconomic stability, energy investment and agribusiness. The Bank had provided US$1.5 billion in budget support and, in June 2026, approved a Country Partnership Framework through 2033 focused on private-sector-led growth and sustainable employment.

The World Bank was also working on a guarantee of up to US$2 billion to help refinance part of Argentina’s debt and reduce financing costs. The proposal was still subject to approval by the Bank’s executive board when announced in April. The bargain is institutional: budget support and guarantees in return for reforms, project execution and social-protection measures.

The Rio Manso in Argentine Patagonia, a pristine river running through the region's abundant natural resources. (File photo)

The United States: Largest Investor and Political Partner

The U.S. government’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement describes the investment climate for U.S. companies in Argentina.

Argentina and the United States signed an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment in Washington, according to Argentina’s Centre for International Economics. Argentina and the United States signed an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment in Washington, according to Argentina’s Centre for International Economics.

Washington offers market access, political backing and potential official financing through the Export-Import Bank of the United States and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.

The corridor links Argentina’s natural-resource exports to ports, transmission networks, roads, railways and data infrastructure.

U.S. investor concerns remain. The assessment identifies continuing obstacles: remaining foreign-exchange and capital controls, difficulties repatriating funds connected to certain pre-2025 transactions, high taxes, rigid labour legislation and uncertainty over the timing of further currency liberalisation. The timing of further currency liberalisation depended on economic conditions.

China: Lithium, Infrastructure and Strategic Persistence

China remains one of Argentina’s most consequential foreign actors even as President Javier Milei’s government has moved closer politically to Washington. Local reporting summarised by the Buenos Aires Times said Chinese investment in Argentina exceeded US$23 billion, with China financing, constructing or purchasing assets in sectors including Vaca Muerta shale and northern lithium.

China’s model differs from that of the IMF or World Bank. Chinese state-linked banks can provide project or sovereign financing. Chinese companies participate directly as owners, contractors and operators. They seek long-term supply, construction and commercial positions, and projects may be bundled with diplomatic relationships and strategic access.

In May 2026, Argentina’s government approved a joint venture led by Ganfeng Lithium Group to expand a lithium mine in Jujuy, together with Lithium Argentina AG, whose shares trade in the United States, and Argentina’s provincial company Jujuy Energía y Minería Sociedad del Estado, or JEMSE.

The project illustrates the structure of Argentina’s mining economy. Ganfeng brings capital, processing capacity and access to the global battery supply chain. Lithium Argentina brings project ownership and technical capabilities. JEMSE and the province bring public-sector participation and access to the resource. Argentina receives export revenue, royalties, employment and infrastructure.

Argentina’s relationship with China has also involved a renminbi currency-swap arrangement. The swap gives Argentina a source of liquidity and can reduce immediate pressure on dollar reserves, but it creates repayment obligations and deepens financial dependence on Chinese institutions. The strategic tension is that Buenos Aires may want Chinese financing and trade while Washington prefers reduced Chinese influence in sensitive infrastructure, telecommunications, energy and minerals.

Buenos Aires at sunset, capital of Argentina and centre of the nation's economic and political power. Photo: Michelle Maria, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Energy: The Largest Foreign-Capital Opportunity

Energy is the principal arena in which foreign capital, national policy and geopolitical competition converge. State energy company YPF is developing the “Argentina LNG” project, backed by Eni and XRG.

The project would be among the largest foreign-linked investment programmes in Argentine history. Its importance rests on four connected assets: Vaca Muerta’s shale gas, pipelines to the coast, liquefaction facilities and long-term LNG export contracts. Foreign participants bring capital, engineering, LNG expertise and access to buyers.

The RIGI regime is designed to make very large, long-term projects more bankable through tax, customs and foreign-exchange protections. Its attraction is strongest in capital-intensive sectors where investors must commit billions before revenue begins. The RIGI regime is designed to make very large, long-term projects more bankable through tax, customs and foreign-exchange protections.

In July 2026, the government announced that U.S.-Argentine company Meitner Energy would invest in a 300-megawatt modular reactor at the Atucha site. This project connects foreign investment with Argentina’s nuclear capabilities and with the global race to commercialise small modular reactors.

European companies remain important. The Argentina LNG plan involves Eni, Italy’s major energy company, and XRG, the international investment arm associated with the United Arab Emirates’ energy interests. Eni brings upstream gas, project development and LNG expertise. XRG brings international energy investment, capital and access to global commercial networks.

The Rules of the Game: Capital Controls and Repatriation

Argentina’s foreign-exchange framework generally permits foreign investment, but repatriation by nonresidents remains subject to specific exemptions and, in other cases, prior approval from the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic, known as the BCRA.

Under the BCRA’s foreign-trade and exchange rules, nonresidents generally require prior BCRA approval to access the foreign-exchange market for repatriation. Prior approval is not required for certain categories, including repatriation of principal and income from portfolio investments in instruments listed on locally authorised markets, unlisted mutual funds composed of those instruments, and sight or term deposits held at Argentine financial institutions.

The BCRA reported that Communication “A” 8226, dated 2025, authorised access to the foreign-exchange market for payment of dividends to nonresident shareholders derived from profits in financial statements for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. Communication “A” 8230 of 16 April 2025 allowed nonresident investors to access the foreign-exchange market without prior approval for repatriation of new investments made and transferred through that market.

The latest official figures show the volatility of flows. Argentina recorded net transactional foreign-direct-investment inflows of US$1.794 billion in the first quarter of 2026.

The BCRA reported US$1.891 billion in distributed profits and dividends in the first quarter of 2026.

What It Means for a Foreigner

For an expat, investor or curious global reader, Argentina foreign capital in 2026 is a system of conditional access. The country offers genuine opportunities in energy, mining, agriculture and digital infrastructure, but the terms are set by lenders and partners who want repayment, reform or resources.

A foreigner considering investment should first understand the foreign-exchange rules. The BCRA’s consolidated rules dated 14 September 2026, incorporating Communication “A” 8481, separately regulate repatriation of direct investments and other foreign-currency purchases by nonresidents. The exact eligibility conditions must be verified through an authorised financial institution because the general framework requires documentary evidence that the transaction is genuine and correctly classified.

The International Finance Corporation, the World Bank Group’s private-sector arm, and IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, are actively partnering with companies investing in Argentine logistics infrastructure, energy and mining. They bring long-term loans, political-risk credibility, environmental and social standards, and the ability to mobilise commercial banks. In return, projects must meet financial, governance, environmental and social requirements.

Japan also remains relevant to Argentine agricultural exports. Japan also remains relevant to Argentine agricultural exports. European, Japanese and Gulf investors generally seek the same core protections as U.S. investors but may be less directly tied to Washington’s geopolitical agenda.

What to Watch

The central question for 2026 and beyond is whether Argentina can complete the transition from stabilisation to sustained private investment. The timing of further currency liberalisation depended on economic conditions. That decision will shape repatriation, dividends and new investment more than any single project announcement.

The IMF programme’s semiannual reviews through 2029 will be key markers. Each review unlocks approximately US$700 million and signals whether Argentina is meeting its fiscal, monetary and structural commitments. A failed review would complicate access to other lenders and private capital.

The Argentina LNG project and the Ganfeng lithium expansion are long-term bets that will take years to produce revenue. Their progress will reveal whether the RIGI regime can deliver the stability that capital-intensive projects require. The Andes–Atlantic Corridor initiative will test whether U.S. strategic interest translates into concrete infrastructure financing.

Finally, watch the balance between Washington and Beijing. Argentina wants Chinese financing and trade while the United States prefers reduced Chinese influence in sensitive sectors. How Buenos Aires manages that tension will determine the shape of Argentina foreign capital for the rest of the decade.

China has financed, constructed or purchased assets in sectors including Vaca Muerta shale and northern lithium.

What is the IMF programme for Argentina?

The IMF approved a 48-month Extended Fund Facility for US$20 billion in April 2025.

Can foreign investors repatriate money from Argentina?

Nonresidents generally require prior approval from the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic to access the foreign-exchange market for repatriation. Certain categories, including portfolio investments in locally listed instruments and new direct investments made through the official market, are exempt from prior approval.

What is the Argentina LNG project?

State energy company YPF is developing the “Argentina LNG” project, backed by Eni and XRG. It would be among the largest foreign-linked investment programmes in Argentine history.

What is the RIGI regime?

RIGI is Argentina’s Special Investment Regime for Large and Medium-Sized Firms. It offers tax, customs and foreign-exchange protections to make very large, long-term projects more bankable. World.title: Flávio Led 15 States, Lula 12 in Brazil’s First Round
World.content:
Neither Flávio Bolsonaro nor President Lula won Brazil’s presidential election outright on Sunday 4 October 2026, so the two meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October. Flávio, a senator for the conservative Liberal Party (PL), has 47.04% of valid votes. Lula, of the leftist Workers’ Party (PT), has 45.15%, according to the Superior Electoral Court (TSE).

Flávio finished first in 15 of the 27 states, including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. Lula finished first in 12, led by the nine states of the Northeast. For US readers, this is a polarised, two-way race over the largest economy in Latin America, with the real and Brazilian stocks next in line to react when markets open on Monday.

Key Facts —Result. Flávio Bolsonaro 47.04% (56,098,129 votes), Lula 45.15% (53,845,563 votes), a gap of 2,252,566 votes or 1.89 points, at 99.96% of polling stations counted (TSE, 22:56 Brasília time on 4 October; 21:56 US Eastern). —Turnout. Abstention was 21.08%, or 33.5 million of 158.7 million registered voters. Blank and null ballots together came to about 6.0 million. —States. Flávio led in 15 states and Lula in 12. Amapá is the closest, with Lula ahead by 225 votes at 100% counted. —Minas Gerais. Flávio leads with 48.24% to Lula’s 43.32% in Brazil’s second-largest electorate, a state that has backed the national winner in the deciding round of every presidential election since 1989. —Governors. Ten are elected, five states go to a governor runoff on 25 October, and twelve are still open in the official count. —Next. Runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026, polls close at 17:00 Brasília time (16:00 US Eastern).

Live map See every state on the live map The official TSE count for president, governors and the Senate, with every candidate’s share and the state map. Open the live results →

How the 27 States Voted

The TSE count shows a country split by region. Each card below lists a region’s states in alphabetical order, with the first-place candidate in bold. Shares are of valid votes.

Northeast: Flávio 0, Lula 9 Alagoas Lula 54.7%, Flávio 40.4% Bahia Lula 66.1%, Flávio 28.6% Ceará Lula 63.3%, Flávio 31.3% Maranhão Lula 64.0%, Flávio 30.9% Paraíba Lula 61.3%, Flávio 33.1% Pernambuco Lula 63.5%, Flávio 31.0% Piauí Lula 71.0%, Flávio 24.1% Rio Grande do Norte Lula 59.8%, Flávio 34.8% Sergipe Lula 62.7%, Flávio 30.6%

South: Flávio 3, Lula 0 Paraná Flávio 59.9%, Lula 31.2% Rio Grande do Sul Flávio 55.6%, Lula 35.7% Santa Catarina Flávio 66.7%, Lula 25.0%

The pattern is clear in the numbers. Lula won all nine Northeast states, with his best result in Piauí (71.0%) and Bahia (66.1%). Flávio won the whole South, the whole Centre-West and the whole Southeast, with his best results in Roraima (71.1%), Rondônia and Santa Catarina.

The North was split: Flávio led in Acre, Rondônia, Roraima and Tocantins, while Lula led in Amapá, Amazonas and Pará. Amapá is the closest state in the country. Lula leads there with 45.71% to Flávio’s 45.67%, a gap of 225 votes with all polling stations counted.

Minas Gerais, the Swing State

Minas Gerais is Brazil’s second-largest electorate, with 16.4 million registered voters, behind only São Paulo. It is also the state analysts watch as a bellwether. On Sunday Flávio won it with 48.24% (5,777,009 votes) to Lula’s 43.32% (5,187,765 votes), a lead of 589,244 votes or 4.9 points, at 99.98% counted.

That is a shift from 2022. Lula carried Minas in that year’s runoff, 50.20% to 49.80%, a margin of roughly 50,000 votes, according to press tallies of the TSE count. Flávio’s lead this time is about 590,000 votes.

History gives the state its reputation. CNN Brasil and the news site ND Mais both report that Minas has backed the eventual national winner in the deciding round of all nine presidential elections since 1989. Minas voted for Fernando Collor in 1989, Fernando Henrique Cardoso in 1994 and 1998, and Lula in 2002 and 2006. It then voted for Dilma Rousseff in 2010 and 2014, Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and Lula in 2022.

The record shows that Minas does not lean one way. The PT candidate won the state in five of the six deciding rounds from 2002 to 2022. The exception was Bolsonaro in 2018. A right-wing lead in the first round is therefore unusual in recent years, but it is not unknown.

Two cautions apply. A first-round lead is not a deciding round, and nine elections are a small sample. The Minas result is the state’s verdict on 4 October, and the runoff on 25 October is open.

Governors: Who Won and Who Faces a Runoff

Brazil elected 27 governors on Sunday. A candidate needs more than half of the valid votes to win in the first round. The TSE marks each race as elected, runoff or not yet decided. Our full state-by-state coverage is in our governors report.

In these states the TSE had not yet marked a winner when we pulled the data. We name the leader and the share counted, and nothing more.

Omar Aziz (PSD, centre-right) leads with 40.6% (99.82% counted), ahead of Professora Maria do Carmo (PL, right), 24.5% Bahia: Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT, left) leads with 55.8% (99.75% counted), ahead of ACM Neto (União Brasil, centre-right), 43.8%

Party directions follow the Rio Times party guide on our live results page. The PL won outright in Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Rondônia and Roraima. The PT leads in Bahia, Ceará and Piauí, and its candidate trails Cleitinho Azevedo of Republicanos by a wide margin in Minas Gerais.

The Senate

Brazilians also chose 54 of the 81 senators on Sunday, two thirds of the chamber. The Senate has no runoff, and the new senators take office in February 2027. The seat-by-seat count is in our Senate report.

Who Is Who

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL, right) is a senator and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Lula (PT, left) is the sitting president, in office since 2023.

Augusto Cury (Avante, centrist) is a psychiatrist and best-selling author who took 2.89%. Renan Santos (Missão, right) co-founded the activist group MBL and took 2.24%. Ronaldo Caiado (PSD, centre-right) is a former governor of Goiás and took 2.18%. Romeu Zema (Novo, pro-market right) is a former governor of Minas Gerais and took 0.27%.

What It Means for the Runoff

The gap is 2,252,566 votes, or 1.89 points. Together Flávio and Lula hold 92.2% of valid votes. All other candidates combined took 7.8%, or about 9.3 million votes, which is more than four times the gap.

Those voters are the pool both campaigns will court. The runoff also arrives with five governor races on the same ballot, in Acre, the Federal District, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro and Tocantins. Whether the 33.5 million people who stayed home vote on 25 October is a second unknown. Our turnout report has the detail, and the runoff explainer covers the rules.

Why It Matters for the US

Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and a major supplier of oil, iron ore, coffee and soy. The real, the Ibovespa stock index and US-listed Brazilian stocks will be the first to show how investors read the result when trading resumes on Monday 5 October.

US investors hold Brazil through ADRs such as Petrobras and Vale and through funds such as the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ). We quote no prices here, because markets were closed when the count was finalised. Our Monday market reports will track the moves.

On the data calendar, the central bank publishes its weekly Focus survey of economists on Monday morning. September inflation (IPCA) follows on Friday 9 October. Both give investors a read on the economy the next president will inherit. The Brazil election guide explains how the system works.

What It Means for You

If you live in or travel to Brazil, the next election day is Sunday 25 October, with polls open from 08:00 to 17:00 Brasília time. Foreign residents who are not naturalised Brazilian citizens cannot vote, but the day can affect transport and security around polling places. Check local notices before you plan.

What Is Not Known

The TSE has not finished the count, so the final figures may move by small amounts. It has not marked a winner in twelve governor races. We have no primary-source report of who the eliminated candidates will back in the runoff, and no way to know how the 33.5 million absent voters will act. We make no forecast.

Who won the first round of Brazil’s presidential election?

Nobody won outright. Flávio Bolsonaro has 47.04% of valid votes and Lula has 45.15%, with 99.96% of polling stations counted, according to the TSE. They meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026.

How many states did Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula win?

Flávio Bolsonaro led in 15 of the 27 states, covering the South, the Centre-West, the Southeast and part of the North. Lula led in 12, including all nine states of the Northeast.

Did Minas Gerais vote for the right?

Flávio Bolsonaro leads Minas Gerais with 48.24% to Lula’s 43.32%, at 99.98% counted. Lula carried the state in the 2022 runoff, and this result is the first-round count, not the final verdict.

Which states will hold a governor runoff on 25 October?

Five: Acre, the Federal District, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro and Tocantins, according to the TSE count.
