World.title: Badenoch ally attacks Burnham’s ‘hope hard enough’ economic message as ‘absolutely mad’
World.content:
Her fierce attack on Burnham’s speech reveals a more combative approach from Badenoch and her shadow cabinet as the conference in Birmingham gets underway. Whately accused the prime minister of having the “wrong political philosophy and understanding of the economy.”

She left little wriggle room when she defended the party’s approach to the triple lock, a state pension increase guarantee introduced by the Tories — and now being tweaked by Burnham to fund a social care overhaul.

Over the weekend, Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Conservatives would commit to the triple lock “for this parliament” — without making an express pledge to keep it in the party’s next manifesto.

But the shadow work and pensions struck a more defiant tone. “Kemi is absolutely dead clear about it,” Whately insisted in her POLITICO interview. “The triple lock is Conservative policy. The answer to the problems that our country faces isn’t to go after pensioners. The answer is to get people working, and the core to my brief is to make savings from the welfare bill where we’ve got seven million people of working age on out-of-work benefits. Let’s get some of those seven million people into work.”

Childcare drive

Whately also defended the Conservative Party’s pledge to offer free childcare to parents earning over £100,000. The current “cliff edge” means parents in England lose out on tens of thousands of pounds of childcare support when they reach this income.

The former Conservative MP Miriam Cates has questioned whether the policy might harm support for parents who want to stay at home rather than get back into the workplace as soon as possible, and risks treating them as “economic units.”

World.title: 4 reasons for Kemi Badenoch to be cheerful — and 3 looming headaches
World.content:
On the upside

1) Badenoch’s personal ratings are on the up

The British public’s view of the Tory leader has improved sharply since she took over.

YouGov polling last month found 32% of voters now have a favorable view of Badenoch, compared to 47% who view her unfavorably.

It’s hardly stirring stuff, but that net rating — of minus 15 — is 20 points higher than a year ago. And that is beginning to vindicate some party strategists’ belief that the more the public sees of Badenoch, the more it likes her.

Robert Jenrick delivers his keynote speech during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 5, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

Badenoch also has no serious internal competitor trying to remove her, following Robert Jenrick’s defection to right-wing populist Reform UK earlier this year. Jenrick narrowly lost the Tory leadership race to Badenoch in 2024, and was widely seen as hankering for her job before his abrupt departure to Nigel Farage’s army.

“Compared to last year when lots of people were sharpening their knives to bring Kemi down, going into this conference the mood is actually very good,” said one Tory adviser, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Kemi has found her voice and is doing well in taking the fight to Labour.”

2) Farage has had a messy summer

The party’s year has also been helped by the trials and tribulations of their chief opponents.

World.title: Meet the 4 lawmakers vying to lead the Green charge in the EU Parliament
World.content:
All four broadly back a shift from pragmatic dealmaking inside the Parliament toward more offensive mobilization, gearing up for a 2029 EU election in which they hope to reverse heavy losses in 2024 , and getting lawmakers out of Parliament and onto the streets.

POLITICO spoke to all the candidates. The vote takes place on Tuesday, with a press conference scheduled for 6.15 p.m. to announce the winners.

Terry Reintke — the continuity candidate

Germany’s Reintke has helped lead the group since 2022 and is widely expected to win one of the two co-chair posts. “I’m quite optimistic, quite confident,” she said in an interview.

Reintke says she believes the Greens can exert influence through pragmatic dealmaking, but also wants to take a more assertive approach.

Terry Reintke takes part in a vote during a plennary session at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on May 20, 2026. | Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images

The group “is really longing to focus more on external communication … to be more outspoken, to be more with the people, to go more outside of the European Parliament, to be more on the ground,” she said, adding that “this is … a sort of politics that I come from, that I was raised with.”

Such a change does not mean removing the Greens from the majority that supports the Commission, Reintke argued. Despite its rightward shift and rollback of green policies, the group can still secure wins by negotiating, she said, citing as an example the EU’s 2040 climate target, which falls short of Green ambitions but remains in place.

World.title: Five days of intense rainfall leave trail of destruction across Crete
World.content:
Five consecutive days of intense rain and thunderstorms have left flooded land, destroyed roads and serious damage in rural areas across much of Crete, an island counted among the Mediterranean's most important tourist destinations.

 

Measurements by the National Observatory of Athens illustrate the volume of rain that fell, mainly on the island's mountainous regions. According to the network of automatic weather stations operated by the Observatory/meteo.gr, 91 millimetres of rain had been recorded by 15:10 on Sunday alone at Xyloskalo, in the Chania region of western Crete, at the entrance to the Samaria Gorge, one of the island's best-known natural attractions.

Daily rainfall in Crete on 4 October 2026. At Samaria-Xyloskalo and at Semprona in Chania 91 millimetres were recorded Εθνικό Αστεροσκοπείο Αθηνών/meteo.gr

One millimetre of rain corresponds to one litre of water per square metre. This means that 91 millimetres is equivalent to 91 litres of water for every square metre of surface. The National Observatory reported that high rainfall totals were being recorded, mainly in Crete's mountains, for a fifth consecutive day.

Even larger amounts of water were measured on the Lasithi Plateau, a fertile upland basin at an altitude of around 840 metres in eastern Crete. According to the head of the Crete Development Organisation, Thodoris Ninos, about 440 millimetres of rain fell in the area in just two days, or roughly 440 litres per square metre.

Damage on the Lasithi Plateau ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ/ΝΙΚΟΣ ΧΑΛΚΙΑΔΑΚΗΣ

He added that average rainfall in the area over four days of the severe weather reached around 470 millimetres, in a region where total annual rainfall normally ranges between 700 and 900 millimetres.

The huge inflow of water was also evident at the Aposelemis dam, about 30 kilometres east of the city of Heraklion, which is a key source of drinking water for the Heraklion urban area and parts of eastern Crete. The reservoir's reserves rose from around 9.26 million cubic metres on 30 September to more than 12.7 million cubic metres on 4 October.

The difference exceeds 3.4 million cubic metres of water in just four days. The Crete Development Organisation estimates that the level may continue to rise, as water from the Lasithi Plateau is still flowing into the reservoir.

Between 1 October and midday on Sunday, the Fire Service received 485 calls across Crete. Crews carried out 96 pump-outs of floodwater and 101 transfers of people to safe locations. An 80-year-old livestock farmer who had gone missing in Karines, in the regional unit of Rethymno, was found dead, and the authorities are investigating the exact circumstances of his death.

The impact was not confined to eastern Crete. Damage was reported in all four of the island's regional units: Chania in the west, Rethymno in the central-west, Heraklion in the centre and Lasithi in the east. Floods and landslides hit mountain villages, farming and livestock areas, as well as stretches of the coast with heavy tourist activity.

Satellite mapping by Copernicus

Greece has activated the European Union's Copernicus Emergency Management Service – Mapping, under activation code EMSR933, to produce maps of the affected areas through the analysis of satellite imagery.

The data will be used by the authorities to map the flooded areas, assess the damage and plan recovery operations. The request was submitted by Greece's civil protection authority and approved by the European Union.

Lasithi: Plateau turned into a lake

The most serious agricultural damage is being reported on the Lasithi Plateau, one of Crete's key farming areas. Large tracts of land were covered by water and mud, rural roads were damaged and potato and vegetable crops were inundated.

Cretalive, citing local figures, reports that around 3,000 tonnes of potatoes and vegetables may have been destroyed and that roughly 85% of the area's crops lie within the affected plain. The final losses have yet to be calculated.

Devastation in Ierapetra, Crete ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ/ΝΙΚΟΣ ΧΑΛΚΙΑΔΑΚΗΣ

On Lasithi's southern coast, Ierapetra and tourist resorts to the east of the town, such as Ferma, Koutsounari, Agia Fotia and Makry Gialos, were hit by torrents and landslides. Roads were blocked or badly damaged, vehicles were swept away and dozens of people had to be moved from hotels and other accommodation to safe locations.

Rethymno: Rivers overflow and destruction in Mylopotamos

In Rethymno, mountainous Mylopotamos was among the areas that took the heaviest hit. In Zoniana, a river burst its banks and the streets turned into torrents, while mud and debris caused damage to homes, the road network and infrastructure.

Between 30 and 40 residents were evacuated from their homes, according to local reports, while damage to the water supply network left villages without water. On the slopes of Mount Psiloritis there were also significant losses of livestock, with farmers reporting dozens of dead or missing animals.

In the municipality of Amari, damage to the road network and continuing difficulties in getting around led to in-person schooling being suspended on Monday.

Heraklion: Damage from the mountains to the tourist coast

In the regional unit of Heraklion, problems were recorded both inland and along the coast. In the municipality of Malevizi, Cretalive reports extensive damage to the rural road network, boreholes and irrigation systems, particularly in mountain settlements.

The impact was also felt on some of the best-known tourist beaches of northern Crete. Nea Kriti reported large quantities of mud, reeds, wood and other debris washed up on the beaches of Ammoudara and Karteros, while in Hersonissos erosion led to the loss of a significant part of the sandy shore.

Chania: Damage in Platanias and people trapped in Samaria

In western Crete, serious damage was recorded in the municipality of Platanias. In Apopigadi and Palaia Roumata, sections of rural roads became impassable, while the mayor of Platanias told the Athens-Macedonian News Agency of damage to roads, water networks, chestnut orchards and livestock facilities. The municipality plans to request that a state of emergency be declared in the area.

A special operation is also under way in the Samaria Gorge. By Sunday evening, eight employees of the National Park remained stranded in a safe spot after the hiking trail turned into a raging torrent. They were in good health, had food, medicines and means of communication, and had been instructed not to attempt to move until the water level dropped.

Government delegation in the affected areas

On Monday an expanded government delegation is travelling to Crete to assess the damage and coordinate recovery efforts. A meeting is scheduled at the Region of Crete headquarters, followed by site inspections in Mylopotamos, Ierapetra and the Lasithi Plateau.

The delegation includes the ministers for Infrastructure and Transport and for Climate Crisis and Civil Protection, along with government officials responsible for agricultural production and natural disaster recovery.

The recording of damage is still under way, particularly in the farming sector and on the road network. In many areas the full picture is expected to emerge only once the waters recede and access has been restored.

World.title: Why ordinary investors struggle to buy into the robotics boom
World.content:
Anyone hoping to bet on robots taking over factories, warehouses and homes runs into the awkward fact that shares of the start-ups at the centre of the frenzy cannot be bought on a stock exchange.

 

What is available is a carmaker betting its future on robots, industrial groups for which robots are one business among many and a new breed of listed funds charging handsomely for access.

Euronews breaks down the options ordinary investors currently have to gain exposure to robotics, and the risks each one carries.

Buying Tesla for the robots

Tesla is currently one prominent route. As Elon Musk said last year, about 80% of the company's value will come from Optimus, its humanoid robot, while its robotaxis add another robotics angle.

Yet, buying Tesla today still mostly means buying a carmaker. Its automotive business generated $20.5 billion (€18.1bn) of its $28.2 billion (€24.9bn) revenue in the second quarter of this year, almost 75%, while Optimus has yet to record any sales.

"By the end of next year, I think we'll be selling humanoid robots to the public," Musk declared at the World Economic Forum in Davos back in January.

Tesla has since begun building the robot at its Fremont plant in California, but Musk has warned that "Optimus production will be extremely slow at first, as everything is new. This is not like making a car."

FILE. Tesla's humanoid robot Optimus distributes popcorn at a Christmas market stall during its presentation at a mall in Berlin, Germany, 20 Dec. 2025 Christoph Soeder/dpa via AP

"Many Tesla investors own the shares to access Elon Musk's entrepreneurial skills. The vehicle sales keep the lights on and help to fund the more adventurous ideas, including robotics," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at UK investment platform AJ Bell, explained to Euronews.

However, that ambition does not come cheap.

"European car manufacturers typically trade on less than 10 times forward earnings. In contrast, Tesla trades on 165 times forward earnings. That suggests a lot of the 'blue sky' element is factored into the shares, and investors are having to pay up for it," Coatsworth said.

Most robots are not humanoids

Humanoids also draw attention out of proportion to their share of the market.

About 7,000 were sold worldwide last year for industrial and professional use, against 603,000 industrial robots installed worldwide, according to the International Federation of Robotics (IFR).

The industrial leaders rarely offer a clean bet either.

Robots made up 44% of sales at Japan's Fanuc in the year to March and only between 7% and 10% of revenue at Swiss-Swedish group ABB in the last two years.

On top of that, rather than list its robotics arm separately as originally planned, ABB agreed to sell it to Japan's SoftBank for $5.4 billion (€4.7bn).

Germany's KUKA left the stock market in 2022 after Chinese appliance maker Midea took full control. Siemens, meanwhile, makes the software and controllers that run automated factories, not the robots.

A listed fund of private robot makers

None of the options mentioned offers a direct stake in the start-ups themselves, and that is the gap RoboStrategy is trying to fill.

The fund, which began trading on the Nasdaq in May under the ticker BOT, holds stakes in private robotics companies and has publicly traded shares, so anyone with a brokerage account can own a slice of its investments.

Well-known robotics start-ups such as Figure AI, Dyna Robotics and Apptronik each made up close to a fifth of its net assets in June.

The fund is run by Andrew Kang, co-founder of crypto investment firm Mechanism Capital, who wrote on X in May that when he first looked at robotics two years earlier, "most venture capitalists I consulted with recommended not to invest in the space."

Sentiment has turned fast since then.

Robotics start-ups had raised $18.8 billion (€16.6bn) this year by mid-June, more than in record-breaking 2025, according to data platform Crunchbase, which tracks information about private and public companies, including start-up funding rounds.

Vehicles like RoboStrategy exist because companies now stay private far longer.

The median US tech company that listed in 2025 was 12 years old, against only four back in 1999, according to University of Florida professor Jay Ritter, who is known as "Mr. IPO" given his more than 40 years of pioneering research into initial public offerings.

In the US, stakes in private companies are largely reserved for wealthy "accredited" investors. Paul Atkins, chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, said in March that this kind of exposure "should not be reserved for those who satisfy a certain wealth threshold or are deemed to be sufficiently sophisticated."

However, access does come at a price, even for these new funds.

RoboStrategy's shares opened at $27.34 on Friday, about 2.4 times the fund's net asset value of $11.35 per share at the end of August. The fund's shares hit a peak of $59 back in May.

"It's a scarcity premium which can happen with a hot investment area [...] investors might feel it is worth paying a premium to invest in RoboStrategy if it means getting early exposure to companies that could be tomorrow's market champions," Coatsworth explained to Euronews.

That premium can shrink fast.

For instance, buyers in early July paid almost four times the value of the underlying assets and have since lost about a quarter of their money, even though net asset value per share rose by 27% over roughly the same period.

Investors also pay a 2.5% annual management fee, with total yearly expenses of almost 4%, and the fund's private stakes are valued on estimates rather than market prices.

FILE. A technician checks a robot after a fall at the end of the 1,500-meter race during the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, China, 23 Aug. 2026 AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim

"An investment in RoboStrategy is speculative and involves a high degree of risk, including the possible loss of your entire investment," the fund warns on its website.

There is a precedent for investors suffering heavy losses as a fund’s premium shrinks.

Destiny Tech100, a fund holding stakes in private firms such as SpaceX and OpenAI, traded at a premium of around 2,000% to its asset value within two weeks of listing on the New York Stock Exchange in 2024. Its shares closed at $99.79 on 8 April that year, but by 12 April they had fallen to $29 — a drop of about 71% in four days.

"It's important for investors to know what they are getting for their money and to realise when they are paying more than the underlying value of assets," Coatsworth cautioned.

Robotics ETFs

Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) generally trade closer to their net asset value, though they mostly hold listed companies. For example, Roundhill's humanoid robotics ETF counted Tesla, Chinese robot maker UBTech and Hyundai among its biggest holdings at the end of June.

"There are several robotics ETFs on the market that trade at net asset value, meaning that investors don't have to settle for the first thing they find," Coatsworth said.

Even when a robot maker does list, it can be out of reach.

For example, China's Unitree soared 460% on its debut in August on Shanghai's tech-focused STAR Market, where foreign investors generally need a special licence to buy newly listed shares.

Until more of the sector's leaders go public, investors wanting a pure bet on robots will pay for it one way or another, through a carmaker, a conglomerate or a premium.

Also remember, we are a journalistic website and aim to provide the best guides, tips and advice from experts. If you rely on the information on this page, then you do so entirely at your own risk.

World.title: Social reckonings and 90s nostalgia: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
World.content:
The dark side of social media takes centre stage in this week's biggest movie release: The Social Reckoning.

 

A dramatisation of the 2021 whistleblower scandal, it tells the story of former Facebook (now Meta) employee Frances Haugen, who leaked documents revealing the company's prioritisation of profits over public health.

At a time when technological anxieties continue to dominate our lives, it's unlikely to be a comforting watch — but at least there's solace to be found in a trip back to the 90s at London's Tate Britain. The museum has put together a nostalgically joyful showcase of the decade's art and fashion in Britain, exploring how they shaped and were shaped by the rebellious culture of the time.

Similarly, 90s pop rock queen Sheryl Crow is releasing a new album that utilises her old school sound in a rallying cry against the divisions of today.

Keep scrolling to find out more about this week's highlights.

Exhibitions

The 90s: Art and Fashion

Juergen Teller, Young Pink Kate London 1998. Juergen Teller, All Rights Reserved / Tate Britain.

When: 8 October 2026 - 14 February 2027

Where: Tate Britain (London, UK)

Beanie Babies, girlbands, pastel-coloured shell suits — the 1990s were an era of many things. But more than anything, they have come to represent a version of life we will never get back.

The last decade before the internet, social media and smartphones took over, the 90s had an unbridled sense of optimism. This is reflected in the art and fashion of that time, with the Young British Artists (YBAs) movement giving rise to rebellious new visions from the likes of Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin, while designers like Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen transformed the runway into theatrical spaces for subversion. This, in turn, shaped the energy and image of the era, which the Tate Britain explores through a diverse collection of iconic photographs, paintings, clothing and more — expertly curated by former editor-in-chief of British Vogue, Edward Enninful OBE. Find out more here.

Christoph Schlingensief: It’s not my problem anymore, deal with your own shit

Christoph Schlingensief, The African Twin Towers, production photo, 2005. Photo © Aino Laberenz / artwork © The Estate of Christoph Schlingensief.

When: 9 October 2026 - 17 January 2027

Where: Gropius Bau (Berlin, Germany)

From satirical gore-films to political performance art, the works of German artist Christoph Schlingensief remain some of the world's most boundary-pushing. By blending his skills in theatre direction, filmmaking and performance art, he consistently created installations that challenged the political and social issues of the time — many of which feel just as relevant today. Sixteen years after his death, the Gropius Bau museum reflects on his works from the late 1990s to the late 2000s, including Schlingensief's remarkable large-scale installation 'Kaprow City', which was originally created in 2006 for a rotating, labyrinthine room.

Bonus highlight: From 9 October, the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris is showcasing more than 250 works from the late French painter Gustave Fayet’s personal art collection. Find out more here.

Movies

The Social Reckoning

Jeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison in 'The Social Reckoning'. © Sony Pictures

Where: Cinemas

When: 9 October

It's been sixteen years since The Social Network came out — a film about Mark Zuckerberg's creation of Facebook and subsequent bitter legal battles. Since then, social media's rot has continued to spread, resulting in lawsuits, safety concerns and growing distrust against the tech billionaires who now harness so much of the world's power and influence. As depressing as all of this is, it also makes for rich sequel material, which Aaron Sorkin (who wrote the previous movie) has now delivered. Starring Mikey Madison (Anora), Jeremy Strong (Succession) and Jeremy Allen White (The Bear), the movie documents the 2021 whistleblower scandal, which saw a Facebook employee leak damning information about the company to the Wall Street Journal.

Bonus highlight: Andrew Garfield stars in The Uprising, a new action-packed drama about the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. It's out in UK cinemas from 9 October, with a staggered rollout across the rest of Europe to follow.

TV series

Carrie

Samantha Sloyan and Summer H. Howell in 'Carrie'. Photo by Liane Hentscher/Liane Hentscher/Prime

Where: Prime Video

When: 7 October

American filmmaker Mike Flanagan has become a trusted source for two things: supernatural TV series and Stephen King movies. Now he's combined the two with a fresh adaptation of King's 'Carrie' — the story of a young, isolated and bullied girl (Summer H. Howell) living with telekinetic powers. Unlike the previous 1976 and 2013 movies, Flanagan's series reportedly expands on King's original story, re-contextualising it to the present day and developing character backstories along with Carrie's supernatural abilities. Perfect spooky season watching.

Bonus highlight: A TV adaptation of John Steinbeck's 1952 novel 'East of Eden' is out now on Netflix, starring Florence Pugh and Mike Faist.

Music

Sheryl Crow: Pick You Up

When: 9 October

If all you wanna do is have some fun, Sheryl Cole has the perfect pick-me-up in the form of Pick You Up — her 13th studio album. The singer, best known for Americana anthems like 'If It Makes You Happy', brings back her warm 90s rock sound to rekindle a sense of optimism in an increasingly anxious world. The album features 7 new tracks, all of which reinforce the power of communal support in hard times.

Bonus highlights: Swedish musician Kristian Matsson, who goes by the stage name The Tallest Man on Earth, is releasing his first new album in three years on 9 October: 'Just Beyond Endless Mountain'.

World.title: US pulls all B-1 bombers from UK airbase at centre of terror probe
World.content:
The United States confirmed Sunday that it has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford, a British airbase at the centre of a counter-terrorism probe after a mysterious security incident last month.

 

Police were called to the base in southwest England on 27 September after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity. The scare forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.

Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but instead "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counter-terrorism police.

A statement from a Pentagon official said Sunday "we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States." The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."

Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.

Six London-based Britons arrested in the incident, including a UK-Iranian dual national, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.

"I wouldn't have done that," US President Donald Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a "foreign actor" was involved. Iran's embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.

Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base. Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.

World.title: Serb separatist politician Milorad Dodik thanks Trump, Putin as he declares victory in contested Bosnia vote
World.content:
The former president of Bosnia's Serb statelet, Milorad Dodik, said his party had retained power in the entity and its seat on the shared presidency, as preliminary results showed a drop in turnout for Bosnia's general elections.

 

Dodik led the declarations for a dizzying number of posts to be decided in the general elections in a complex system that has held the partitioned Balkan country together since the 1995 peace deal.

The key race was for the tripartite presidency, split between Bosnian Muslims or Bosniaks, and the Serb and Croat ethnic groups. Dodik's Serb nationalists ran on a platform of greater autonomy and secessionist rhetoric.

"If it had not been for (US President) Donald Trump's magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today," he told supporters in Banja Luka, in a speech that also thanked his close ally, Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"But now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners," he added.

Zeljka Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) speaks after the publication of general election results, in Banja Luka, Bosnia, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026 Radivoje Pavicic/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

The 67-year-old was not on the ballot after being convicted of overstepping his powers and banned from the presidency for six years.

But he remains a central figure in the Bosnian-Serb Republika Srpska entity.

With 95% of the ballots counted, according to electoral officials, his candidate, Zeljka Cvijanovic, was firmly on track to retain her spot in the presidency.

Meanwhile, Bosniak presidential incumbent Denis Becirovic also claimed victory after results showed him leading a tighter race for his seat.

"A freedom-loving, anti-fascist and civic Bosnia and Herzegovina is alive," Becirovic, from the Social Democrats party, told supporters in Sarajevo.

Denis Becirovic (SDP) poses for a photo with his wife after declaring himself winner of the Bosniak seat of the tripartite Bosnian Presidency in Sarajevo, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026 Armin Durgut/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Bosnian Croat nationalist candidate Darijana Filipovic also claimed victory in her bid for the Croat presidential seat.

Dodik's party was also projected to retain power in the Serb entity's parliament and local presidency by a large margin.

The US-brokered ‘Dayton agreement’ ended the 1992-95 conflict but entrenched divisions that often paralyse decision-making.

It divided Bosnia into two semi-autonomous entities –s the Serb-run RS and a Muslim-Croat federation – linked by a weak central government.

Turnout dropped nearly 10% from the last election in 2022, to around 42% on Sunday, according to official figures.

A man places his ballot into an electronic ballot box during the general election in Sarajevo, Bosnia, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026 Armin Durgut/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

In the Muslim-Croat federation, Becirovic advocates a path toward the European Union and NATO.

But if Dodik's party returns to the presidency, it would almost certainly mean the political deadlock that has blocked the necessary reforms for years would remain.

After two decades in power, Dodik and his party have repeatedly clashed with the country's central authorities and vocally oppose EU membership.

Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform. They want a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.

World.title: Tooth with jade inlay reveals ancient Maya skill as dentists
World.content:
A single molar can provide new clues about the knowledge and skills of the ancient Maya in dentistry. A study published (source in Spanish) in the journal 'Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports' analyses a lower first permanent molar with a jadeite inlay on its surface and concludes that the tooth was modified while the patient was still alive.

 

The tooth belongs to a pre-Hispanic osteological collection at the Popol Vuh Museum of Universidad Francisco Marroquín in Guatemala. The researchers found a well-defined cavity at the point where the four main cusps of the molar meet, in which the jade piece was firmly fixed with a cementing material.

"The cavity is perfect," explains Elma Vega-Lizama, a dental anthropologist at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico and co-author of the study, in comments reported (source in Spanish) by 'National Geographic'. "It is really a good procedure: well executed, clean."

The location of the inlay is particularly significant. Dental modifications documented among the ancient Maya were concentrated mainly in the anterior teeth, such as incisors and canines, and generally had an aesthetic purpose or were linked to social identity. In this case, however, it is a posterior molar, so the researchers rule out the idea that its function was purely ornamental.

To determine whether the intervention had been carried out before or after death, the researchers used cone-beam computed tomography. The images revealed extensive dystrophic calcification of the pulp chamber, a biological response indicating that the tooth was alive when the inlay was placed. In addition, the pulp chamber was well preserved and showed features consistent with a young adult individual.

The authors point out in the article that this find is "the first documented case of an occlusal inlay in a posterior tooth among the ancient Maya", that is, the first documented case of an inlay in the occlusal surface of a posterior tooth among the ancient Maya. The discovery broadens current interpretations of this civilisation's dental knowledge.

The mystery of its purpose

The exact purpose of the intervention, however, remains unclear. The researchers, from Universidad Francisco Marroquín, the Autonomous University of Yucatán and the Popol Vuh Museum, believe it may have had a therapeutic or palliative purpose, although they also leave open the possibility that it formed part of an unusual symbolic practice. The article stresses that it cannot be proved with certainty whether the inlay was used to fill a carious lesion.

The case is particularly striking because, despite the high prevalence of caries and abscesses among Mesoamerican populations, there is little evidence of interventions intended to relieve these conditions. The researchers also recall that the ancient Maya had considerable experience with dental drilling techniques. According to the study, "less than 4% of the drilling reached the pulp chamber".

The tooth analysed is therefore an exceptional case in Maya dental archaeology. For the authors, it shows that dental modifications in this civilisation were more varied than previously thought and underlines the need to continue investigating the more unusual dental interventions of ancient Mesoamerica.

World.title: Coral reefs are bleaching in extreme heat. Could underwater umbrellas save them?
World.content:
Can an umbrella work underwater? The answer appears to be yes, just not for the reason many might imagine.

 

Around the world, marine heatwaves have put coral at risk of excessive heat stress. When ocean temperatures get too hot, stressed corals can expel the microscopic algae that live in their tissues, causing them to turn white and lose their main source of food – a phenomenon known as bleaching that is occurring with alarming frequency.

A group of scientists in Florida believes that underwater umbrellas could mitigate the damage.

“Heat-related coral bleaching is probably the biggest threat to reefs worldwide,” says Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, lead author of a research article published this week in Frontiers in Marine Science. “Solutions like shading can offer temporary protection on small scales.”

How underwater umbrellas protected Florida corals

The study came together after a record-breaking marine heatwave struck the Florida Keys in 2023.

At most sites, every kind of coral bleached, and branching corals – species that grow in tree- or antler-like formations, such as the aptly named staghorn and elkhorn corals – were almost wiped out. At one inshore site, more than half of the corals researchers monitored lost some or all their living tissue.

“This study stemmed directly from that event: we wanted to provide proof of concept for tools to save targeted corals in similar future events,” says Neely.

The following summer, the researchers selected 40 colonies belonging to two species of brain coral in the lower Florida Keys.

Half were left exposed and half were fitted with floating shades made from PVC frames and nylon mesh – like underwater parasols suspended about 30 centimetres above the coral.

The shades, the researchers stress, were not used to cool the water. Instead, they reduced the intense sunlight and ultravioletradiation that can make bleaching worse.

Divers began monitoring the corals in July 2024 and installed the umbrellas in August, when summer heat intensified. They continued until November, when temperatures cooled, tracking changes in their colour and the algae living inside their tissue.

Despite 2024 seeing the second-highest level of heat stress recorded at the site since 1985, some of the shaded corals began to regain their colour after the umbrellas were installed. The exposed corals became paler during the hottest part of the experiment.

But the umbrellas are still a temporary fix, the researchers stress.

Covering entire reefs would be impractical, so they see it primarily as a way to protect vulnerable corals during extreme heat. Ultimately, though, long-term protection depends on limiting the warming of the seas.

“Scaling is the big limitation of this study,” Neely explains. “Shading is not a cure-all.”

Marine heatwaves are bleaching reefs worldwide

Globally, ocean temperatures continue to break records. On 22 August, the average global sea surface temperature outside the polar regions reached 21.1°C, the highest daily temperature recorded.

Meanwhile, extreme heat is hitting coral reefs more often. In August, the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network reported that bleaching events now occur roughly every five to six years, compared with about once a decade in the past.

Although corals can recover from bleaching when sea temperatures cool, frequent marine heatwaves can leave too little time for damaged reefs to repair themselves.

The most recent global bleaching event began in 2023. Between 2023 and 2024, hard coral cover fell by 8.9 per cent globally – the largest one-year decline on record.

By March 2025, 84 per cent of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures hot enough to cause bleaching, while parts of Australia’s Great Barrier Reef recorded their largest annual losses of living coral in almost 40 years of monitoring.

Although coral reefs cover less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, they are vital to life, both underwater and on land.

They provide food and shelter for at least a quarter of all marine species, including many fish caught for food, and are a natural shield for coastlines.

While underwater umbrellas may be able to prevent marine heatwaves, the Florida study suggests they could give these important creatures at least some protection as temperatures rise.

World.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
World.content:
Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.

Yemen's Saudi-backed government on Sunday announced a new military operation to retake territory held by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, as fighting intensified around the key southwestern city of Taiz.

"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.

The announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.

More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.

The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire [FILE: September 27, 2026] Image: Social Media/REUTERS

How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.

A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.

As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.

The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

World.title: India news: Top court to hear petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar
World.content:
Skip next section Supreme Court to hear petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR decisions

10/05/2026 October 5, 2026 Supreme Court to hear petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR decisions

The Supreme Court on Monday is scheduled to hear a batch of pleas seeking the suspension of Election Commission of India chief Gyanesh Kumar over decisions related to the country's controversial voter roll revisions, allegedly taken unilaterally, India media reported.

Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise — called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — which began last year, has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters by striking their names from electoral rolls

Kumar has been under intense public scrutiny after the Indian Express daily reported that two of his fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.

Kumar heads the three-member commission, which has overseen the voter roll revisions.

The Election Commission of India rejects allegations of wrongdoing and says the process removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Opposition parties and critics allege that the changes to voter lists benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.

Kumar is yet to make a comment on the allegations against him.

On Monday, a three-judge bench, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, is expected to hear petitions over the decisions taken by Kumar allegedly without the approval of the two election commissioners.

One of the petitions is seeking a declaration that the chief election commissioner cannot take decisions for the ECI without the concurrence of the other two Election Commissioners, legal news website LiveLaw reported.

The other seeks a revocation of the 14 reported decisions allegedly taken unilaterally, along with the constitution of an independent judicial inquiry commission or a special investigation team headed by a retired judge of the Supreme Court to probe the allegations against Kumar.

The hearing comes afterthousands of protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai over the weekend to demand Kumar's resignation.

World.title: Hundreds of French schools closed amid protests
World.content:
The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. More protests are planned for Tuesday.

Several hundred schools in France will close totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said.

The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation.

France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why are the schools staying closed?

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended" in some "400-500" high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled."

According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday.

Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons."

He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began.

"There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said.

"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added.

Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday.

Several schools have been damaged amid the protests Image: CLPRESS/ABACA/picture alliance

What are the school protesters saying?

The protesting teenagers at French high schools, called lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities.

They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning.

Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.

He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition.

Violent incidents at the school protests

The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters.

More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.

On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat.

Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort.

The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate."

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."

World.title: Middle East oil exports recover to pre-Iran war levels despite Hormuz attacks
World.content:
Gulf crude exports returned to pre-war levels in September, with producers increasingly relying on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers to bypass Hormuz. Iranian exports remain below the pre-war average.

Middle East crude oil exports, excluding Iran, rose back above pre-war levels in late September despite continued attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, according shipping data from trade intelligence firm Kpler .

Exports exceeded the pre-war average of about 18 million barrels per day (bpd) on four days in the final week of September, reaching 19.5 million to 22.5 million bpd, according to the data and analytics platform.

When the Strait of Hormuz closed following the start of the Iran war, the seven-day average non-Iranian crude leaving the region fell by 72% in 10 days, Kpler said.

How was Hormuz bypassed?

The recovery has relied on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers.

In September, about 40% of crude left the Gulf without crossing Hormuz, compared with only 17% before the Iran war.

According to Kpler, more than 70% of the crude changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman in August. In comparison, almost no Gulf crude changed tankers in the Gulf of Oman before the war.

Additionally, Saudi Arabia also increased exports through the Red Sea, while the UAE used its pipeline to Fujairah.

The primary exporters of crude oil in the region were:

Saudi Arabia

the United Arab Emirates

Iraq

Iran, however, remains the major exception, with its exports still well below the pre-war average, primarily due to US policies.

Attacks on ships around Hormuz continue

Meanwhile, attacks on vessels have continued around Hormuz. At least seven incidents have been reported in recent weeks.

On October 1, a tanker, Kazimah III, was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile, according to maritime intelligence firm Marisks. All crew members were evacuated safely.

World.title: US: FBI arrests woman accused of spying for China
World.content:
A California woman was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport, just before departing for China, with the US officials accusing her of spying on Taiwan's president's son.

US officials announced on Sunday that a woman had been arrested by the FBI and accused of spying for China in the United States.

Wanying Z., 34, of Irvine, California, was detained at at Los Angeles International Airport ahead of a scheduled flight to China.

She faces charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

The woman "traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, at the direction of (People's Republic of China) officials, surveilled a close relative of a Taiwanese government official, sending photos, videos and license plate information to those officials," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in an online post.

He added that Z. "coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection."

The woman is due to appear before a Los Angeles federal court on Monday, Essayli wrote.

Wanying Z. was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport before she was set to fly to Shanghai Image: via REUTERS

Who was the alleged target of surveillance?

The FBI said Z. was spying on a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te. While the US agency did not provide the target's name, they later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, who is reportedly a US resident.

In an X post, FBI Director Kash Patel celebrated the arrest, warning foreign adversaries that "America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations."

"Allegedly surveil a foreign leader's family on US soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening," Patel added.

Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party advocate for Taiwan's distinct identity from China. Their statements often irritate Beijing, which considers the island Chinese territory.

While Washington does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, the United States is the island's most important international supporter and supplier of weapons.

World.title: US pulls bombers out of UK's Fairford airbase after arrests
World.content:
Following a suspected terrorist plot targeting the UK's Fairford airbase, the US Air Force withdrew all its B-1 planes from the site.

A week after several men were detained at the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in the UK's Fairford on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks, a Pentagon official announced that the United States had removed its B-1 bombers from the base northwest of London.

On Sunday, aircraft monitoring sites showed the B-1 aircraft flying out of the UK base.

"While operational security precluded us from ​confirming the movement of our assets and forces ​in real-time, ‌we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home ‌stations in the United States," a Pentagon spokesman wrote ‌in ​a statement.

A dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the British airbase used by the US. London previously allowed the Pentagon to fly sorties out of Fairford against Iranian missile sites which were threatening ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the suspected plot

Last Sunday, police were called to a base in southwest England after a local farmer reported a group of men in several vans engaging in "suspicious" activity.

Investigators blocked off the area and called in the bomb disposal teams. However, no explosives were found in the vehicles. Later, the five British nationals arrested in connection to the incident were released on bail.

US President Donald Trump voiced his disappointment over their release.

On Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that Britain had "strong indications" that Iran was involved in a suspected plot targeting the base.

Iran dismissed the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran to discuss the issue.

World.title: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff
World.content:
Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court.

With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term.

With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote, and Lula has 45%. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the country's electoral court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff on October 25.

Commenting on the outcome, Lula said it was "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round."

"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," the 80-year-old said. "I am very good in the knockout stage."

In turn, Bolsonaro said he was "very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government."

Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo..

You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below.

Right gaining momentum in Brazil

Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election.

"He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva.

"The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said.

He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term.

Lula vows to 'defeat the far right'

Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.

Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de Janeiro Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance

The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."

Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.

Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.

"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.

The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final time Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS

Bolsonaro calls for 'change'

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.

He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.

Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if elected Image: Douglas Shineidr/AFP

The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."

"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."

Brazil's 2022 election rematch

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.

Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."

Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."

Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.

Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."

US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019] Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance

What happens next?

Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.

In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.

Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.

In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.

In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.

Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

World.title: Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
World.content:
Bosnia-Herzegovina's three-member presidency is set to be dominated by nationalists from the three major ethnic groups, including Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, backed by disqualified Serb secessionist leader Milorad Dodik.

Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency.

With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities.

Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik, who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska.

Voters queued in Banja Luka and other cities around the country Image: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/picture alliance

With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote.

Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote.

Nationalist and ethnic political division

Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS).

Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat.

Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric.

The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges.

There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them.

The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.

Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months.

What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district.

These entities are further split into several cantons and communities.

The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia.

Milorad Dodik still powerful figure in Republika Srpska

In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot.

Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022.

After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive.

He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners."

Dodik, wants close ‌ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.

What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.

The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.

Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.

Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.

Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.

But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws.

World.title: Reacciones a los decretos de vivienda y las acampadas en directo | Máxima expectación ante la declaración institucional anunciada por Sánchez a las 9.00 en Moncloa
World.content:
El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha anunciado una declaración institucional a las 9.00 en La Moncloa y ha cancelado el resto de su agenda del día. El anuncio ha generado una expectación máxima en el Gobierno y en toda la política española. Todo está listo para que Sánchez aclare sus planes sobre el adelanto electoral que la mayoría del Gobierno y del PSOE dan por hecho después de la derrota de los dos decretos de vivienda. Esta declaración llega después de que el presidente haya mantenido numerosos contactos durante el fin de semana con miembros de su Ejecutivo y líderes socialistas para decidir el curso de la legislatura. El desencadenante ha sido la derrota en el Congreso, el pasado viernes, de los dos decretos elaborados por el Gobierno como respuesta a la movilización social que ha seguido al desahucio en Madrid de una mujer de 87 años, Maricarmen Abascal. Junts tumbó los decretos al unir sus votos a los del PP y Vox y pese a que el Ejecutivo había negociado con los independentistas catalanes parte del contenido. Entre las filas socialistas es mayoritaria la opinión de que Sánchez disuelva ya las Cortes y convoque elecciones lo antes posible. Si lo hiciera este mismo lunes, el decreto podría publicarse en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) al día siguiente. A partir de entonces, empezarían a contarse los 54 días que fija la ley para la jornada electoral, que tendría lugar el 29 de noviembre.

EL PAÍS ofrece de forma gratuita la última hora de la protesta por la vivienda. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete.

World.title: Humanizar la educación ‘online’, o por qué los docentes son más importantes que nunca
World.content:
La formación virtual pivota sobre el profesorado para lograr una mayor oferta de recursos, exprimir las posibilidades de las plataformas y estimular la interacción y la autonomía del alumno

Cuando se habla de educación online, la atención se bifurca habitualmente en dos direcciones íntimamente relacionadas: hacia las posibilidades de la plataforma digital educativa y hacia las posibles dificultades que el alumno afrontará a lo largo de su aprendizaje, desde mantener la atención hasta la frialdad de aprender sin estar rodeado físicamente de otras personas. Sin embargo, todas estas cuestiones dependen, en gran medida, de la capacidad del profesorado en conseguir que la experiencia, de principio a fin, se humanice lo suficiente como para no echar de menos la presencialidad continuada.

Y esa humanización pasa, desde el principio, por intentar que el alumno no se sienta solo ante el contenido. Hay formas: con tutorías telefónicas, videollamadas, mensajes de voz, vídeos personalizados, clases en directo... Como explica la docente Ana Belén Salinas, en esas conversaciones se estrecha la relación y, “de ese modo, conoces a los alumnos un poco más, sabes de dónde partes y cómo puedes ayudarles”.

Ana Belén Salinas, psicopedagoga y profesora en el grupo tecnológico-educativo Educa Edtech. Mónica Martínez Aguilar

Para establecer ese vínculo, el docente tiene que hacer un esfuerzo mucho mayor que en un aula presencial, reconoce Salinas. De hecho, su inteligencia emocional y su empatía son fundamentales para transformar una plataforma en un espacio seguro de aprendizaje. Así lo afirma Ramón Sánchez, compañero de Salinas en el grupo tecnológico-educativo Educa Edtech: “Damos un toque humano y real. Si no, es muy difícil convencer al alumno de la autoridad de los conocimientos”.

Los grandes retos para el docente

Salinas es psicopedagoga y profesora e imparte formaciones relacionadas precisamente con la docencia. Esta granadina de 47 años comenzó en el oficio hace 21, cuando la educación a distancia consistía en enviar por correo libros físicos y cuestionarios que el alumno devolvía por sobre franqueado. “Yo no llevaba portátil a la facultad, vengo de un mundo analógico”, recuerda.

Hoy, es ella la primera que debe seguir aprendiendo para adaptarse a la tecnología que luego servirá para la educación online. Su adaptación pasa por distintas formaciones pero, también, por lo que ha absorbido de compañeros “mucho más jóvenes que nacieron en la época tecnológica”, asevera. “No queda otra: la gente trabaja, tiene que conciliar y quiere seguir aprendiendo. Las clases online son una buena opción y, por suerte, los docentes podemos actualizarnos”.

No todos lo ven así: la resistencia de los docentes al cambio es uno de los principales desafíos en España a los que se enfrentan las instituciones que quieren ofrecer una formación online de calidad, según se puede ver en el siguiente gráfico.

Desafíos de las instituciones educativas para ofrecer formación 'online' de calidad

Una vez que el docente se adecúa al formato y a las plataformas, es él quien debe adaptar las clases a partir de lo aprendido. Y el principal error es pensar que esto consiste simplemente en trasladarlo a la pantalla, como indica Andrea Carolina Rojas, pedagoga infantil y docente en Educa Edtech. “Dar clases en línea tiene su propia metodología: no basta con grabarla o con subir unos contenidos”. Para Rojas, se deben diseñar experiencias de aprendizaje adecuadas para el entorno digital: “Es importante utilizar un lenguaje cercano, facilitar espacios de interacción, dar una retroalimentación personalizada y mostrar disponibilidad para orientar al estudiante”, recomienda.

Andrea Carolina Rojas, pedagoga infantil y docente en Educa Edtech. Mónica Martínez Aguilar

Por toda esta mano humana, insiste en que la tecnología no puede sustituir a un docente: “Al contrario, se valorará todavía más aquello que aporta el profesional, como su capacidad para interpretar contextos, acompañar y tomar decisiones pedagógicas”.

Consejos para aprender ‘online’

Aunque sus virtudes son la flexibilidad, el alumno tiene que conseguir ser constante y continuar motivado para aprovechar al máximo este tipo de formación. Sánchez, docente en la Facultad de Actividad Física y Deporte de la misma institución, ofrece una serie de pautas fundamentales. La primera es crear un horario: “Tienen que organizar qué tiempos tienen disponibles para el aprendizaje y que sean innegociables”. El espacio también ha de ser adecuado, sobre todo, libre de distracciones.

Para facilitar la adherencia a la formación, el alumno debe implicarse y utilizar todas las herramientas a su alcance. Los docentes insisten en que no debe ser un ejercicio pasivo; no se puede considerar que ha habido un aprendizaje real si un alumno se limita a pasar páginas o liquidar un curso en un fin de semana. Requiere tiempo de maduración y reflexión. Además, Sánchez subraya como fundamental que encuentren una vía para aplicar lo teórico en el ámbito práctico o profesional.

Ramón Sánchez, docente en la facultad de Actividad Física y Deporte en Educa Edtech. Mónica Martínez Aguilar

Por último, la comunicación directa: no estancarse ante dudas complejas y utilizar el contacto con el docente para recibir pautas claras que permitan seguir avanzando. “La clave es ese contacto humano, esa capacidad de tranquilizar, de alumbrar los conocimientos”, reflexiona Sánchez. Los docentes de Educa Edtech también se relacionan entre sí. Desarrollan su trabajo en el Edificio Educa Edtech, en Granada, equipados con micrófonos y auriculares. En ese mismo espacio cuentan con cabinas insonorizadas, y es allí donde se recluyen cuando deben impartir una masterclass o realizar una videollamada.

Lo que las empresas valoran

La formación virtual es una alternativa ideal para todo tipo de personas y profesionales, explica Elísabeth San Juan, quien cuenta con más de seis años de experiencia en el área de Business tutorizando formaciones de Recursos Humanos y gestión del talento de Educa Edtech. Sobre todo, para profesionales en activo que necesitan conciliar la vida laboral y personal, para personas que no tienen un acceso fácil a los centros educativos o para quienes quieran libertad. “Son los propios alumnos quienes marcan su ritmo de estudio, adaptando y ajustando el aprendizaje a sus verdaderos intereses”, describe San Juan.

A su vez, responde a una demanda de los empleadores. “Hoy en día las empresas buscan perfiles interesados en aprender de forma continua”, señala esta experta: “Haber realizado formación online demuestra autodisciplina, buena gestión del tiempo, autonomía y competencias digitales, que son cualidades clave en el mercado laboral actual”, insiste. Porque algunas compañías, una vez que el candidato es contratado, implementan itinerarios formativos online que permiten a sus empleados la escalabilidad del aprendizaje y la actualización inmediata de competencias.

“Cursar una formación ‘online’ demuestra autodisciplina, buena gestión del tiempo, autonomía y competencias digitales, cualidades clave en el mercado laboral actual” Elísabeth San Juan Docente en la Facultad de Recursos Humanos en Educa Edtech

Por todo, la formación online no debe entenderse como una alternativa de menor valor a la presencial, como señala Rojas: “Se trata de una modalidad con unas posibilidades propias que, cuando está bien diseñada y acompañada, puede ofrecer una experiencia educativa de gran calidad”.

World.title: Ignacio Calvo de Mora (Bodegas Benjamin de Rothschild & Vega Sicilia): “Mi querida suegra dice que tengo gusto de champán y bolsillo de cerveza”
World.content:
El responsable de la bodega riojana reconoce que un fin de semana perfecto pasa porque el Real Madrid gane al Barça en el Bernabéu

Ignacio Calvo de Mora (Oporto, 53 años) es el director general de Bodegas Benjamin de Rothschild & Vega Sicilia (Macán), el proyecto conjunto con sede en Samaniego (La Rioja) de estas dos familias tan ligadas al mundo del vino.

Pregunta. ¿Cuál es su idea de felicidad perfecta?

Respuesta. Al estar normalmente toda la semana fuera de Madrid, mi felicidad absoluta es quedarme en casa con la familia, salir a pasear con Paco nuestro perro, aperitivo largo con amigos bebiendo alguna copa de Macán y acabar el fin de semana en el Bernabéu ganando al Barcelona.

P. ¿Cuáles son sus aficiones cuando está fuera de la oficina?

R. Mis aficiones actuales preferidas son la de poder probar nuevos vinos y conocer nuevos restaurantes en diferentes pueblos o ciudades, ya sea en familia o con amigos.

P. ¿Cuántas horas necesita dormir para sentirse bien?

R. Al hacerme mayor tristemente cada vez duermo menos, pero mínimo necesito seis o siete horas.

P. ¿Qué aplicaciones son las que más usa en su teléfono móvil?

R. Infelizmente las relacionadas con el trabajo, desde la movilidad; taxis/Uber en el extranjero, aerolíneas, sin olvidar las de los bancos e IG. A nivel más personal, WhatsApp, Spotify, radio y StepsApp.

P. ¿Qué viaje guarda con más cariño? ¿Qué destinos tiene pendiente?

R. Desde hace unos años estoy viajando mucho por temas comerciales de Macán por los diferentes continentes, y me encantaría poder volver con la familia a alguno de los países para enseñárselos, en especial Japón y Sudáfrica que me fascinaron.

Pero dicho esto, me encanta siempre ir a Portugal, no solo por mi vinculación familiar sino también porque allí lo encuentro todo, gastronomía, familia, playa, golf..

P. ¿Qué grupos o tipo de música no pueden faltar en su play list?

R. Al estar todo el día viajando escucho muchísima y muy variada, me encanta de todo, desde Julio Iglesias, Maria Dolores Pradera, Manzanita, etc hasta Prince, Guns & Roses… pero quizás lo que más acabe por escuchar sea el pop español de los años 80, 90 y 2000.

P. ¿Recomienda algún libro que haya leído recientemente?

R. Acabo de leer “del tirón” una trilogía de Mikel Santiago que tiene lugar en diferentes lugares del país vasco, y me encantó. Eso sí, infelizmente todo ya por eBook porque cada día veo menos.

P. ¿Es aficionado a las series de televisión? ¿Cuáles son sus favoritas?

R. Las veo buscando distracción y simultáneamente con mi mujer. Todas las que sean de suspense, históricas, policiacas o comedia, nos encantan.

P. ¿Qué defecto le gustaría corregir de su personalidad? ¿Y qué virtud destacaría?

R. Mi querida suegra dice que tengo gusto de champan y bolsillo de cerveza, y algo por destacar, sería la lealtad sin duda.

P. ¿Le gusta la gastronomía? ¿Qué restaurantes suele elegir para comidas de negocios? ¿Y para comidas con amigos o familiares?

R. Me apasiona. Y mis restaurantes para todo son sin duda los caseros con producto y a poder ser con algo de cuchara, y tengo la suerte que el que lo tiene todo a nivel superlativo está en La Rioja, La Alameda. En Madrid me encanta De La Riva, Rafa, Horcher para celebrar algo especial y recientemente estuve en Caja de Cerillas que me gustó mucho.

P. ¿Qué consejo le han dado que tiene siempre presente? ¿Qué consejo le gusta dar?

R. Tengo presente todos los que se refieren a preservar los valores, empezando por la familia, siguiendo por la amistad, la educación, la gratitud, el respeto o la cultura del esfuerzo. Y en cierto modo intento también trasladarlos.
