World.title: Croatia Suffer Heaviest Defeat in History in 7-0 Loss to England
World.content:
Croatia hosted England at Rujevica in Rijeka in the third round of Nations League A, Group 3. Both sides went into the match with three points, each having beaten the Czech Republic and lost to Spain. After a win against the Czechs in Prague and a defeat to Spain in Seville, Croatia welcomed England for a 6 pm kickoff, but the evening turned into the darkest in the national team’s history.

Due to a UEFA sanction, no tickets were sold for the match, but the stands were far from empty, as around 6,000 children from primary schools and football academies across Croatia, accompanied by their coaches, turned out to support the Vatreni.

Lineups:

CROATIA: Livaković, Stanišić (Šutalo 76′), Vušković, Gvardiol, Perišić, Modrić (Jakić 56′), Kovačić (yellow card), Baturina (Vlašić 46′), P. Sučić (Mario Pašalić 46′), Ivanović, Musa (Matanović 46′)

ENGLAND: Pickford, Quansah, Konsa, Guehi, Hall (Gibbs-White 80′), Anderson (Lewis-Skelly 80′), Scott (Garner 69′), Saka, Gordon (Eze 69′), Bellingham, Kane (Rogers 69′)



Match report

German referee Sven Jablonski got the match underway, and England threatened from the start, with Livaković ready for Gordon’s third-minute effort. The visitors took the lead in the eighth minute after Joško Gvardiol played a loose pass into the middle. England pounced, and Jude Bellingham slipped in an unmarked Kane. The England captain had time to compose himself and lifted the ball over Livaković from around ten meters to make it 1-0.

By the 20th minute, England were in total control, with Croatia unable to get out of their own half. A minute later, England struck again, this time through Bellingham. Livaković denied Gordon a sitter in the 25th minute, and at the half-hour mark Croatia were still searching for their first attempt on the England goal. In the 35th minute, Perišić delivered a good cross into the box, but Pickford punched clear.

England crowned their dominance with a third goal in the 39th minute, as Gordon finally beat his club teammate Livaković at the third attempt. Croatia registered their first shot on target in the 41st minute from a Stanišić cross, though it posed no danger to England. Moments later came Croatia’s first real chance, but after weaving through the English defence, Kovačić’s finish lacked accuracy.

England added a fourth right on the stroke of half-time. In the 45th minute, Bellingham crossed from the left to find Bukayo Saka completely alone five meters out, and the Arsenal forward had no trouble making it 4-0. Just one minute of stoppage time was added, and Croatia went into the break completely powerless after England’s show of strength at Rujevica.

Croatia made three changes at half-time, with Musa, Baturina and Petar Sučić staying in the dressing room and Matanović, Vlašić and Mario Pašalić coming on. Matanović nearly made an immediate impact in the 48th minute with a powerful strike from distance that flew just wide of the post. But the nightmare continued in the 53rd minute, when Kane grabbed his second of the night to make it 5-0.

Bellingham was off target with another England chance in the 56th minute, and Croatia captain Luka Modrić then made way for Kristijan Jakić. Croatia won their first corner of the match in the 62nd minute, but Pickford claimed Perišić’s delivery. In the 68th minute, Saka netted his second to put England 6-0 up, and Kovačić was shown a yellow card shortly after.

England manager Thomas Tuchel made a triple change in the 69th minute, bringing off Kane, Scott and Gordon for Rogers, Garner and Eze. Croatia brought on Šutalo for Stanišić in the 76th minute, while England replaced Hall and Anderson with Gibbs-White and Lewis-Skelly in the 80th.

Croatia’s heaviest ever defeat had been the 6-0 loss to Spain in the 2018 Nations League, and that record came under threat in the 72nd minute when Saka nearly added a seventh. Croatia brought on Šutalo for Stanišić in the 76th minute, while England replaced Hall and Anderson with Gibbs-White and Lewis-Skelly in the 80th.

Croatia’s players were left fuming in the 83rd minute when Franjo Ivanović went down in the box after a challenge from Konsa, but referee Jablonski waved away their penalty appeals. Four minutes later, the record was gone. In the 87th minute, Morgan Rogers collected a long ball from Bellingham in the Croatian half, raced clear on the counter, sent Livaković the wrong way and slotted home to make it 7-0, the heaviest defeat in Croatia’s history.

Croatia meets Spain next on Tuesday at Poljud.

World.title: Zadar Connected Year-Round: Winter Flights to Munich Confirmed, Expansion to Paris, London or Venice
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – Zadar is set to become connected year-round, with winter flights to Munich now confirmed, and expansion to Paris, London or Venice being actively eyed.

The new year-round air route between Zadar and Munich should be only the beginning of the further expansion of Zadar’s air connectivity with Europe, County Prefect Josip Bilaver said in response to journalists’ questions after a working meeting at the Zadar County House with Croatian Roads Management Board President Ivica Budimir and associates. O23 reports how Bilaver recalled that the possibility of introducing a year-round connection was announced about a year ago, and that operations during the winter months have now also been confirmed. He emphasised that the first reactions from citizens have been extremely positive.

“Munich is a major international air hub from which you can continue travelling practically to the entire world. Our wish is to have more such routes and we believe this should only be the beginning,” Bilaver said. He added that talks have already been held with other airlines, as well as with Croatia Airlines, and that further expansion of the year-round route offer is expected next year.

“As a county, together with the tourist boards, cities and municipalities and the tourism sector, we are ready to support such projects. Representatives of the tourism sector already several months ago expressed their readiness to participate in co-financing the routes. When we have concrete routes and proposals, we will also discuss concrete amounts,” the Prefect announced. He stressed that year-round air connectivity is important not only for tourism, but also for better connecting the residents of Zadar County with the rest of Europe and indeed the world.

“A good indicator will be precisely the Munich route, for which we expect good occupancy. After that we will see whether there is a possibility of connecting Zadar with some other major European centre. Split, for example, has a connection with Rome, but I believe there is no need for us to compete with them on the same route in the winter period. I would like Zadar to get a connection with some other major European centre such as Venice, Paris or London and thus further expand its year-round connectivity,” County Prefect Bilaver concluded.

World.title: Railway Mega-Project Would Position Croatia as Important Transit Hub
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – The recently announced and sighed railway mega-project has a high chance of positioning Croatia as an important transit hub.

The future Adriatic-Ionian railway corridor would bring many benefits, and its importance is also recognised by the European Commission. Europe must be better connected, that’s the premise that guided the signatories of the initiative “Adriatic-Ionian Railway Corridor. Transport Connectivity is deemed to be the Foundation of Development and Resilience”, and finalising the documents, the first step has been taken towards a future railway corridor that will connect Italy, Slovenia and Croatia with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania and Greece. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that Croatia could benefit greatly in this story, as the new corridor would specifically link Trieste, Koper, Rijeka, Zadar, Šibenik, Split, Ploče, Bar, Durrës and Greek centres along the Adriatic-Ionian route.

better connectivity for all

The initiative was signed on Friday by Member of the European Parliament and member of the Committee on Transport and Tourism Nikolina Brnjac, Zadar County Prefect Josip Bilaver, representatives of the coastal counties, and State Secretary in the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure Žarko Tušek. The aim of the initiative, it was said at the conference, is to better connect Croatia by rail with neighbouring countries and the rest of the Adriatic-Ionian region and to encourage joint investments in transport infrastructure, Hina reports.

“I don’t even need to say how important this is for the railway connection of Ploče, the Port of Ploče, with the ports of Split, Zadar, Šibenik and Rijeka. At the same time, for the first time it would enable the railway connection and financing of Istria County, Kvarner and Dalmatia with the rest of Croatia and with the European network,” said Brnjac, emphasising that the next step is a meeting with stakeholders from the governments of the countries through which the route would pass. The initiative will, she said, also influence the reconstruction of existing railway corridors as well as the construction of new lines. Tušek noted that without a modern railway there can be no strengthening of logistics capacities and position in the TEN-T network. He also highlighted the need to integrate the Istrian railways into the complete Croatian network, adding that study documentation for the Učka railway tunnel is currently being prepared. In this regard, he also announced that next year a tender will be issued for the Učka project, that is, the lowland railway project and the connection of Rijeka to that lowland railway.

financing the future adriatic-ionion corridor

Returning to the Adriatic-Ionian corridor, the question of its financing also needs to be raised. Brnjac said that 81 billion euros of EU money is currently available until the next financial framework, of which 35 billion for transport, 30 for energy and 17.5 for military mobility, and that is why this initiative was launched, working on opening the regulation of the Trans-European Transport Network.

“When the regulation tender is opened, then the Adriatic-Ionian corridor would become an integral corridor and then we can have funds for further financing,” she stressed, noting that the only known deadline is that a large conference on this topic will be organised in the European Parliament at the beginning of next year. More specifically speaking, the final conference is planned in Brussels, when the initiative will be handed over to European Commission Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism Apostolos Tzitzikostas, who, she said, has recognised the importance of this initiative.

All the signatories are aware of the importance of the said corridor for Croatia both in terms of connectivity and tourism, so HŽ Infrastruktura Management Board President Damir Lončarić emphasised that the Adriatic-Ionian railway corridor is a strategic issue for the state. “HŽ Infrastruktura is ready to make a full contribution in terms of expert and operational support for this project,” Lončarić added. The sheer importance of this massive project is further heightened by the security and geopolitical circumstances in Europe, as the war in Ukraine has shown how important alternative and reliable transport routes are for the economy, energy and military mobility. In addition, a more modern railway would enable faster freight transport, relieve road traffic and stronger inclusion of Croatian ports in the international chain.

World.title: Croatian Subjects Found to Have Forever Chemicals in Them Speak Out
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – Croatian subjects found to have so-called forever chemicals in them have spoken out, with one man from Lika having been found with the highest levels of all.

Gospić lawyer Vjekoslav Bušić, better known to the public as one of the founders and prominent representatives of the Citizens’ Initiative “Gospić is Our Home”, revealed in a report by Slobodan Mufic for Index that he has the worst findings among the ten Croatian participants in the study on the presence of PFAS compounds in the blood, also known as “forever chemicals”.

“I spoke with the other participants in the study and it turned out that the highest values of the four long-chain PFAS were found in me, even though I’ve only been living in Gospić for the last three and a half years. Interestingly, my wife is clean as a whistle. Her findings are phenomenally low, and we have practically the same lifestyle habits and eat the same food,” said Bušić.

7 from gospić, one from pula and two from knin

The study was commissioned by the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament. The biological analyses were carried out by the Institute for Occupational Medicine of the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, and the toxicological interpretation of the results was done by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. In addition to the seven people from Gospić, two more from Knin and one person from Pula were tested.

A total of 110 people from Croatia, Italy, Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain, Denmark and Finland took part. Among the participants were also women of reproductive age, residents of areas near the chemical industry and trade union representatives, which shows that this is not a randomly selected representative sample of the European population.

All four analysed long-chain PFAS compounds (PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS and PFOS) were found in all 110 participants. However, in 27 of them, or 25 percent, the sum was above the health-based reference value set by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). Of the ten Croatian participants included in the study, six had a sum above the reference value – that is, 60 percent. The sum of the four long-chain PFAS compounds in the study was compared with the reference concentration of 6.9 nanograms per millilitre of blood. Exceeding that value does not mean that a person will develop a disease, nor does it constitute a diagnosis. It is a health-based reference value linked to EFSA’s assessment of long-term exposure to PFAS compounds and possible effects on the immune system.

Bušić emphasises that he has no reliable explanation for his findings: “It’s difficult for me to assess what the cause could be; I can only speculate. I thought it might be because in the last year and a half I have really often walked around the silos in the former PPK Velebit. Maybe the problem is inhaling those particles – I don’t know myself.”

how dangerous are these forever chemicals?

“On the other hand, toxicologists warn that heavy metals, which were also found in the illegally disposed hazardous waste in Gospić, are in the long term much more toxic and dangerous to human health than those ‘forever chemicals’. In any case, the findings are what they are, but one should not draw some final and alarming conclusions about carcinogenicity from them. It seems to me that all of this is still quite unresearched,” says Bušić, and adds:

“I still believe that I live in one of the cleanest and best-preserved areas in all of Europe. It’s important that it remains so and that the remediation of the waste in Gospić is carried out in the best possible way. And who knows, maybe I ‘picked up’ the PFAS while I was living in Zagreb.” The testing was carried out in the first days of July this year in Brussels. Bušić says that the people from Gospić received a link where they could apply online: “We didn’t even know how many people were participating in the study; in the end we realised that there were ten of us from Croatia. Apart from the seven of us from Gospić, the application of one person from Pula and two people from Knin, also members of an association, was accepted.”

The office of Croatian MEP from the Greens/EFA, Gordan Bosanac, organised the participation of ten Croatian volunteers and their trip to Belgium for blood sampling. In June, Bosanac described the project as a study of people deliberately selected from areas with possible increased exposure to PFAS, for example near landfills or industrial plants.

“Given our situation, this was a good signal that we should perhaps carry out some biomonitoring on a wider circle of people. Especially on those who live relatively close to the silos in Gospić or those who worked at the Rakitovac municipal landfill, where that hazardous waste was also brought. And it would be interesting to see the findings of the people who worked for Josip Šincek, who transported and unloaded that waste,” said Bušić.

Josip Šincek is a Varaždin entrepreneur and the main suspect in the USKOK investigation into illegal waste management; investigators suspect that through related companies he organised the import and transport of plastic, mixed and medical waste from Croatia and abroad. In Gospić, his company operated from 2021 in the former PPK Velebit complex in Bilajska Street, where tens of thousands of tonnes of illegally disposed and partly hazardous waste were later discovered.

World.title: Plenković: Without Government Measures, Inflation Would be 7%
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – PM Andrej Plenković has stated that without government measures, inflation would currently be 7% in Croatia.

The Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) recently published that the year-on-year inflation rate measured by the consumer price index in September amounted to 4.7 percent, and 0.9 percent compared to August. Poslovni reports that it accelerated by 0.5 percentage points compared to August on an annual basis, and by 0.8 percent compared to July.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković warned on Friday after a meeting with Bavarian Prime Minister Markus Söder that without government measures inflation would have been 35 percent higher and would have stood at around seven percent, instead of the 4.7 percent that is the first estimate by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) for September, Hina reports.

The DZS earlier today published that the year-on-year inflation rate measured by the consumer price index in September amounted to 4.7 percent, and 0.9 percent compared to August. It accelerated by 0.5 percentage points compared to August on an annual basis, and by 0.8 percent compared to July. Energy prices had the greatest impact on the rise in inflation, rising by 20.5 percent year-on-year in September, while food, beverages and tobacco rose by only 0.2 percent, and non-food industrial products fell by 1.4 percent.

“What is good is that other segments are going downwards; there we have succeeded with measures in mitigating the growth. Without government measures, the overall inflation rate would have been 35 percent higher – it would have been around seven percent,” Plenković said in response to journalists’ questions.

He also recalled that prices of motor fuels are lower due to the government’s weekly interventions and stated that at the moment blue diesel is 10 cents cheaper, eurosuper 20 cents cheaper, and eurodiesel as much as 32 cents cheaper than the prices that would have been formed without government measures.

He added that there is still room to mitigate the rise in fuel prices through interventions, because Croatia is in good time asking the European Commission for permission to exceptionally lower excise duties even below the minimum threshold set by European regulations. A new government intervention is expected next Monday.

World.title: UK nuclear umbrella comments prompt Estonia defense debate
World.content:
A remark by the head of the Royal Navy about the UK's nuclear umbrella for Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) partners has prompted debate in Estonia over whether it can deliver on regional defense.

Experts say no separate guarantee is being offered, and that conventional capability — not nuclear reassurance — is what matters most for Estonia and the region.

The JEF is a UK-led defense cooperation framework covering the Nordic and Baltic countries, one of its main aims being to strengthen deterrence in the Baltic Sea region. The jointly developed crisis-response measures complement NATO, and the Joint Expeditionary Force is intended to be the first responder in the event of a threat. The UK is the sole nuclear power in the 10-member state JEF.

Royal Marines General Gwyn Jenkins, who is First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff, told "Aktuaalne kaamera": "The Baltic Sea is vital to the UK's security – I draw no distinction between our own territorial waters in the Atlantic or in the North Sea, and in the Baltic; we are all part of the same operational space."

Jenkins recently told Finnish paper Iltalehti that the JEF also offers partner countries its so-called nuclear umbrella. According to security expert Meelis Oidsalu, this does not in fact mean that any separate guarantee is being offered, while the British are not changing their existing nuclear policy.

"There is no actual need for any of that, as their longstanding doctrine provides for the protection of NATO allies, and that public doctrine does not say that this has to be an Article 5 operation. So perhaps we were simply being reminded of something important," Oidsalu said.

Oidsalu added that during periods of attritional warfare or a limited war of conquest, the threshold for using nuclear weapons is very high, hence why the UK should actually focus more on developing conventional capabilities.

"They recently held a defense review, and it found that an enormously large sum of money ultimately goes on funding a questionable nuclear capability, while funding for the army and, to some extent, naval capabilities has been somewhat poor. They have already taken some steps in drone warfare, but not as much as they could," Oidsalu continued.

According to Oidsalu, this also raises the question of how capable the British will be in the future of fulfilling the role as regional military leader.

Reserve Maj. Gen. Neeme Väli likewise said the UK has been constantly plagued by a lack of resources on military matters, and that this had impacted on deployments to Estonia.

"For example, the UK's plans concerning the deployment of a brigade to Estonia changed only a few months ago. Initially, there was talk of an armored brigade, but now entirely different capabilities are being discussed. I personally think this statement is also connected to the fact that there simply are not as many resources as originally planned," Väli told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Former defense minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) was less skeptical, saying: "I would by no means underestimate British capabilities. It is in our interests that they not only say these things but also act on them. And I believe they will."

There are currently 900 British troops in Estonia. The new contingent arriving in Estonia next year will be about 300 personnel larger than the current one. The UK's land deployment to Estonia has been its largest worldwide for several years now.

Estonia is also in talks with France, also a nuclear power but not part of JEF, to join its enhanced nuclear deterrence initiative, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said last month.

World.title: Expert: Russia attacking civilian infrastructure as it has made no front line gains
World.content:
Russia's escalating attacks on Ukraine and threats against the West are signs of its failure to achieve a breakthrough on the battlefield, former ambassador to NATO Jüri Luik tells ERR in an interview.

What do you make of Russia's so-called new approach, with its emphasis on long-range strikes and unrestricted attacks on civilian infrastructure?

First, of course, it shows that Russia has been unable to break through the front line and the Ukrainians are now actually managing to retake territory. So the Russians really have only one option left and that is long-range bombardment. They have also begun bombing civilian targets, which is a war crime.

They are clearly testing whether they can reach a point where the Ukrainians simply surrender because their cities are no longer habitable: bridges are destroyed, reservoirs are destroyed, power plants are destroyed. But it is hard to imagine that actually happening. The bombing will certainly continue, but it will not break the Ukrainians' resolve.

In addition to terrorizing Ukrainian cities, Russia is also trying to exert greater pressure on the West. As part of these attacks on cities, embassies have been warned to leave because it is going to become very dangerous. Then there is all the rhetoric about having arms factories that produce weapons for Ukraine in their sights and using nuclear weapons if necessary. The hybrid attacks being carried out in the West have also become more dangerous. What should we make of all this?

As for the Russians' demand that embassies leave Kyiv, they have actually done this several times already and it is clear that no embassy is going to leave Kyiv because of it. It is a form of propaganda pressure.

If anything, the opposite is true. Chancellor Merz was in Ukraine just yesterday and demonstrated very clearly what he actually thinks of the Russians' threats, particularly given that he also brought an economic delegation and businesspeople with him. It was all a signal to the Russians that we do not take their warnings seriously.

To what extent could this intimidation nevertheless have an effect, for example, on societies in Western or Southern Europe? We have a somewhat different attitude here because we have been hearing threats like these all along, but there have been quite a few alarming articles in the international media in recent months. Could that eventually have an impact? Russia does not even have to do very much itself if we are already frightening ourselves.

There are a great many analyses in the international media that are often completely baseless and interpret one Russian move or another as a threat indicating that some kind of attack on NATO countries is being planned. There is actually no such information. It is simply a case of fear making things seem worse than they are.

Of course, we all have to remain vigilant. And there is no doubt that these articles can influence public opinion. But it seems to me that solidarity among European countries in support of Ukraine remains quite strong at present.

Putin's threats are also very specific — the issue of Kaliningrad, for example. I do not think the general public across Europe necessarily knows exactly what Kaliningrad is or what issues are associated with it. So for now, I do not think this will have a significant impact.

This week, Putin spoke at length about his views at the Valdai Forum. He portrayed the current situation as one in which Russia is under attack and has to defend itself and so on, which turns the logic completely on its head. But there was also an interesting moment when he said Russia had gained 1,300 kilometers of territory during September. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, for example, went so far as to compare the claim to hallucinations because it differs so greatly from what they are actually seeing on the front line. What could that tell us? Is Putin simply trying to portray the situation more favorably or could he himself already be receiving distorted information?

He is certainly trying to portray the situation more favorably. When analyzing the Valdai speech, we also have to bear in mind that much of it was intended for his domestic audience, even though it is said to be aimed at an international audience. In reality, of course, it was disseminated primarily in Russia.

If you look at the speech analytically, there was not very much that was new: Russia is not to blame, Russia was forced to start the war because Russia was threatened and so on. He has essentially been saying this all along; the only question is the exact wording.

Perhaps the accusation about a possible blockade of Kaliningrad and the statement that Russia could use nuclear weapons in response added a new dimension, although Putin has threatened the use of nuclear weapons before as well.

How has the West and NATO responded so far to Russia's increasingly brazen approach?

I think NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte's response was very good. First, he said that NATO is a defensive alliance and, of course, no one intends to attack Kaliningrad militarily. That is completely absurd.

The Russians know that very well, too, because they have simply withdrawn all their forces from Kaliningrad. If they genuinely believed someone intended to attack Kaliningrad, they obviously would not do that.

In fact, we now have this paradoxical situation in which Kaliningrad's location among NATO countries — within NATO's perimeter, so to speak — actually protects Kaliningrad. Not a single Ukrainian drone has struck Kaliningrad. So, paradoxically, the situation is precisely the opposite.

The second point, and a very important one, is what Rutte said about NATO defending every inch of its territory. Whenever the Russians make some kind of threat, it never hurts to reiterate that NATO has Article 5 and that we will defend our territory. And that is what Rutte did.

More generally, though, NATO is a rather blunt instrument. It is designed for war and, naturally, when it comes to everything below the threshold of warfare, NATO as an organization has difficulty determining how to respond. Not every action is something to which you can respond by immediately going to war.

So when it comes to provocations that remain below the Article 5 threshold, NATO cannot do very much directly. NATO member states, however, can. And NATO provides the security framework that allows countries to act more boldly. It also enables them to provide assistance to Ukraine because we have to recognize that if countries were entirely on their own, they would be much more cautious about giving their weapons to Ukraine.

There is still a degree of risk involved, but because collective security exists, each individual country is more willing to give its weapons to Ukraine. So NATO plays a very important role here, but it is not a direct striking force.

When we talk about these increasingly dangerous hybrid attacks — here in Estonia, there was also discussion this week about the Milrem case — how could countries respond to Russia in the face of such attacks?

There are several options and I think some of them are probably not public and fall within the realm of other kinds of activities. But there is, of course, political and diplomatic pressure, as Estonia applied by summoning the Russian chargé d'affaires.

Most importantly, however, there should be more and more support for Ukraine. In Estonia's case, military aid may no longer be particularly noteworthy in itself, but everything we do to urge the European Union to impose sanctions more actively and forcefully and everything we do to restrict the entry of combatants into the European Union — these are all countermeasures in response to these provocations.

And I think the most powerful response actually came from [German Chancellor Friedrich] Merz. Clearly also in response to the Leipzig provocation where there was an attempt to attack civilian aircraft with armed drones, Merz went there and put an enormous military aid package on the table. I think that message in itself was quite significant.

Is there any hope of hearing something about peace talks in the near future or is that essentially a dead issue for the time being?

I think it is essentially a dead issue, although that does not mean there will be no meetings or news about it.

On the one hand, Putin harshly criticized the Europeans, but when it came to the United States, he was much more nuanced and stressed that Russia is interested in negotiations. He also raised one specific issue — the question of Ukrainian neutrality.

That, of course, demonstrates what we have always known: For Putin, the issue is not only Ukraine as a territory, but also what Europe's postwar security system will look like. And we can see that he is already trying to shape it through his statements. This is part of his negotiating tactics, which we naturally have to watch very closely. None of this is in our interests.

World.title: Estonia mulls longer truck driver hours in emergencies to secure supplies
World.content:
The Climate Ministry says it wants truck drivers to be allowed to work longer in emergencies to help prevent disruptions to supplies of essential goods.

Estonia is continuing to prepare for a variety of crises which could affect the country, and the transport sector is included in these preparations.

The ministry is preparing a legislative amendment which would allow professional drivers to work longer hours and take less rest than current law allows in emergency situations. This may be necessary, for example, to ensure supplies of essential goods such as medicines or motor fuel during a crisis.

Priit Tuuna, chief specialist at the Ministry of Climate's roads and railways department, told ERR that Estonia has not faced a situation in recent years in which an exemption from working and rest time requirements has been needed. However, that does not mean the country should not be prepared for such situations, he added.

"The coronavirus period was difficult, but it did not directly create a need for operational intervention on our part. However, if we look at neighboring countries and European Union countries in general, unforeseen situations can arise in which rapid action is needed. Natural disasters have happened, for example, and some countries have suffered major storm damage. In such cases, the need for transport has also risen," Tuuna said.

In such situations, the working and rest time requirements could be relaxed by ministerial regulation. For instance, the daily driving time could be extended, the daily rest period shortened, or the deadline for a driver's next rest period could be postponed.

Though longer working hours also increase driver fatigue and the risk of traffic accidents, the ministry says this temporary risk is still smaller than the harm society would suffer if the supply chain for essential goods were to be disrupted. As is the case right now, employers would still remain primarily responsible for ensuring that employees get sufficient rest during a crisis.

"Even now, under normal circumstances, it is the company's own responsibility to ensure that the way its staff's work is organized does not conflict with the rules laid down by law. If an emergency situation arises, it will also be very clearly specified that, for example, one additional hour of driving is permitted. Both the employer and the driver must then comply with that," Tuuna said.

Kersten Kattai, head of the national road transport association (Eesti Maanteetranspordiliit), said he did not believe there was a significant risk that professional drivers would become excessively fatigued during a crisis, particularly when everyone would likely be on heightened alert.

"We still assume that emergencies are emergencies and that both professional drivers and the people assigning them work will retain their common sense and good judgment," Kattai said.

Under the Estonian Constitution there are two definitions covering a state of emergency and a state of war, plus two lesser tiers; of these latter two, the "Emergency situation" (eriolukord) was declared during the Covid crisis.

World.title: Dmitri Moskovtsev: Citizenship carries deeply personal meaning
World.content:
The meaning of citizenship is deeply personal. For some, it is important that the entire family share the same citizenship; for others, it is about having the opportunity to participate more actively in Estonia's social and political life, Dmitri Moskovtsev writes.

It is easy for us to ask why a person who has lived in Estonia for 10, 20 or more years is still not an Estonian citizen. From the outside, the path may seem simple: learn the language, pass the exams, submit the documents and become a citizen. In reality, it can mean years of studying, paperwork and waiting, as well as significant costs in many cases.

We can see this particularly clearly now in the case of permanent residents of Estonia who are citizens of the Russian Federation and want to become Estonian citizens. In August, the cost of renouncing Russian citizenship rose sharply. While the cost associated with the process could until recently be just over €300, it now costs €2,376.

ERR recently reported on the experience of one new Estonian citizen whose path to Estonian citizenship took nearly three and a half years, with renouncing Russian citizenship taking the most time. They had to wait months for a consular appointment and some of the required documents expired in the meantime.

The high fee, long waits and complicated process are increasingly giving people the impression that renouncing Russian citizenship has been made so difficult that it seems almost insurmountable and that there is no point in even starting the journey toward Estonian citizenship. Our task is to counter this discouraging narrative by showing that, alongside the obstacles, there are also concrete opportunities and support available for applying for Estonian citizenship.

For many people, €2,376 represents several years of savings or simply a sum their family budget cannot afford. Of course, Estonia did not impose this fee. We cannot influence another country's procedures, waiting times or state fees, but that does not make the obstacle any smaller for the person involved. When we discuss why someone is not yet an Estonian citizen, we must also take into account circumstances that depend neither on the Estonian state nor on the applicant's own will.

Not everything can be explained by a lack of desire

In public debate, we occasionally hear that if someone had really wanted Estonian citizenship, they would have obtained it long ago. That may be true for some people, as citizenship is a conscious choice and not all noncitizens living in Estonia want Estonian citizenship. Research shows, however, that the situation cannot be explained simply by a lack of desire.

According to the 2023 Estonian Integration Monitoring survey, 48 percent of permanent residents surveyed who did not have Estonian citizenship wanted to obtain it. Among Russian citizens, the figure was 50 percent. Among residents with undetermined citizenship, it was 60 percent at the time.

A comprehensive study of residents with undetermined citizenship published in 2025 showed an even greater willingness to obtain Estonian citizenship. Given the opportunity, 79 percent of respondents would choose Estonian citizenship, while 65 percent said they were prepared to apply for it. The study also clearly highlighted the obstacles. The most frequently cited barrier was attaining the required B1 level of proficiency in Estonian, but a lack of money and time, age and limited awareness of the process also pose problems.

These figures do not mean that all these people will submit citizenship applications tomorrow, but the desire is not confined to survey responses. Russian citizens submitted 465 applications for Estonian citizenship to the Police and Border Guard Board in 2025, followed by another 217 in the first seven months of 2026.

Next to requirements, we must talk about what citizenship provides

There are specific requirements for applying for Estonian citizenship. Applicants must know Estonian, be familiar with the Constitution and the Citizenship Act and meet the other conditions established by law. Citizenship is a legal relationship between an individual and the state that entails both rights and obligations.

Alongside these requirements, it is also important to talk about what being a citizen means to people personally. In the latest Integration Monitoring survey, people who wanted Estonian citizenship cited the opportunity to participate in Estonian public life and vote in elections as one of its main benefits.

In our work at the Integration Foundation, we see that the meaning of citizenship is deeply personal. For some, it is important that the entire family share the same citizenship; for others, it is about having the opportunity to participate more actively in Estonia's social and political life.

For some, Estonian citizenship provides greater legal certainty as well as the rights and opportunities that come with EU citizenship. For others, becoming an Estonian citizen represents long-awaited confirmation that their legal status finally reflects the reality of their lives: their family, work, home and future are in Estonia.

If we talk more as a society about the value of Estonian citizenship and what it means to be a citizen, it may also give some people an additional incentive to take concrete steps toward citizenship.

Support does not mean lowering the bar

We cannot take the exam for someone or make the decision for them. Nor can we arrange for them to renounce another country's citizenship. What we can do is help them understand the next step in applying for citizenship and what support the Estonian state provides along the way.

It is important to us that people do not give up on the path to citizenship simply because they do not know where to start or what to do next or because the entire process has been portrayed as hopelessly complicated.

The Integration Foundation's role is to make the path to Estonian citizenship as clear and manageable as possible. People can come to us even with beginner-level Estonian and work step by step toward the required proficiency level, receive support in preparing for the citizenship exam and get advice throughout the process. In cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Culture, we provide free language courses, opportunities to practice Estonian and civic education.

In my view, we need to pay more attention to civic education than we have in the past so that residents whose native language is not Estonian have a better understanding of how the Estonian state and society function, the shared information space, national defense and opportunities to participate and have a say in public life.

Behind the requirements, services and statistics, however, we must see the individual: the person who goes to Estonian classes after a day at work, the person preparing for the B1 exam, perhaps not for the first time, the person gathering documents and waiting months for a response from another country's consulate and perhaps also the person who has to find more than €2,000 to renounce their current citizenship.

These efforts should not be taken for granted. When someone becomes an Estonian citizen after a journey lasting years, that choice deserves to be noticed and recognized. Instead of asking, "Why only now?" perhaps we should say: "Welcome to the ranks of Estonian citizens!"

World.title: Object that halted Helsinki–Tallinn ferry traffic turns out harmless
World.content:
An object found in the sea that halted ship traffic from Helsinki on Saturday evening is likely part of an old shipwreck, Finnish authorities said. The shipping lane was reopened overnight.

At 7:20 p.m. Saturday, Finnish police received a report from the Border Guard about a funnel-shaped metal object in the southern part of the Kustaanmiekka Strait, in a shipping lane used by passenger vessels. Police and the Coast Guard then cordoned off the area. Police asked the Finnish Navy for assistance in identifying the object, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported.

Fintraffic, the agency responsible for monitoring maritime traffic, told Finnish news agency STT that the restricted sea area was south of Särkkä and Suomenlinna and west of Vallisaari. Ships arriving at and departing from the Katajanokka terminal and the Olympia Terminal in Helsinki's South Harbor are among those that pass through the area.

Finnish police has ongoing operation in Gulf of Finland since 8pm local time, ferry traffic between Estonia and Finland temporarily stopped as the shipping lane is closed by authorities. Place is near Kustaanmiekka just outside Helsinki, no further info given. https://t.co/Mt9mR3X56Z — Aki H Heikkinen (@akihheikkinen) October 3, 2026

The Finnish Navy, which arrived to identify the object, said its preliminary assessment was that it was a very old mechanical part from a shipwreck. The Helsinki Police Department said in a statement issued at around 2:30 a.m. that the object was not an explosive device.

Authorities lifted the restrictions on the sea area and police left the scene.

The object will be towed to Santahamina for further examination at a later date, Yle reported.

The Viking XPRS' departure from Helsinki was delayed due to the discovery. Source: Viking Line

A passenger aboard Viking Line's XPRS told the newspaper Ilta-Sanomat on Saturday evening that the vessel was unable to depart Helsinki for Tallinn on schedule because of the discovery. The ship was due to depart at 8 p.m., but according to Yle, it did not leave the port until 2 a.m. Sunday.

World.title: Authority recommends removing a third of Jõgeva County manors from protection
World.content:
During a review of manor heritage in Jõgeva County, the National Heritage Board recommended removing one-third of the area's architectural monuments from state protection.

"We reviewed 133 architectural monuments listed as manor heritage. As a result of the assessment, our preliminary proposal is that protection should continue for 85 sites, while state protection should be ended for 48," said Anita Staub, head of the National Heritage Board's built heritage department.

The National Heritage Board has been reviewing and updating its list of monuments since 2023 and Jõgeva County is the first county where manor heritage has also been reviewed as part of a pilot assessment.

Estonia has nearly 5,000 architectural monuments, with manor heritage accounting for more than half of them. Staub said manors in five counties have been reviewed over the past year, with Jõgeva County the first for which the analysis has also been completed.

The National Heritage Board has offered owners advice to help restore valuable protected buildings, but Staub acknowledged that in some cases, properties were added to the list rather arbitrarily.

"For example, during the Soviet era, when the first inventories were carried out, quite a few buildings were placed under protection even though there had actually been no proposal to protect them. I would say that manor heritage was placed under protection very broadly and extensively and in many cases the buildings were already in quite poor condition when they were first protected," she said.

The National Heritage Board's recommendations are not final. The assessment results will be presented to the Jõgeva County community in the coming week and only after that will the board decide which buildings to remove from the list. The assessors themselves do not always agree.

Staub cited Võisiku Manor as an example, saying it prompted heated debate: "Historically, Võisiku Manor has been a very special place. It is also the setting of 'The Czar's Madman,' an important work in Estonia's literary history. However, in the 20th century, the main building in particular was extensively altered and a very large addition was built onto it, significantly affecting the historic setting. Based on our assessment, we are currently proposing that state protection of the buildings in this manor complex be ended."

In addition to Jõgeva County, manor heritage assessments have also been carried out in Pärnu, Lääne, Hiiu and Saare counties. The National Heritage Board plans to gradually review all buildings listed as manor heritage, but the process will take time.

"We are hearing from across Estonia, 'When will you get to our county?' But I have to say that this is a fairly resource- and time-intensive project. It involves different fields; for example, we have also brought in archaeologists because manor heritage is not just about buildings — it often includes archaeological heritage as well. Assessing these five counties alone took 10 months," Staub said.

The goal is to review and assess all manor heritage sites by the end of 2028.

More information about plans for the manor heritage assessment is available on the National Heritage Board's website.

The Jõgeva County report will be presented in Puurmani on Tuesday, October 7.

World.title: Effect of research paper mills enough to start affecting LLM query results
World.content:
Scientific paper mills and AI-generated content are posing a growing threat to research integrity, while retractions reveal only a fraction of the problem, TalTech researcher Anton Sokolov says.

In early September, a Novaator experiment showed how easily co-authorship of a scientific paper can be purchased on the black market from paper mills. With just a few WhatsApp messages, 20 days and $800, it is possible to become an author of a scientific paper ready for publication. But misconduct involving authorship is only one part of a much broader problem concerning the integrity of scientific literature.

After the experiment was published, Anton Sokolov, a doctoral student at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and a researcher at the Tyche Institute, contacted Novaator. As part of his own research, he has taken a closer look at what happens to bogus science once it makes its way into databases. Among the sources Sokolov uses in his research is the Retraction Watch database, which compiles retractions of scientific papers and other cases involving research integrity from around the world.

"If we look at Retraction Watch's public database, there are about 61,000 retracted papers from 2010 to 2025. Currently, about two papers per thousand are retracted each year. The number of retractions shows how much is being cleaned up, not how much garbage remains," Sokolov said.

As part of his research, Sokolov compiled a dataset containing nearly 15,000 retraction records focusing on computer science literature. Analysis of the data showed that violations directly related to authorship accounted for less than 2 percent of cases. "But the small proportion does not mean that authorship is rarely sold. The notice shows what the publisher was able to prove, not how much is actually being sold," he explained.

The latter is precisely what makes the issue difficult for publishers. Such transactions usually take place in private conversations and there is nothing in the published text that unequivocally indicates that authorship was purchased.

For this reason, Sokolov said, retraction notices much more frequently cite problems with peer review. "A single notice usually lists several reasons at once, with peer-review problems cited in about seven out of 10 cases," he added.

Computer-generated content has also become an increasingly serious problem in academia in recent years. According to Sokolov, for example, the most common reason for retractions in computer science and artificial intelligence is computer-generated text, accounting for about one-third of cases.

In 2023, the number of officially retracted scientific papers exceeded 10,000 for the first time. Sokolov said, however, that the figure reveals little about the true prevalence of problematic papers because the vast majority of retracted papers came from large-scale cleanup programs by a handful of academic publishers. "The number of retractions simultaneously measures the problem itself, its detection and classification and a publisher's ability to see cases through to completion — not the actual prevalence of problematic authorship or the use of artificial intelligence," the researcher said.

Cases involving Estonian scientists

Retraction Watch, a website that monitors research integrity, also lists papers co-authored by Estonian researchers. "As of September, there are 13 retractions linked to Estonian institutions and 11 of them involve co-authors from other countries. About half are older cases, involving issues such as duplicate publication or errors in analysis. The rest are more recent, dating from 2023 onward and involve problems with the review of the papers or their data," Sokolov explained.

According to Retraction Watch data, one retraction linked to Estonia is also flagged as involving a paper mill. "But that does not show whether any of the authors here purchased authorship," Sokolov said.

The researcher believes the impact of paper mills could also extend to artificial intelligence systems. Because large language models are trained on material found online and in scientific publications, flawed or manipulated research can also make its way into them. "The risk is real and it has already been measured. In a study published last year, a language model was asked to assess retracted or questionable papers. In more than 6,500 assessments, it did not mention the retraction even once," the researcher said.

The problem is that artificial intelligence may absorb bogus scientific material even before a paper is officially retracted. The publicly available text-screening tool Problematic Paper Screener has flagged tens of thousands of papers as questionable. According to Sokolov's preliminary pilot calculation, more than 20,000 of these papers had not been retracted as of June.

One possible solution, he said, would be to use digital signatures to verify authorship of scientific publications. "At the moment, an author of a scientific paper is simply a name in the text. In Estonia, we use our ID cards to sign contracts and applications; similarly, each author could digitally sign off on their contribution," Sokolov suggested.

He said digital identification of authors and other parties involved in scientific publishing would help increase transparency and make it more difficult to manipulate authorship. "This has not yet been implemented, but we plan to continue this research," he said.

World.title: Cranberry harvest booms in Estonia's bogs as pickers seek extra income
World.content:
Estonia's bogs are full of cranberries this year, and there is no shortage of people eager to pick them. For some, it is a hobby; for others, a chance to earn extra money.

Cranberry pickers say the berries are good this year and plentiful. Even after making the long trip to the Emajõe‑Suursoo bog, you still meet many people who have also come to gather the large red berries.

Most pickers arrive by boat across Lake Peipus.

"Using a boat is convenient: if you pick a lot of cranberries, it's hard to carry them out of the bog. But with a boat, it's easy. The cranberries grow right near the water. You take a potato sack or a sugar sack, throw it into the boat, and haul it out. I think that's the main thing. And besides, boating is pure romance," said Tauno Laasik, initiator of the Peipsi Toit regional food network.

"It's much closer when you come by boat. If you go on foot, you have to walk almost two kilometers across the bog," said cranberry picker Jekaterina.

"For many, this is a hobby, but here at the edge of the bog there are quite a lot of people who pick cranberries to earn a bit of money for the winter. These are serious masters — they can pick 100 liters a day. Then they sell the berries to buyers and earn a decent amount as extra income for winter," Laasik added.

Cranberries. Source: Cjboffoli/Wikimedia Commons

According to Kristel Vilbaste, who has studied cranberries for many years, more and more people prefer to sell their berries directly through social media rather than to collection points.

"I looked at the ads: prices range from €6 to €10. But some people don't notice that the price is listed per liter, not per kilogram. €6 per liter is almost €10 per kilogram. So you should pay close attention to what exactly you're buying. The berries are very good and tasty. We had a lot of rain this year, so they're juicy. And there was enough sun too," Vilbaste said.

She added that because of the large amount of water in the bogs this year, it's best to wear high rubber boots — and not forget a reflector, since berry picking often continues into the dark.

World.title: Colts top Commanders in NFL London game
World.content:
Los Angeles – Indianapolis running back Jonathan Taylor ran for two touchdowns as the Colts defeated the injury-hit Washington Commanders 30-13 on Sunday in the NFL’s latest foray in London.

Taylor had ample opportunity to unveil his London-themed celebration, miming sipping tea after finding the end zone late in the first half at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and again early in the third quarter to give the Colts a 17-6 lead.

“I just think that any time we have an opportunity to put a great product on the field and showcase the game that we love (to) fans all across the world, on the international stage, we always try to put our best foot forward,” Taylor told NFL Network.

“The crowd was electric, the energy was amazing and I can’t wait to come back to London.”

The Commanders, already missing star quarterback Jayden Daniels with a dislocated left elbow, saw veteran backup Marcus Mariota depart with a right knee injury in the opening minutes.

Mariota — who led Washington to an upset win over the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks last week — was replaced by rookie seventh-round draft pick Athan Kaliakmanis.

Kaliakmanis came up with some impressive plays, connecting on passes of 48 and 47 yards, but had an 87-yard TD nullified by a penalty.

The contest was one of nine NFL international games this season and the first of three in London this month.

It launched a Sunday slate that will feature the Las Vegas Raiders hosting the Kansas City Chiefs in a battle of unbeaten AFC West division rivals.

The Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers also put their perfect 3-0 records on the line.

Buffalo quarterback Josh Allen takes a historic rushing touchdown streak into the Bills’ home game against the New England Patriots.

With two rushing TDs in each of the first three games, Allen became the first quarterback to rush for multiple touchdowns in three straight games.

He could become the first player in NFL history — regardless of position — to record multiple rushing TDs in four straight games to start the season.

The 49ers host the Denver Broncos and the Vikings host the Miami Dolphins.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate rises against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar experienced an increase on Sunday in both Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,580.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,579.5 Iraqi dinars on Sunday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,585 Iraqi dinars and 1,575 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate increased, fluctuating between 1,580.5 and 1,580 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars for every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq probes US flag desecration during Sovereignty Day parade
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered on Sunday the formation of an investigative committee in response to an incident in which a US flag was desecrated during the recent parade marking the Sovereignty Day in Baghdad.

The spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed that the individuals involved in the incident had already been arrested.

According to reports, military vehicles of Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) were filmed driving over large US and Israeli flags laid across the roadway during parade processions marking “Sovereignty Day,” which commemorates the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission in Iraq.

The footage gained international attention after US Congressman Joe Wilson shared it on social media, publicly criticizing Iraq’s state sovereignty.

Al-Zaidi, as commander-in-chief, strongly denounced the crime, highlighting the legal and diplomatic need to respect friendly countries’ emblems and authorized foreign embassies.

The prime minister urged the committee to conclude its work quickly so that those involved can face legal responsibility under Iraqi law.

World.title: Spy chief Clayton, the Trump loyalist tech bosses trust on AI
World.content:
Washington – Jay Clayton, Donald Trump’s pick for AI czar, is the nation’s top spy, and a rare figure trusted by both the president and the tech bosses determined to keep the AI boom roaring.

The 60-year-old lawyer, who will keep his post as director of national intelligence, is unlikely to question the central place of artificial intelligence in the US economy, even as opposition to the technology grows among American voters.

“Jay Clayton is a golden asset for the administration because he’s so well respected by tech leaders as well as many in the government,” said Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co, an investment company.

“He is not a typical Beltway bureaucrat,” Ives added, calling the appointment “bullish for the industry because you can’t just have a regular political appointee.”

A regular golf partner of Trump, Clayton entered politics when Trump picked him to lead the Securities and Exchange Commission, the national markets regulator, in 2017.

A longtime Wall Street lawyer at Sullivan & Cromwell, where he represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis, Clayton ran the market regulator without ruffling feathers. He brought cases against crypto companies, an industry that has since become closely aligned with Trump and his family.

His wife, Gretchen Butler Clayton, worked as a wealth manager at Goldman Sachs but stepped down when he joined the government in 2017.

– No David Sacks –

Trump picked Clayton to lead the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York at the start of his second term, where he took on cases dear to the president, including a probe ordered by Trump into ties between prominent Democrats and the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

His office also signed off on controversial subpoenas against New York Times reporters days before his confirmation hearing for the intelligence post. The Senate confirmed him in July.

But Clayton is no David Sacks, the Silicon Valley venture capitalist who held the AI role at the start of Trump’s second term.

Clayton has no technology background, but does hold an engineering degree from the University of Pennsylvania, where he also earned his law degree, as well as an economics degree from the University of Cambridge.

“Jay Clayton doesn’t have the same deep background in technology that Sacks brought to the role, but he has a rich federal resume and significant experience navigating the federal bureaucracy,” said Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“He also seems to be highly in sync with the president’s thinking right now — though of course we have seen plenty of examples of other advisors that started out that way but ultimately fell out of favor,” Mehta added.

Carl Tobias, a law professor at the University of Richmond, said juggling two major jobs would be a challenge, though Trump has handed multiple roles to trusted officials in his second term, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

– National security –

“Jay Clayton ultimately is going to have to do what the president wants,” said Connor Martin, a national security fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

But by giving the AI portfolio to the nation’s top spy, Trump seemed to be accepting arguments that the technology poses real dangers for cybersecurity and is key to the geopolitical rivalry with China, he added.

A tech industry source in Washington said the industry largely welcomed the appointment, but cautioned against expecting major change.

“Jay Clayton is not going to preside over some big regulatory effort,” the source said. “If he brings coherence to the policy, or provides details that bring clarity, those would be wins.”

Clayton will not be the only voice in Trump’s ear on AI, however.

Sacks, along with tech bosses including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, will continue to hold significant sway over how the president approaches the industry.

Elon Musk is also back in Trump’s good graces after their falling out in 2025.

Clayton takes on the role days after tech bosses signed a commitment at the White House to self-police their AI models, an accord Trump called “morally binding.”

Mehta said he expected Clayton to coordinate the government more effectively while sticking to Trump’s goal of not slowing the industry.

“But at the same time, the problems he is facing — like around AI safety and sentiment — are bigger and harder now, and they are happening at a much faster clip,” he said.

World.title: Trump confirms national intelligence chief as new AI czar
World.content:
Washington – US President Donald Trump on Sunday confirmed national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as head of a new White House task force on artificial intelligence, amid increasingly vocal warnings from researchers about the technology’s potential dangers.

Under Clayton, the new Super Intelligence Force — Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence — will ensure that the United States “continue to lead the world” in AI development, the president posted on his Truth Social platform.

Trump said the force had also been tasked to “protect the interests, and improve the lives of all Americans.”

Clayton will become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump’s second term before stepping down.

Sacks continues to advise the president on AI, as does Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Trump said last month he would create an AI force modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal efforts.

A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers’ assets.

He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry.

Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers.

Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.

He has no background in the tech industry.

The appointment would come as AI researchers warn of the technology’s potential dangers, following cases of AI systems going rogue and hacking outside systems.

Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology.

Tech bosses at a White House meeting this week signed a commitment to self-police AI, an accord Trump described as “morally binding.”

Attitudes toward AI have soured in Washington, with lawmakers increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow its development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.

Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which tech giant OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, beginning with a July breach of Hugging Face — a widely used platform for sharing AI models.

Clayton told the Wall Street Journal on Saturday that Trump had insisted the new task force ensure US primacy in the AI field, amid stiff competition from China.

“The risk of not being first is high,” Clayton told the Journal.

“Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people.”

World.title: Iraq’s financial revenues hit $30 billion in seven months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Finance revealed on Sunday that the country’s total revenues reached approximately 39.09 trillion Iraqi dinars (nearly $30 billion) until the end of July 2026, with oil revenues accounting for about 78 percent of total state resources.

The revenues from oil exports totaled over 30.35 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $23.24 billion). In comparison, non-oil revenues amounted to 8.74 trillion Iraqi dinars (nearly $6.7 billion), which represented about 22 percent of the total income.

The figures indicated that total revenues of 39.09 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $30 billion) were offset by total expenditures of approximately 65.42 trillion Iraqi dinars (about $50.09 billion), resulting in a deficit of 26.32 trillion Iraqi dinars ($20.15 billion).

Iraq’s financial revenues between January and April surpassed 31.16 trillion Iraqi dinars ($23.6 billion).

Oil sales during the first four months of 2026 produced 26.12 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $19.9 billion), accounting for 84 percent of overall state income, while non-oil revenues were around 5.04 trillion Iraqi dinars (around $3.84 billion).

Iraq’s significant reliance on oil as the primary source of its national budget exposes the country to vulnerabilities stemming from global crises that impact the oil sector.

The government’s reliance on oil to address the deficit forces it to seek external or internal loans, underscoring its struggle to manage public finances efficiently and revealing a deficiency in developing alternative revenue streams.

World.title: Iran tells US there is no military solution to Middle East war
World.content:
Tehran – Iran’s top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States’ war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.

A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.

The main point of contention remains Iran’s attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday another tanker struck by an unknown projectile.

“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.

“There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he continued, adding “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.

The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.

Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.

The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.

On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz “reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room”, though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.

The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel’s origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.

– Focused on Hormuz –

Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.

Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.

Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Sunday characterised the latest US counterproposal as being “in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues”.

“We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required “an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions”.

The United States and Israel have characterised the war as being necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons — a goal it has long denied pursuing — though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.

The United States has not struck Iran since September 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.

US media outlet Axios reported that Washington has deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to help protect key energy facilities from possible Iranian retaliation.

It also reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group were heading to the Middle East, where they could join two other US carrier strike groups already in the region.

Axios reported that top Trump cabinet members met Friday to discuss the war in Iran, as well as the conflict in Yemen, where the Tehran-backed Houthis have been fighting government forces and attacking Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Russia strikes hit Kyiv as Germany’s Merz visits
World.content:
Kyiv – Russia struck another major bridge in Kyiv on Sunday, soon after Germany’s chancellor arrived on a surprise visit to show European support in the face of an upsurge in attacks.

Air raid sirens blared repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, including as Friedrich Merz met President Volodymyr Zelensky at the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a Russian attack drone on Tuesday.

Zelensky told him that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.

“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” noted Merz.

“These barbarous attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are war crimes that are being committed daily here.”

Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike had damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge — one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of the city over the Dnipro river which have been struck in recent days.

Images posted on messaging channels appeared to show a missile slamming into the structure, sending up a fireball as traffic crossed.

Klitschko has said that Kyiv — largely spared from the devastation wrought near the frontlines in nearly five years of conflict — should now be on a war footing due to the upsurge in attacks.

A spate of round-the-clock attacks has hit residential areas, petrol stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure while near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.

Merz said as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”.

“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he added.

Ukraine wants more Western military support, including advanced interceptors to shoot down Russia’s new fast-moving, jet-powered drones.

On Sunday, Zelensky promised “important agreements”. Government sources in Berlin said they were expected to shake hands on a new package of military support worth more than $1 billion.

It includes combat drones and satellite technology to help Ukraine hit Russian launch sites, as well as for the joint production of anti-jet drones, the German sources said.

“This support addresses the most significant current gap in Ukraine’s air defence system. The impact is expected to be rapid and tangible,” a source said.

– Military support –

Merz this week called for unity against Russia within NATO and the European Union as well as his own country, where the far-right, Moscow-friendly AfD opposition is on the rise.

There have been increasing fears in Europe that it could find itself in Russia’s crosshairs, including from covert attacks, if it is not stopped in Ukraine.

On Saturday, Russia warned foreigners and diplomats to leave Kyiv, saying “massive” new airstrikes would hit the city.

The Russian foreign ministry declared in a statement that “responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning”.

Moscow had issued a similar warning in May, but leaders from countries supporting Ukraine have defied the Russian warnings and continued to make visits.

“The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!” EU ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on X on Sunday.

Mathernova told AFP separately that “nobody is moving”, although European embassies always had contingency plans, including for winter, she added.

Russia has admitted deliberately targeting Ukraine’s energy sector as winter approaches. Last year, similar attacks knocked out power and heating for days on end as temperatures plummeted to -20C.

In Kyiv, which is home to some three million people, residents have begun mulling what to do if that happens again. The government has also suggested that the vulnerable and disabled should consider leaving.

Merz’s trip was expected to announce some 350 million euros to help provide generators, transformer stations and for grid repairs, German government sources said.
