World.title: EDB backs Kazpost’s Islamic financing platform with $100,000 grant
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 5. The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) and Kazpost signed an agreement on developing a pilot digital platform for Islamic financing during the AI & Digital Bridge 2026 forum in Astana, with EDB providing a $100,000 grant for the project.

This was announced by the EDB's press service.

The agreement was signed by EDB Deputy Chairman of the Management Board Ruslan Dalenov and Kazpost Chairman of the Management Board Bekezhan Zhakeev.

The grant will be provided from EDB’s Technical Assistance Fund to develop a digital platform that will allow retail customers to purchase goods online in installments through the Murabaha Islamic financial product, using Kazpost’s international delivery service Keruen.

The project envisages the development of the platform and the methodology required to provide the Islamic financial product, bringing the purchase of goods, financing and delivery together in a single digital solution.

The launch of the platform is expected to expand Kazpost’s financial services and create an additional digital channel for access to Islamic financing for individuals and businesses.

“EDB consistently supports the development of modern financial solutions that expand access to financing and create new opportunities for businesses and people in the region. Together with Kazpost, we are launching a pilot project that combines digital technologies, Islamic financial instruments and the extensive infrastructure of the national operator,” Dalenov said.

Zhakeev said the project would help develop Kazpost’s digital financial services and make access to Islamic financing more convenient for individuals and businesses.

The project is being implemented in cooperation with the Islamic Development Bank Group under a memorandum signed between EDB and the Islamic Development Bank Institute in June 2024.

AI & Digital Bridge 2026 took place on October 1–3 at the EXPO International Exhibition Center in Astana. Organized by the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of Kazakhstan, Astana Hub, and the Astana city administration, the forum has attracted more than 1,500 speakers from over 100 countries, 500+ investors, and 600+ startups.

World.title: Four ways to incorporate fresh asparagus into dinner this week
World.content:
It's the perfect time to be cooking asparagus.

Blossoms and hay fever concerns aside, spring is really about asparagus season. A time for asparagus lovers to rejoice and an annual opportunity for sceptics to get onside.

From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these four recipes will help you embrace those delicious green spears while they are affordable.

One-pot pasta is a speedy weeknight dinner with hardly any washing up. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

With a cooking time of just 15 minutes and minimal prep, this one-pot pasta recipe from Heidi Sze combines about two bunches of asparagus and a lot of staple ingredients.

Lemon and capers will help brighten the dish and either tinned or cooked salmon fillet could be substituted for the tuna, she says.

You can make this vegetarian galette ahead of time and keep it in the fridge for up to three days. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Hetty Lui McKinnon's galette recipe is an unfussy and adaptable vehicle for your favourite spring vegetables.

The corn could be replaced with fresh peas, podded broad beans, green beans, thinly shaved fennel, broccoli, or crunchy sugar snap or snow peas, Hetty says.

And it can be enjoyed either warm or at room temperature, making any leftovers a potentially perfect work lunch candidate.

Hetty Lui McKinnon's hearty sauce transforms a salad into a main meal. (ABC Everyday: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Another recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon, who says this salad is "high on texture and assertive with spring vibes".

If you're not familiar with sauce gribiche, it brings together vinegar, cornichons, capers, mustard and chopped hard-boiled eggs.

"The iconic French sauce is part chunky vinaigrette, part punchy mayonnaise," according to Hetty.

This rich and silky quiche will feed 8-10 people. (ABC News: Thalia Ho)

This quiche recipe from Thalia Ho is simple to assemble and includes beginner-friendly pastry.

Asparagus, lemon and goats' cheese is a tried and tested flavour combination, but Thalia says "you can play around with the filling, depending on taste, craving and what's available".

World.title: Runner honours mother in epic Perth to Sydney relay for DV awareness
World.content:
Running across the Nullarbor every night for two weeks under the unfiltered glow of the Milky Way, Hayden Sumner turned his mind to his mother and other victims of domestic violence.

"I thought back to those victims and the nights they probably go through," he said upon completing an epic cross-country trek from Cottesloe Beach in Perth to Bondi Beach on Sydney's east coast.

"The sun comes up and I get to have a bowl of cereal and a terrible coffee and get on with my day but for them, the struggle doesn't stop."

The group ran from Cottesloe Beach in Perth to Bondi Beach in Sydney. Pictured is runner Jordan Nuks. (Supplied: Project Australia)

As part of Project Australia, Mr Sumner and five other ultra-endurance athletes took part in the 4,000-kilometre relay over 15 days in a bid to raise money and awareness for domestic violence support service Beyond DV.

Athletes ran around the clock, with someone on the move every second of the day and night.

"Whilst running under the Milky Way and the Eyre Highway with no lights around you is incredible … [the nights] were pretty long and grinding," Mr Sumner said.

"Just the monotony of every hour jumping up and putting your shoes on and getting back out there."

In between running shifts, athletes rested and refuelled in one of three support vehicles that accompanied the runners.

Every athlete ran about 666km over two weeks, with each taking part for a different reason.

The athletes ran around the clock for 15 days. Pictured is runner Jamie Hunter. (Supplied: Project Australia)

Mr Sumner said his motivation was his mother, who died by suicide when he was 7 years old.

"As I grew up, I learnt [her death] was largely due to her struggles with domestic violence," he said.

"She had years and years of abusive partners, she was in and out of hospital … so I felt very defenceless when I heard that.

"I was only a little kid. I couldn't do anything then, but I guess I can do something now.

" We can't change the past, but we can try and change the future. "

Mr Sumner ran 785km solo in 2025 in support of advocacy group Beyond DV, which will receive fundraising proceeds from the group's Perth to Sydney relay.

The organisation provides support to women and children affected by domestic violence, including financial literacy programs, employment support and long-term independence strategies.

The runners arrived in Bondi after 15 days on the road. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

At the finish line outside Bondi Pavilion on Monday afternoon, the runners wrapped each other in tearful hugs.

"So do we want to turn around and go back?" runner Katie Brock joked.

Mr Sumner said he "couldn't be more proud" of his running mates.

World.title: Australia's Rugby League World Cup squad is a sign of the changing times
World.content:
The depths of Australia's star power means the Kangaroos will always name squads oozing with class and Kevin Walters's combination for this year's World Cup is no exception.

It's a side with major success stories, young and old and in-between.

James Tedesco's return three years after his last Test caps the 33-year old's resurrection and after he ran the ball to hell and back in the grand final to win the Clive Churchill Medal, there can be no doubt that, at an age where many players best days are only just a memory, he is once again the best fullback in the world.

Walker among six Kangaroos debutants The grand final sides feature in the Kangaroos squad for the Rugby League World Cup, with James Tedesco back in and Sydney's Sam Walker and Newcastle's Bradman Best among six debutants.

The inclusion of Dolphins flyer Jack Bostock, who will almost certainly see a Test debut in the World Cup opener given the side's shortage of wingers, heralds the start of a new generation wearing green and gold.

At 26, David Fifita is no longer a youngster in rugby league terms but his looming Australian debut is both a long time coming and well-earned following his strong finish to the year with Souths.

The one-time prodigy has longed seemed a player of limitless possibilities but only now, eight years after his NRL debut and three years since he last played for Queensland, will he get the chance to be a Kangaroo.

But the Australian squad also reveals the new truths about representative football, that the disconnect between State and Origin and Test matches is wider than ever before and may never be stitched back together again.

The disconnect between Origin and Test football has never been wider. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

It's a process that began with Origin's gradual but unmistakeable rise past Test football as rugby league's biggest stage then continued when a host of players chose to represent Pasifika nations over Australia while retaining their Origin eligibility.

The final change came earlier this year when the NRL allowed players to represent New Zealand or England and still being available for Origin selection.

Both of those eligibility changes reflect the changing face of rugby league and the people who play it and the game is better for them.

But it does require a reset of over a century's worth of thinking that interstate football is the pathway to national selection.

This has not been true for some years now, but there's a reason old habits have a hard time dying.

And while Australia will never be hard up for talent, some of the more eyebrow-raising picks prove this old adage is as antiquated as Kangaroo tours that travel to England by boat.

Robert Toia would have been a walk-up start for Australia but has chosen Tonga. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Not one of the Queensland outside backs is in the side at all. Kalyn Ponga, Robert Toia, Jojo Fifita, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all would be, but they're playing for other nations while Selwyn Cobbo is injured.

That's how we end up with Brisbane's Kotoni Staggs, a fine centre who had a tough year, making the side despite being dropped by New South Wales for the Origin decider after a horror night in Game II at the MCG.

Latrell Mitchell missed the entire series through injury and has only started one match in the past five months but he's made it, while Tom Trbojevic is a likely starter on one wing despite not having played rep football for two years and not playing a match on the flank since 2018.

Tom Trbojevic will play his first Test match in two years. (AAP: Darren England)

Likewise of the 12 men who played in the forwards for New South Wales, only Blayke Brailey, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Cameron Murray have made the squad.

Hudson Young and Payne Haas are both out with injury, but Haumole Olakau'atu and Addin Fonua-Blake will both line up for Tonga while Victor Radley is with England.

So Reuben Cotter makes the squad despite an underwhelming season with the Cowboys and a lacklustre series for Queensland.

His selection over Dolphins hardman Max Plath, who does a similar job with similar attributes whilst offering the same versatility and is coming off a far superior season for club and state, is perhaps the hardest pick to understand.

How Plath became Queensland's newest Origin hero The players who fill the spaces in between the stars are the secret to Queensland's Origin dominance and in Max Plath the Maroons have found yet another player who knows just how to do it.

Plath, along with Newcastle's Fletcher Sharpe and South Sydney's Tallis Duncan can count himself most aggrieved at missing out but it's hard to take up too much issue with Walters's squad, even if it's short of wingers.

This is the hand the Australian coach has been dealt for his final tournament before he departs to take over Super League side St Helens.

The eligibility changes and the fact that Test football misses out on players who pick up injuries during club seasons that are getting longer and longer all the time means sometimes his options are a bit more limited than he would have liked.

Australia are still the pick to win the World Cup and will be warm favourites in every game they play, beginning with their tournament opener against New Zealand next Thursday night in Sydney.

Walters is attempting to solve a puzzle no other Kangaroos coach has ever had to face and there is no one-size-fits-all philosophy in the battle between fitness, function and form when it comes to selecting a player.

But when numbers are scarce, and for the Kangaroos they're a lot shorter than they used to be, the first two are more important than the last.

World.title: The FBI calls this type of cult 'modern-day terrorism'. It has found its way to Australia
World.content:
Emma* thought she had made a friend online. Instead, the 14-year-old found herself sucked into a sinister, sadistic online cult.

Warning: This article contains graphic content and references to self-harm and suicide.

The teenager lives in Western Australia, but police believe the person who lured her is somewhere in the Caucasus.

She is among a growing number of children targeted by what the FBI describes as "modern-day terrorism", which has been linked to reports of suicide, animal torture and school shootings overseas.

"I had no choice. I got told that I had to self-harm for him," Emma says.

" I had to use my body to make him happy. "

With the support of her parents, the teenager has decided to share her experience with 7.30 to prevent other children falling victim.

Incited to commit ritualistic deeds

Emma, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, loved to play Roblox.

"You can role-play, you can dress up your avatar, you can buy currency on the game," she says.

Helplines: The Kids Helpline: 24-hour support on 1800 55 1800

Lifeline: 24-hour support for all Australians on 13 11 14

About 1.7 million Australian children aged between 6 and 13 use the online gaming platform.

"I met this guy … he said that I was really good at the game," Emma says.

The teenager says she was asked to move to Discord, another platform that allows file-sharing and interactions through messages or video chat.

Seemingly innocuous questions like her age and what school she went to turned into requests for "selfies" and then more explicit content.

"Then he started asking me for, like, pics that were not good … [telling] me 'if you don't do this, I will leak you,'" she said.

At this point, the perpetrator had gathered enough information to identify Emma and her parents. He even found their contact numbers.

Then things escalated further.

Emma was told to self-harm by a member of the online group. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

Emma was incited to self-harm. She was also told to carry out and film sinister acts, including using her blood to write a username on a wall.

Running her hand along her scars, Emma explains that the group glorified gore.

"They made me upset, but I was too scared to tell my parents. That's the main thing. I never told my parents about any of this," she says.

One day the teenager was told to live stream her suicide.

When she refused, they messaged her father.

Emma's father was shocked by what had occurred to his daughter. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

"When I opened it … it was like a collage of pictures and it was ... blood, cuts, pornographic stuff. I felt sick and scared at the same time," Emma's dad says.

"I didn't really know what it was about ... I had no idea that it was going to be even bigger than that."

Written in blood

The person who targeted Emma is part of a global network.

7.30 has been monitoring some of their encrypted messaging group chats for months.

Some of the messages sent as part of the online group. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

They share material, including videos of self-harm.

There are also photos of walls and bathtubs covered in satanic symbols and usernames written in what appears to be blood.

AFP cybercrime commander Graeme Marshall has been investigating child exploitation for years, both nationally and internationally. He says these networks are unlike anything he has ever seen.

Australian Federal Police cybercrime commander Graeme Marshall. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

"It's all about status within the group," Commander Marshall says.

"And that compels the perpetrators to continue to try and coerce their victims into doing ever greater self-harm or other activities.

" The other alarming thing that we have seen is that some of the victims then are also coerced to become offenders. "

These groups go by different names, but the most notorious is 764.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Daryna Zadvirna at Zadvirna.Daryna@abc.net.au.

It was created by a Texas teenager six years ago and named after the zip code of his town.

Bradley Cadenhead was 15 at the time and is currently serving an 80-year prison term.

US cybercrime expert Keven Hendricks says the ideologies that underpin groups like 764 are not new.

A sample of messages sent within the online cult chat. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

"[The] mixing of demonology and Satanism with neo-Nazi tropes, antisemitic tropes ... it's like you throw everything into a stew and you let it sit. It just starts to bubble and, really, that's how this all built up," Mr Hendricks says.

"But at its core it was always about harassment, and it was about online trolling."

Mr Hendricks, who has previously worked in law enforcement, says police agencies around the world face the same challenge.

"It's just very hard to stamp out an ideology that just regurgitates itself and evolves," he says.

'Brainwashed' into a 'dark place'

Emma's case is among 19 referrals made to the WA Police Force (WAPF) cybercrime squad in the past 18 months.

"She was brainwashed, intimidated, threatened into a dark place she couldn't get out of," says WAPF cybercrime chief Peter Foley.

"It is a scary place, a dark place and we've got children that have been isolated … they will not engage with their parents, their teachers or friends and they will not come to police.

"Those children are out there."

Emma was too scared to tell her parents but then the perpetrator leaked content to them. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

Detective Superintendent Foley says there are different tactics used to intimidate victims into complying and not reporting the group.

One is doxxing, which means publishing someone's personal information online, to allow others to contact or locate them or their family.

7.30 has seen multiple examples of doxxing, where dossiers with the target's phone number, address and even the names and workplace of their parents had been posted online, encouraging others to harass them.

Swatting is another. It is when someone makes a fake emergency call with the aim of tricking a tactical law enforcement unit into raiding an unsuspecting person's home.

Detective Superintendent Foley says any child could be at risk and is urging parents to be vigilant about their children's behaviour.

Western Australian police cybercrime chief Peter Foley. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

"When they start hiding their devices, hiding the content of the devices … if they start to isolate themselves … these are some of the risk indicators we see," he says.

In June, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) travelled to London for a meeting of The Five Eyes — an intelligence-sharing alliance made between the UK, US, Canada, New Zealand and Australia.

Combating sadistic online exploitation was high on the agenda.

"We engage broader than the Five Eyes. We also engage through Europol, with our European counterparts," Commander Marshall says.

The AFP launched a task force to disrupt and dismantle these networks last year.

Commander Marshall would also like to see more proactive measures in areas like health and education to prevent the crimes from occurring in the first place.

"I still struggle to believe that we can have kids as young as 11 perpetrating these types of crimes," he says.

"There's a lot of ability to have those earlier interventions that actually produce better outcomes for our youth than having to go in and either safeguard a victim who's already been harmed or lay a criminal charge against a very young offender."

'Industry-wide challenge' says Roblox

7.30 asked Discord and Roblox how confident the platforms were that the systems they had in place were enough to protect children from grooming and exploitation.

In a statement, Roblox said these "horrific crimes" were "an industry-wide challenge" and it took them extremely seriously.

"We have dedicated teams and systems working proactively to identify and remove content and users associated with these criminal networks, and we collaborate with law enforcement to help bring them to justice," the statement reads.

Emma's parents want platforms like Roblox to be more accountable. (Brent Lewin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Discord said it was "deeply committed to user safety".

"We use a combination of advanced technology and trained safety teams to proactively find and remove content that violates our policies," says a Discord spokesperson.

"Unlike social media platforms that use algorithms to select content and maximise engagement, our service strives to enable organic, real-time interaction and connection."

Both platforms are currently exempt from Australia's age-restricted social media ban.

Australia's online safety regulator released a report last week, finding "significant gaps" in how gaming platforms protect children online.

"Australian children have a right to play online without being exposed to predators, sexual extortionists, violent extremist content or other harmful material," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said.

"While we have seen some safety improvements as a result of sustained regulatory pressure, including the recent court-enforceable undertakings we accepted from Roblox, there is still significant work to be done."

Emma's parents want the platforms to be more accountable.

They say it is "terrifying" knowing that her abuser is still at large and could be targeting other kids.

"They were pretty much getting her to destroy herself," Emma's mum says.

"It's heartbreaking as parents to watch her go down."

While the wounds on her body have healed, Emma is still recovering from the psychological impact.

"The things I've done were really, really bad and I regret each bit," she says.

" I don't want other people ending up like how I ended up. "

*Emma is not her real name

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: IS-linked Australians in Iraq face 'risk of unfair prosecution', HRW warns
World.content:
Grave concerns are being raised for 13 Australians believed to be held in Iraqi jails on suspicion of links to the Islamic State (IS) group, with Human Rights Watch (HRW) warning they face inhumane treatment and potential execution.

The organisation has accused the Albanese government of "outsourcing" its responsibilities with regards to the group, given it has explicitly insisted it is making no efforts to repatriate the men to Australia despite calls from Iraq to take them back.

The Australian Government declined to comment on the circumstances of the individuals for legal and security reasons.

The ABC understands the government is not repatriating people from Iraq.

The 13 Australians were among almost 5,700 men and boys transferred to Iraq from Syria by the United States military in a hastily arranged mission earlier this year, as Syrian government forces swept through territory once held by Kurdish authorities.

In early September, Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council announced it had finished interrogations of the men and would move to begin prosecutions.

Australians set to face Iraqi trial Local Iraqi authorities say they have finishing interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.

In a report released on Monday afternoon, HRW said Iraq had a long history of torture and unlawful executions within its prison system, and argued that should sound alarm for countries such as Australia.

"I think a lot of countries of origin of these detainees, including Australia, would like to think that sending them to Iraq is a 'mission accomplished'," HRW's senior counterterrorism adviser Letta Tayler told the ABC.

"Iraq is a sovereign state; in the past, these men and boys were being held by a non-state actor inside war-torn Syria.

"So on the surface, this might look a lot better, this might look like an improvement and certainly conditions are better in Iraq, relatively speaking.

"But the bottom line is these men in particular still face a real risk of unfair prosecution followed by execution."

Australian men believed to be held in Iraq

Perth-born paediatrician Tareq Kamleh, who has been dubbed "Dr Jihad", is thought to be among the Australians in jail in Baghdad.

Tareq Kamleh travelled to Syria in 2015 to join the Islamic State group. (Facebook: Tareq Kamleh)

Yusuf Zahab, now believed to be in his early 20s, is also thought to be in the group, having been detained by Kurdish forces in north-eastern Syria in 2019 when he was still a teenager.

He was taken to Syria from Australia by relatives wanting to live under IS rule when he was just 12 years old.

It has been reported he was injured in an IS attack on the Syrian prison where he was held in 2022, and had previously been suffering from tuberculosis behind bars.

HRW said a family member had told it that Kurdish authorities had agreed to release him, but he was transferred to Iraq just days before they arrived to take him home.

That was around the same time a group of Australian women tried to flee the Al Roj camp in Syria to begin their perilous journey back to Australia.

Not clear if death penalty will be waived

Ms Tayler said sources had told HRW that Iraqi authorities had said "a number of countries" had approached them "requesting that they waive the death penalty for their nationals if convicted".

But she said there was no "official commitment" that Iraq would do that, and no confirmation from her discussions that Australia was one of them.

That is despite Australia's history of advocating against the death penalty.

"Iraqi authorities have said that they will abide by international fair trial standards," Ms Tayler said.

"And I do get the impression from several sources I spoke with, both inside and outside the Iraqi government, that there is a strong commitment to do so on the part of ranking Iraqi judiciary members.

"However, Iraq does have a long substantial record of fair trial violations, including the use of confessions extracted apparently through torture.

"And so can Iraq really change this record almost overnight? Can it initiate reforms to make these trials truly fair, particularly given this international push to have all of these men prosecuted as soon as possible?"

Iraqi authorities have called for greater support as it deals with the burden of the cases.

The Albanese government has insisted it is not doing anything to help bring the men back to Australia.

The office of Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong has been contacted for comment.

"Surely a country [Australia] of this size and stature with a robust democratic system and judiciary is capable of bringing home 13 men," Ms Tayler said.

"One of whom, at least, is himself a victim of ISIS and has been detained since childhood."

Ms Tayler went on to say that Australia is capable of assessing whether any of the men should be prosecuted, and if they are, process them through domestic courts.

"It's long past time for Australia and other countries to stop outsourcing responsibility for its nationals, to entities overseas, to captors overseas," she said.

"I do believe that Iraq has good intentions, at least at the highest level, to do what it can. But this is a near impossible burden to have dumped into Iraq's lap."

World.title: Samoan PM apologises for 'heil Hitler' salute at family event in 2007
World.content:
Samoa's prime minister has apologised after video emerged showing him giving a Nazi salute while saying "heil Hitler".

Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt issued a statement on social media saying the video was recorded at a private family gathering in Savai'i in 2007 and was not intended for the public.

According to the Samoa Observer, which first reported the video on Sunday, the 7-second clip shows Mr Leuatea Schmidt holding a microphone in his left hand before encouraging a group of about 13 people to raise their right hands and say the phrase.

The camera then reportedly pans across the gathering, showing others repeating the phrase with their right arms raised.

In the statement, Mr Leuatea Schmidt — who has German and Samoan heritage — said he rejected Nazism, antisemitism and racism in all forms.

Why devotees of Samoa's new PM say he's 'chosen by God' Supporters are fervent in their enthusiasm for Samoa's new prime minister, but voters who are more sceptical of Laaulialemalietoa Polataivao Fosi Schmidt, question his motives.

"I recognise that those words and gesture were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt and I apologise for using them," he said.

"They do not reflect my personal beliefs, nor the values of the Government or people of Samoa as in the public record of statements I made since becoming Prime Minister."

Germany controlled Western Samoa — now known as Samoa — from 1900 until World War I.

German rule left a lasting imprint on Samoa, from colonial buildings and infrastructure to families descended from German settlers.

The Samoa Observer reported that the video was filmed at a family reunion.

Mr Leuatea Schmidt was deputy speaker of Parliament at the time, having won a seat in the general election the previous year.

(Supplied)

He became prime minister in 2025 following a snap election after former prime minister Fiame Naomi Mata'afa failed to pass the national budget.

Mr Leuatea Schmidt said his government remained committed to a constitutional democracy founded on respect for human dignity and the rule of law.

The report was published two days after Mr Leuatea Schmidt's government reaffirmed a ban on the Samoa Observer, barring the newspaper access to the prime minister and coverage of government events and functions.

Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt became prime minister in 2025. (Facebook: Government of Samoa)

Previously, the Government Press Secretariat lodged a formal complaint to the Media Council on a number of articles the paper published, deeming them to a have "breached the standard of Media Ethics".

The editor of the Observer has said the ban on the paper attending the prime minister's press conferences would not stop it from doing its job.

The Media Council's decision on the matter has not yet been released.

World.title: NBL owner pays state $577 a week to rent stadium
World.content:
The Tasmanian government has effectively been leasing out a stadium to property developer and NBL owner Larry Kestelman for less than it would cost to rent most houses in the area, a parliamentary report has found.

The Public Accounts Committee found the proposed sale of Wilkinsons Point, home to the Derwent Entertainment Centre, to Mr Kestelman has exposed "serious and longstanding failures" in the management of a public asset and negotiations should be paused until some of its recommendations are implemented.

The Derwent Entertainment Centre, also known as MyState Bank Arena. (ABC News: Scott Ross)

The report into the sale of Wilkinson's Point found that despite six years of negotiations between the Tasmanian government and Mr Kestelman's LK Group, there is no binding sale, no business case and no agreed master plan.

It also found that the LK Group was effectively leasing the Derwent Entertainment Centre (DEC) for less than $30,000 a year.

"Larry Kestelman is a billionaire," Shadow Treasurer Dean Winter said.

" He has already sold the JackJumpers for a reported $35 million, while his company, a separate entity, is now leasing MyState Bank Arena for less than a family pays in rent for a family home in Glenorchy. "

The base rate rent for the DEC is $200,000 a year, adjusted for CPI.

But the Tasmanian government pays the LK Group $175,000, meaning Tasmania makes less than $30,000 a year, or approximately $577 a week.

Larry Kestelman and Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff at a JackJumpers game in 2022. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The report and Mr Winter accused the government of "overstating the revenue and failing to disclose the hiring fee" during the committee process.

"The $175,000 annual subsidy was completely hidden from the Parliamentary Public Works Committee during its 2020 review," Mr Winter said.

" In the hearing, the government overstated revenues. They have never disclosed the $175,000 annual payment back to Kestelman's company. "

The committee said the agreement did allow for LK Group to pay a percentage rent subject to the performance of the DEC, but none had been paid.

The Tasmania JackJumpers celebrate their 2024 NBL Championship win at the DEC. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The committee found that the proposal to sell the land to Mr Kestelman began through Glenorchy City Council, before the state government took over when it acquired the DEC and the land surrounding it in 2020.

Since that time, the Tasmanian government has been working exclusively with the LK Group to sell the land with a price tag of about $6 million.

In February 2025, Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced that the government had agreed to sell the Crown land at Wilkinsons Point to the LK Group "at a value determined by the valuer-general to enable the development" of:

A multi-use retail precinct,

A family resort; and,

A hotel complex.

A report released later that year by the auditor-general found "significant shortcomings in advice and process" and a lack of a government business case to support the policy.

Then in an incoming government brief provided to Business and Industry Minister Felix Ellis following July's state election, the Department of State Growth warned that activating the site could cost taxpayers $100 million.

The departmental brief also detailed that there was "no certainty of development or contribution to costs from LK Group".

"The department's current recommendation is to cease negotiations on sale of land and consider offering the surplus land to open market," the note said.

The committee found a key area of disagreement was how much the car park would cost and who should pay for it.

The department estimated it would cost $100 million, while LK Group thought it would be about half that. It is unclear whether this has been resolved.

In April Mr Kestelman told the committee negotiations were suspended, in part due to the car park, and he was prepared to walk away if necessary.

Talks have since resumed.

In its report, the committee found that no agreement exists on how infrastructure costs will be shared between the government and LK Group, "notwithstanding years of negotiation on this point".

Wilkinsons Point sits on 15 hectares of Crown land, and is the site of the Derwent Entertainment Centre. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Winter said the premier appeared to be "hell-bent on giving Larry Kestelman a good deal, but not at all interested in the interests of Tasmanians".

"Taxpayers face an estimated infrastructure footprint approaching $100 million for car parking, road realignments, and site servicing, with zero agreement on cost-sharing.

"This isn't commercial negotiation; it is complete mismanagement of public assets.

" You do not sell off $100 million in public liabilities for a $6 million headline price without a business case, without market testing and without binding development guarantees."

It recommended that the government pause negotiations until it completes a number of recommendations, including tabling a report that sets out the status of negotiations, any revised development proposal, estimated public costs and progress on the auditor-general's recommendations.

It also recommended that the lease agreement between the government and the LK Group be reviewed.

Asked about the report's findings, government minister Nick Duigan said the government remains committed to the opportunities.

"Wilkinson's Point represents a massive opportunity for Greater Hobart in terms of new housing, activating Dowsing Point," he said.

World.title: Nobel Peace Prize won't go to Trump this year, experts say
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has been "ruled out" of contention for Nobel Peace prize, according to experts and analysts.

The 2026 winner will be announced on October 9.

Last year, Venezuelan politician María Corina Machado was awarded the peace prize for her "struggle to a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy", according to the Nobel Peace Prize Committee.

A few months later, in January 2026, she presented it to Mr Trump, saying it was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.

While the committee for the prize said the award was not transferable, Mr Trump said it was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".

The US president has repeatedly stated over the years he would like to receive the award and had been vocal about his wishes ahead of it being awarded last year.

"They will never give me a Nobel Peace Prize. It's too bad. I deserve it, but they will never give it to me," Mr Trump said during a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House in February 2025.

This year, the deciding body will be mindful of picking someone who can withstand pressure from Mr Trump, according to Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo.

"I think last year's events around the Nobel Peace Prize, María Corina Machado giving it to Trump afterwards, will affect some of the considerations that they make," he said.

"One worry the committee might have is whether awarding it to someone could put them under pressure from Donald Trump … I think the committee will consider whether the award does more harm than good."

So who is up for the prize and what does it mean?

What is the Nobel peace prize?

The Nobel Peace Prize was named after Alfred Nobel. (AP: File)

The Nobel prizes, which are also handed out for outstanding achievements in physics, chemistry, literature and peace, come with a prize amount of 12 million Swedish Krona ($1.7 million).

They were created by wealthy Swedish chemist and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, who bequeathed funds for "prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind".

Best known as the inventor of dynamite, Nobel was also a poet and linguist who could speak Russian, French, English and German by the age of 17.

The five original prize categories reflect interests closest to his heart.

Nobel chose the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences to select the winners of the chemistry and physics prices, the Swedish Academy to choose the literature winner, the Karolinska Institute to award the physiology and medicine prizes, and a committee chosen by the Norwegian parliament to choose the peace prize winner.

Who is a frontrunner for the peace prize?

This year, that committee has received nominations for 287 candidates — a mixture of political figures and organisations.

The shortlist is not made public, but Mr Gjerløw is considered a top forecaster.

He said the International Space Station (ISS) would be a candidate for the peace prize because it was a rare symbol of global cooperation at a time when multilateralism was crumbling and many countries had retreated to narrower national interests on Earth.

Mr Gjerløw's list also includes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney due to him standing up to Mr Trump over US tariffs.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney could be a contender. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

It also mentions Ukrainian children's advocate Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children; Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, a grassroots relief network; and the Committee to Protect Journalists after the deadliest two years for reporters since record-keeping began nearly 45 years ago.

Could Trump win the prize?

Mr Trump has reportedly been nominated for the peace prize by the leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan, but Mr Gjerløw says his chances of being awarded it are "quite low".

This year's peace prize comes at a time marked by the most war and conflict in decades, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Can a Nobel Peace Prize be revoked, refused or given away? While it can be gifted, refused or displayed, the Nobel Peace Prize itself — once awarded — belongs to its original recipient forever.

Shawn Davies, a senior analyst at the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, which monitors conflict, said Washington had gone from a guarantor of the postwar order to a violator of it in some cases.

"I don't even think his own base would believe" Mr Trump could win the prize now, "given how he's stuck in what looks like a forever war in Iran," Mr Davies said.

Nelson Wiseman, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, said: "Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel."

"If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are," he said.

Famous recipients and criticism

Only five people have won multiple Nobel prizes and American chemist and peace activist Linus Pauling is the only person to receive two unshared Nobel prizes.

Some awards have aged poorly, such as Egas Moniz's 1949 medicine prize for the since-discredited practice of lobotomy.

Many peace prizes have also been criticised, including those for Henry Kissinger, Yasser Arafat, Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

Failure to give the prize to Mahatma Gandhi before his death in 1948 is also seen by many as an oversight.

Only 20 of the prize's 112 individual laureates have been women in its 125-year history.

In the past 15 years, eight women have won the prize individually, compared to just six men.

ABC/wires

World.title: Merrett has become a Hawk. This is how they are likely to land King next
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Merrett has become a Hawk. This is how they are likely to land King next Michael Gleeson October 5, 2026 — 5:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In striking contrast to last year’s protracted, ugly and ultimately failed move, this year Zach Merrett became a Hawthorn player on the opening day of trade period. Merrett will move to Hawthorn in exchange for picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft and a future second-round draft pick. The 31-year-old Merrett, who just won a record-equalling seventh Crichton Medal as Essendon’s best and fairest, has signed a four-year deal worth $1 million a year with the Hawks. Outgoing Essendon midfielder Zach Merrett. Ruby Alexander Hawthorn’s best offer for Merrett last year was three first-round draft picks – selections 10 and 22 at the time in the 2025 draft year – their first round pick in this year’s 2026 national draft and fringe midfielder Henry Hustwaite (who was delisted by the club last week). The swift move to secure Merrett this year suggests Hawthorn are confident that they can spend their draft capital believing they won’t need to use it to form part of a trade for restricted free agent Ben King from Gold Coast.



It indicates the Hawks are confident the Suns will not match their offer for King and instead accept a first-round draft pick – currently selection seven – as compensation. On Tuesday, young Hawthorn forward Aidan Schubert will fly to the Gold Coast and be joined by his parents – flying up from the family home in Gawler, South Australia – to tour the Suns’ facilities and consider a move after just one year at the Hawks. Aidan Schubert played one game for the Hawks in his first season. AFL Photos via Getty Images The move for Schubert is a standalone trade, separate from the King free agency move, but the Hawks being open to trading the player they took in last year’s national draft clearly creates goodwill for the Suns not to match the contract terms for King. Having arrived at Hawthorn as pick 23 last year, a future second-round selection is likely to form the basis of the deal this year.



Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period day one: Zach Merrett’s trade to Hawthorn becomes official; Pies gain Hogan but trade Pendlebury Schubert, who played one game for the Hawks this season, was shocked and disappointed to discover the Hawks were open to trading him. For Hawthorn, however, after securing King and then re-signing Calsher Dear, there was a tight squeeze for spots for key forwards in a starting line-up in this year’s preliminary final that already included Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis and Mabior Chol. The last year has changed a lot of things for the Hawks, with the club moving swiftly this year to engage with Essendon about a trade. “You do look and learn from what you do from previous trade periods, and we’ve done that,” Hawthorn list boss Mark McKenzie said earlier on Monday about the Merrett negotiations. McKenzie said the form of midfielder Cam Mackenzie and the emergence of Josh Ward in this year’s finals series in particular would not be harmed by Merrett’s arrival.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The Bombers gave up Merrett without a fight. This is why it was the right move Sam McClure Sports reporter “I think the strength of Sam [Mitchell] and the coaching group is that they’ve been able to show their ability to move around players and play them in different positions, so the versatility of some of these guys – Cam’s played a bit more forward at times and wing, and Josh Ward’s done that as well,” McKenzie said. “So it was great this year to see the development of those players. But don’t be surprised to see a lot of those players, whether it is a new player who comes into the football club playing in a different position as well at times. “I think the strength of the coaching group has been able to use that mechanism to go half-back, wing, midfield, or forward with a lot of our midfielders. So, I wouldn’t think that’ll change him anytime soon.” That said, Merrett will play midfield.

World.title: Storm to break south-east dry spell with more rain on the way
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Storm to break south-east dry spell with more rain on the way Courtney Kruk October 5, 2026 — 5:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Residents across south-east Queensland are preparing for a “dynamic” weather shift with severe thunderstorms predicted across the region on Tuesday, following an extremely dry September across the entire state. Patchy, light rain was possible across inland parts of Queensland, including through the Darling Downs and into the south-east on Monday, before shifting on Tuesday afternoon, the Bureau of Meteorology said. “For the first time this spring, we are looking at potential for a decent sized storm outbreak in Queensland,” senior meteorologist Angus Hines said. Severe thunderstorms are predicted across parts of south-east Queensland on Tuesday, with the potential for flash flooding, large hail and damaging winds. Brittney Deguara/Brisbane Times Areas likely to be hit by severe thunderstorms include Brisbane, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, parts of the Burnett Region and west towards Toowoomba.



Hazardous weather conditions are also possible, with the bureau warning of the potential for damaging wind gusts, large hailstorms above two centimetres and flash flooding. Related Article Weather This feels like the warmest winter in Brisbane in years. But is it? “Not everyone will probably pick up a storm tomorrow,” Hines said. “But the areas that do, it’s certainly going to … bring some pretty disruptive weather.” The possibility of rain is welcome news for Queenslanders following an “extremely dry” September, with the state recording only 1.4 millimetres of rain for the entire month. Tuesday’s storm wasn’t expected to fill the gage, but suburbs directly impacted by the system will enjoy a short, heavy downpour.



“Unfortunately, when it comes to rainfall, some places who have been really dry will get a good soak of rain,” Hines said. “For some it might it too much too fast, and for others, you probably won’t get as much as you’re looking for.” Australia and the Pacific Ocean is currently in the grip of a strong El Nino weather pattern, the bureau said, which many people assume means only dry weather or a drought season. Hines said this is not always the case, with current modelling showing a high chance of above-average rainfall for south-east Queensland and other parts of the state in coming months. “We don’t have summer long-range forecasts … but we have got an elevated chance of above-average rainfall in a large part of Queensland over this coming three-month period,” he said.



Related Article Extreme weather What flash droughts and a super El Nino will mean for your summer “El Nino doesn’t always lead to drought … [but it does] tend to bring elevated heat … [and] push the average temperature then above and beyond a typical summer. “So every chance we’ll be dealing with a pretty hot burst of weather [in coming months], but maybe that’ll be hot and muggy and sticky as opposed to hot and dry.” The Bureau said showers are possible on Wednesday and Thursday, though Tuesday remained “the most dynamic” weather day. World.title: You can come to my suburb by bus, train, bike or boat. And, like us, never leave
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After 17 years of countless moves while renting around the inner west, I thought I knew every suburb in the area. When finally looking to buy, we discovered Hurlstone Park, a pocket of Federation charm and gardens demurely tucked away at “the Paris end of Canterbury Bankstown” (according to one of our regular Herald letter-writers, alluding to our style and many canine companions, I’m sure). May May Lau with her dog Sansa, stopping to smell the flowers in Hurlstone Park. Janie Barrett You can arrive here on foot from a nearby light rail stop, on a bike via the Greenway, by bus, by train (well, by a replacement bus for the foreseeable future) and by boat via the kayak launching platform down at the Cooks River, with its abundant bird life, magical sunsets and popular play and picnic areas. Hurlstone Park is still a place of quiet Sundays and backyards; in ours we host frogs, skinks, ringtail possums, native bees and birds (recently a young white-faced heron). During the cooler months I am reminded, by the sounds of hollering that reach us from the fields of Ewen Park, of my now-grown children’s rite of passage playing for one of the oldest football clubs in Australia, the Hurlstone Park Wanderers. We honour our past here. The silhouette of our small group of shops has changed little since the suburb’s development alongside the railway, around 1900. We still have a butcher, a grocer, baker and land agent, but lost our boot maker a few years ago. Being young at heart, we’ve embraced the arrival of cafes and small bars. You’ll find us at HP Bowlo on a Friday evening, when the winning ticket of the “best meat raffle in Sydney” elicits applause and excited barking. Con Anagnostou in Con’s Handmade Shoes, photographed in 2023, prior to his death. Janie Barrett The main street of Hurlstone Park, Crinan Street, is lined with small businesses. Janie Barrett Crinan Street at golden hour. Janie Barrett



In Hurlstone Park we are the sum of our parts – local artists preserve our streetscapes and our many musicians get us together on weekends; my good friend pipes at the Cenotaph on Remembrance and Anzac Days. A photographer beautifully portrayed us during the harsh lockdowns of the COVID-19 pandemic, and a lady I know has run a huge charity jam stall for eons. Community groups revegetate and clean up our much-loved river area, increasingly known as Goolay’yari, (pelican dreaming), reminding us of this place’s cultural history as fishing grounds. Ballet teacher Mel Coady ran an online class during lockdown while her daughters Ella and Indi danced along at their studio. Brook Mitchell We are newcomers, of 25 years, to this enchanting place; our neighbours put down roots some 40 to 60 years ago, from Vietnam, Lebanon, Greece, Portugal and Italy. We increasingly encounter young family groups strolling alongside our planted verges, too. There’s little crime to report, although the pinching of fruit and plants from our wondrous gardens sometimes lights up the local Facebook page. This is a place where I’ve forged fantastic friendships and made unexpected connections, like meeting a European designer who was pictorially documenting the “tile risers of Hurlstone Park”, and corresponding with a man photographing the leadlights of inner western homes. Our potent community spirit has seen us punch above our weight in the face of multiple threats to turn our village into just another railway station with a shopping mall and shoddily-built apartment blocks. We have stood our ground against developers, past councillors and the state government. I love this place so much, some years ago I walked its leafy streets for many weeks documenting its built character; this eventually led to council heritage studies and protections, announced to a cheering crowd at the old council chambers in Campsie. The Hurlstone Park Association rallied the community when the state was imposing planning changes and the metro conversion of our rail line, and you can largely thank the good people of Hurlstone Park, through their numerous and quality submissions, for preventing the wrecking of many of the historic railway buildings between Sydenham and Bankstown. Another local mounted a successful campaign to have art, instead of advertising, plastered across our railway bridge. Hurlstone Park sits on a wobbly political stool; many of us feel inner westy, and Bankstown is a long way along congested Canterbury Road. We are old-fashioned but progressive. The first-ever Greens councillor came from here and served for many years. There’s tension in the air with the housing debate and the looming Metro opening.

World.title: The ‘slaughter, pummel, smash or ram’ culture at ANZ exposed by a ‘hypocrite’
World.content:
Analysis BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace culture The ‘slaughter, pummel, smash or ram’ culture at ANZ exposed by a ‘hypocrite’ Nick Bonyhady October 5, 2026 — 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former ANZ trader, Etienne Alexiou, was described as a “hypocrite” by Justice Nye Perram in a judgment published on Monday. But there was at least one key point where the Federal Court judge found Alexiou to be correct. Alexiou, who was sacked amid the fallout from a partially forgotten scandal more than a decade ago, had long argued that he was a whistleblower. Former ANZ trader Etienne Alexiou leaving the Federal Court in Sydney last October. Louie Douvis He told the court that he had spoken out about trading malpractice in the early 2010s and claimed a colleague had said he would “slaughter” a rate used to set the interest on vast amounts of short-term loans, thereby manipulating the market and making money. Perram did not agree Alexiou was a whistleblower. He was a man who had spoken with colleagues of “ramming speed straight at a jap bird” and then claimed, in court, he was talking about whaling.



ANZ had sacked him for that kind of language and Perram found Alexiou’s evidence at times “unconvincing and blameworthy”. “The fact that Mr Alexiou is a hypocrite about this does not logically entail that he is wrong and, on this occasion, I am satisfied that he is right,” he said. But Alexiou was no Robinson Crusoe. His remarks about “ramming” were made to counterparts at UBS and CBA. And as Perram put it, they paint a picture of a wider ‘nasty and brutish’ world characterised by the British philosopher Thomas Hobbes, that Alexiou inhabited. Internally, “the workplace in which Mr Alexiou worked was Hobbesian,” Perram said. Traders were paid multimillion-dollar annual bonuses. “Their pursuit no doubt contributed to the – at least – martial language evident on the trading floor where, as the facts of this case show, the Dionysian urge to slaughter, pummel, smash or ram seems to have been a virtue worthy of public confession.”



Related Article Banks scolded in BBSW stoush Swearing was pervasive. Getting drunk was common, even among senior management. Reckless, dangerous and “sexist behaviour which did not by any means stop short of sexual harassment” happened openly. “The attitude to women that is revealed is particularly problematic.” Alexiou himself had been interviewed for his job, which he got in 2011, on an evening that began at a wine bar, continued to a Chinese restaurant, and ended at a strip club called the Men’s Gallery in the Sydney CBD. The evening was driven by a senior man in the ANZ trading division, but the group included a female human resources staffer from the bank. It was a “a radical departure from what most people would regard as normal in the workplace”, said Perram, with some understatement. If the interview set the tone, things escalated in March 2013 at a dinner in a conference hosted by the bank in the Hunter Valley. After dinner, ANZ’s then-managing director of global markets, Steve Bellotti, took an interest in a young woman identified only as P.



“[Bellotti] (and another male employee) then sexually harassed P by badgering her for her room number, blocking her from leaving and manhandling her,” Perram found. The incident ended only when another bank employee asked whether P would like him to call security. Related Article Big four After axing 3500 jobs, ANZ chief’s grand plan has a long way to go “If this was the conduct of the people at the top of global markets then it is not difficult to see what impact that was likely to have had on the culture of the (mostly) male employees beneath them,” Perram said. “It paints a picture not only of unconstrained loucheness and irresponsibility but also of a culture where sexist behaviour towards women was normalised and where the sexism went as far as harassment.” “Since the fish rots from the head, I find that this culture permeated down to the traders for whom senior management was responsible and that the workplace was affected by it to a non-trivial degree.”



Alexiou embraced the culture, Perram found, but he was not fully of the “the smash, ram, pummel and slaughter set”. The former trader was an introverted man trying to fit in amidst his boorish workplace, Perram said. While the whistleblowing claim and talk of a $100 million judgment came to nothing, Alexiou won a breach of contract claim, likely worth about $5 million. The bank itself settled allegations around the interest rate setting device for $50 million in 2017 and admitted some of its traders had attempted to engage in “unconscionable conduct”. ANZ, under new leadership, has made a concerted effort to clean up its internal culture. Bloomberg ANZ is on its third chief executive since Alexiou was sacked in 2015. Bellotti – who was contacted for comment – left that year too. In striking contrast to last year’s protracted, ugly and ultimately failed move, this year Zach Merrett became a Hawthorn player on the opening day of trade period. Merrett will move to Hawthorn in exchange for picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft and a future second-round draft pick. The 31-year-old Merrett, who just won a record-equalling seventh Crichton Medal as Essendon’s best and fairest, has signed a four-year deal worth $1 million a year with the Hawks. Outgoing Essendon midfielder Zach Merrett. Ruby Alexander Hawthorn’s best offer for Merrett last year was three first-round draft picks – selections 10 and 22 at the time in the 2025 draft year – their first round pick in this year’s 2026 national draft and fringe midfielder Henry Hustwaite (who was delisted by the club last week). The swift move to secure Merrett this year suggests Hawthorn are confident that they can spend their draft capital believing they won’t need to use it to form part of a trade for restricted free agent Ben King from Gold Coast.



It indicates the Hawks are confident the Suns will not match their offer for King and instead accept a first-round draft pick – currently selection seven – as compensation. On Tuesday, young Hawthorn forward Aidan Schubert will fly to the Gold Coast and be joined by his parents – flying up from the family home in Gawler, South Australia – to tour the Suns’ facilities and consider a move after just one year at the Hawks. Aidan Schubert played one game for the Hawks in his first season. World.title: Storm to break south-east dry spell with more rain on the way
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Storm to break south-east dry spell with more rain on the way Courtney Kruk October 5, 2026 — 5:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Residents across south-east Queensland are preparing for a “dynamic” weather shift with severe thunderstorms predicted across the region on Tuesday, following an extremely dry September across the entire state. Patchy, light rain was possible across inland parts of Queensland, including through the Darling Downs and into the south-east on Monday, before shifting on Tuesday afternoon, the Bureau of Meteorology said. “For the first time this spring, we are looking at potential for a decent sized storm outbreak in Queensland,” senior meteorologist Angus Hines said. Severe thunderstorms are predicted across parts of south-east Queensland on Tuesday, with the potential for flash flooding, large hail and damaging winds. Brittney Deguara/Brisbane Times Areas likely to be hit by severe thunderstorms include Brisbane, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, parts of the Burnett Region and west towards Toowoomba.



Hazardous weather conditions are also possible, with the bureau warning of the potential for damaging wind gusts, large hailstorms above two centimetres and flash flooding. Related Article Weather This feels like the warmest winter in Brisbane in years. But is it? “Not everyone will probably pick up a storm tomorrow,” Hines said. “But the areas that do, it’s certainly going to … bring some pretty disruptive weather.” The possibility of rain is welcome news for Queenslanders following an “extremely dry” September, with the state recording only 1.4 millimetres of rain for the entire month. Tuesday’s storm wasn’t expected to fill the gage, but suburbs directly impacted by the system will enjoy a short, heavy downpour.



“Unfortunately, when it comes to rainfall, some places who have been really dry will get a good soak of rain,” Hines said. “For some it might it too much too fast, and for others, you probably won’t get as much as you’re looking for.” Australia and the Pacific Ocean is currently in the grip of a strong El Nino weather pattern, the bureau said, which many people assume means only dry weather or a drought season. Hines said this is not always the case, with current modelling showing a high chance of above-average rainfall for south-east Queensland and other parts of the state in coming months. “We don’t have summer long-range forecasts … but we have got an elevated chance of above-average rainfall in a large part of Queensland over this coming three-month period,” he said.



Related Article Extreme weather What flash droughts and a super El Nino will mean for your summer “El Nino doesn’t always lead to drought … [but it does] tend to bring elevated heat … [and] push the average temperature then above and beyond a typical summer. “So every chance we’ll be dealing with a pretty hot burst of weather [in coming months], but maybe that’ll be hot and muggy and sticky as opposed to hot and dry.” The Bureau said showers are possible on Wednesday and Thursday, though Tuesday remained “the most dynamic” weather day. World.title: You can come to my suburb by bus, train, bike or boat. And, like us, never leave
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After 17 years of countless moves while renting around the inner west, I thought I knew every suburb in the area. When finally looking to buy, we discovered Hurlstone Park, a pocket of Federation charm and gardens demurely tucked away at “the Paris end of Canterbury Bankstown” (according to one of our regular Herald letter-writers, alluding to our style and many canine companions, I’m sure). May May Lau with her dog Sansa, stopping to smell the flowers in Hurlstone Park. Janie Barrett You can arrive here on foot from a nearby light rail stop, on a bike via the Greenway, by bus, by train (well, by a replacement bus for the foreseeable future) and by boat via the kayak launching platform down at the Cooks River, with its abundant bird life, magical sunsets and popular play and picnic areas. Hurlstone Park is still a place of quiet Sundays and backyards; in ours we host frogs, skinks, ringtail possums, native bees and birds (recently a young white-faced heron). During the cooler months I am reminded, by the sounds of hollering that reach us from the fields of Ewen Park, of my now-grown children’s rite of passage playing for one of the oldest football clubs in Australia, the Hurlstone Park Wanderers. We honour our past here. The silhouette of our small group of shops has changed little since the suburb’s development alongside the railway, around 1900. We still have a butcher, a grocer, baker and land agent, but lost our boot maker a few years ago. Being young at heart, we’ve embraced the arrival of cafes and small bars. You’ll find us at HP Bowlo on a Friday evening, when the winning ticket of the “best meat raffle in Sydney” elicits applause and excited barking. Con Anagnostou in Con’s Handmade Shoes, photographed in 2023, prior to his death. Janie Barrett The main street of Hurlstone Park, Crinan Street, is lined with small businesses. Janie Barrett Crinan Street at golden hour. Janie Barrett



In Hurlstone Park we are the sum of our parts – local artists preserve our streetscapes and our many musicians get us together on weekends; my good friend pipes at the Cenotaph on Remembrance and Anzac Days. A photographer beautifully portrayed us during the harsh lockdowns of the COVID-19 pandemic, and a lady I know has run a huge charity jam stall for eons. Community groups revegetate and clean up our much-loved river area, increasingly known as Goolay’yari, (pelican dreaming), reminding us of this place’s cultural history as fishing grounds. Ballet teacher Mel Coady ran an online class during lockdown while her daughters Ella and Indi danced along at their studio. Brook Mitchell We are newcomers, of 25 years, to this enchanting place; our neighbours put down roots some 40 to 60 years ago, from Vietnam, Lebanon, Greece, Portugal and Italy. We increasingly encounter young family groups strolling alongside our planted verges, too. There’s little crime to report, although the pinching of fruit and plants from our wondrous gardens sometimes lights up the local Facebook page. This is a place where I’ve forged fantastic friendships and made unexpected connections, like meeting a European designer who was pictorially documenting the “tile risers of Hurlstone Park”, and corresponding with a man photographing the leadlights of inner western homes. Our potent community spirit has seen us punch above our weight in the face of multiple threats to turn our village into just another railway station with a shopping mall and shoddily-built apartment blocks. We have stood our ground against developers, past councillors and the state government. I love this place so much, some years ago I walked its leafy streets for many weeks documenting its built character; this eventually led to council heritage studies and protections, announced to a cheering crowd at the old council chambers in Campsie. The Hurlstone Park Association rallied the community when the state was imposing planning changes and the metro conversion of our rail line, and you can largely thank the good people of Hurlstone Park, through their numerous and quality submissions, for preventing the wrecking of many of the historic railway buildings between Sydenham and Bankstown. Another local mounted a successful campaign to have art, instead of advertising, plastered across our railway bridge. Hurlstone Park sits on a wobbly political stool; many of us feel inner westy, and Bankstown is a long way along congested Canterbury Road. We are old-fashioned but progressive. The first-ever Greens councillor came from here and served for many years. There’s tension in the air with the housing debate and the looming Metro opening.

World.title: The ‘slaughter, pummel, smash or ram’ culture at ANZ exposed by a ‘hypocrite’
World.content:
Analysis BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace culture The ‘slaughter, pummel, smash or ram’ culture at ANZ exposed by a ‘hypocrite’ Nick Bonyhady October 5, 2026 — 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former ANZ trader, Etienne Alexiou, was described as a “hypocrite” by Justice Nye Perram in a judgment published on Monday. But there was at least one key point where the Federal Court judge found Alexiou to be correct. Alexiou, who was sacked amid the fallout from a partially forgotten scandal more than a decade ago, had long argued that he was a whistleblower. Former ANZ trader Etienne Alexiou leaving the Federal Court in Sydney last October. Louie Douvis He told the court that he had spoken out about trading malpractice in the early 2010s and claimed a colleague had said he would “slaughter” a rate used to set the interest on vast amounts of short-term loans, thereby manipulating the market and making money. Perram did not agree Alexiou was a whistleblower. He was a man who had spoken with colleagues of “ramming speed straight at a jap bird” and then claimed, in court, he was talking about whaling.



ANZ had sacked him for that kind of language and Perram found Alexiou’s evidence at times “unconvincing and blameworthy”. “The fact that Mr Alexiou is a hypocrite about this does not logically entail that he is wrong and, on this occasion, I am satisfied that he is right,” he said. But Alexiou was no Robinson Crusoe. His remarks about “ramming” were made to counterparts at UBS and CBA. And as Perram put it, they paint a picture of a wider ‘nasty and brutish’ world characterised by the British philosopher Thomas Hobbes, that Alexiou inhabited. Internally, “the workplace in which Mr Alexiou worked was Hobbesian,” Perram said. Traders were paid multimillion-dollar annual bonuses. “Their pursuit no doubt contributed to the – at least – martial language evident on the trading floor where, as the facts of this case show, the Dionysian urge to slaughter, pummel, smash or ram seems to have been a virtue worthy of public confession.”



Related Article Banks scolded in BBSW stoush Swearing was pervasive. Getting drunk was common, even among senior management. Reckless, dangerous and “sexist behaviour which did not by any means stop short of sexual harassment” happened openly. “The attitude to women that is revealed is particularly problematic.” Alexiou himself had been interviewed for his job, which he got in 2011, on an evening that began at a wine bar, continued to a Chinese restaurant, and ended at a strip club called the Men’s Gallery in the Sydney CBD. The evening was driven by a senior man in the ANZ trading division, but the group included a female human resources staffer from the bank. It was a “a radical departure from what most people would regard as normal in the workplace”, said Perram, with some understatement. If the interview set the tone, things escalated in March 2013 at a dinner in a conference hosted by the bank in the Hunter Valley. After dinner, ANZ’s then-managing director of global markets, Steve Bellotti, took an interest in a young woman identified only as P.



“[Bellotti] (and another male employee) then sexually harassed P by badgering her for her room number, blocking her from leaving and manhandling her,” Perram found. The incident ended only when another bank employee asked whether P would like him to call security. Related Article Big four After axing 3500 jobs, ANZ chief’s grand plan has a long way to go “If this was the conduct of the people at the top of global markets then it is not difficult to see what impact that was likely to have had on the culture of the (mostly) male employees beneath them,” Perram said. “It paints a picture not only of unconstrained loucheness and irresponsibility but also of a culture where sexist behaviour towards women was normalised and where the sexism went as far as harassment.” “Since the fish rots from the head, I find that this culture permeated down to the traders for whom senior management was responsible and that the workplace was affected by it to a non-trivial degree.”



Alexiou embraced the culture, Perram found, but he was not fully of the “the smash, ram, pummel and slaughter set”. The former trader was an introverted man trying to fit in amidst his boorish workplace, Perram said. While the whistleblowing claim and talk of a $100 million judgment came to nothing, Alexiou won a breach of contract claim, likely worth about $5 million. The bank itself settled allegations around the interest rate setting device for $50 million in 2017 and admitted some of its traders had attempted to engage in “unconscionable conduct”. ANZ, under new leadership, has made a concerted effort to clean up its internal culture. Bloomberg ANZ is on its third chief executive since Alexiou was sacked in 2015. Bellotti – who was contacted for comment – left that year too. He is now an investor with a particular interest in cryptocurrencies. “The conduct considered by the court relates to events involving employees no longer with the bank that occurred more than a decade ago that falls short of the standards expected at ANZ,” a bank spokesman said.



“ANZ has continued to strengthen its culture, leadership accountability and workplace standards, and remains committed to providing a respectful, inclusive and safe environment for all employees.” At least some of the exposure that led to that change came from a most imperfect messenger.
