World.title: Demand surges for telehealth ADHD assessments
World.content:
Telehealth services are offering assessments for ADHD, as some people seeking a diagnosis for the condition don't want to wait months for an in-person consultation.

Since February, GPs and nurse practitioners have been able to diagnose ADHD and prescribe medication for it.

It isn't mandatory for GPs and nurse practitioners to specialise in ADHD, meaning many GP practices aren't offering the service.

That means many people are turning to virtual assessments instead. After suspecting for a few years that she may have ADHD, Nikki (who didn't want her surname used) decided to act last year.

She had seen that GPs would soon be offering assessments so, after hearing about the long wait times and high cost of getting diagnosed through a psychiatrist, she thought she'd see her doctor when the rules changed.

But when February rolled around, her Palmerston North GP gave her the news she didn't want to hear.

"So I went to my GP and said 'Hey I'd like to do this, and she was like huh we don't do that here in Palmy, we haven't got a collective of GPs to be able to do that yet, maybe in July we might have one, do you want to wait?' And I was like no."

Frustrated she had waited longer for no reason; she was referred to an online telehealth service.

Her teenage son was also diagnosed through telehealth, and she said for both of them it was pretty much smooth sailing, bar the cost.

"You go to book and it was like $972 and you had to pay upfront, so I kind of prioritised [my son's] one first, and then I did mine a few months later."

Stuart Cowley (left). Supplied

Despite the cost, Stewart said that finally getting a diagnosis was more than worth it.

"It's changed our lives, we can concentrate. My son in particular can sit at the desk I bought him five years ago which is amazing, and for me it just means I can pay attention more in meetings."

After spending his whole life being labelled a 'poster boy' for ADHD, at 53, Stuart Cowley decided it was time to get assessed.

Like Nikki, he'd heard about the GP changes and decided to wait for nearly a year until they were brought in.

"We did some research into looking into getting it done privately and then we held off specifically for the reason that I would have preferred to go to my own GP obviously having that connection already and her understanding me as a person."

But, like Nikki, his GP didn't offer the service.

Cowley ending up choosing a telehealth service and was diagnosed by a psychiatrist.

He said the hour and half online consultation was simple, and two weeks later he received the diagnosis he was expecting, something he said had been a gamechanger.

"If we'd had known the GPs weren't going to be doing it then we could have got it underway a lot quicker."

Stuart Cowley and Nikki are part of a growing number of Kiwis getting assessed for ADHD via telehealth.

One of those services is ADHD Simple, which also operates in the UK and Australia.

Founder Cameron Houston set up the company after struggling to get his own ADHD diagnosis in New Zealand.

Once he had established the service overseas, he decided to launch in New Zealand after hearing about the changes allowing doctors and nurse practitioners to assess for ADHD.

"It's been a bit of a rollercoaster, demand has been very high, very quickly, I think as soon as we established a name for ourselves, and what we stood for and what we were able to deliver, demand has, I'd say that demand in the early stage has outstripped supply."

Not everyone is convinced by the online model, with some clinicians worried about the level of service offered over the phone.

President of the Royal New Zealand College of GPs, Dr Luke Bradford, said while it was a positive for those living rurally, telehealth had its drawbacks.

"They're not able to do the complete job and they're often not following up either, often there's a diagnosis, and 'ok we think they've got it', and starts giving notes back to the GP as opposed to an ongoing treatment plan, and they can't see and examine the patient in person.

"So, I don't think it's the best model for this, but it certainly is an option, given the examination is essentially verbal as opposed to putting your hands on someone to examine."

Psychiatrist Dr Caleb Armstrong has been doing ADHD assessments via telehealth service, Validus, since 2019.

He said telehealth was now a standard part of healthcare, and the level of service and experience clinicians were offering was more important than the form in which it was delivered.

"Whether a service is telehealth or not is not much of a marker of its quality. It's been well established for many years that telepsychiatry for instance is equivalent for outcomes, and much better for access compared to going and having to see a doctor in person."

Dr Bradford said he worried that telehealth providers could be missing out on checking blood pressure and doing echocardiograms, both important checks during an ADHD diagnosis.

World.title: High Court urged to acknowledge Bill of Rights breach in recent electoral changes
World.content:
Courts do not need to declare recent electoral changes breach the Bill of Rights Act (BORA), because any future government would already know, according to the Crown.

But Christopher Carrol - who is seeking a declaration of inconsistency in the High Court regarding the government's controversial 13-day voter enrolment deadline - says given the concession from the Crown the Bill of Rights Act had been breached, there was a need for the court to both acknowledge and respond in some manner.

Justice David Boldt, presiding over the case, said he would not be silent on the "seriousness" of the breach: "The only question is whether that needs to be a declaration, or whether something… a bit lower voltage will do the trick."

Peter Gunn, representing the Attorney-General, said Carrol's argument was "unconvincing".

"What is the court actually going to be telling Parliament, even a new Parliament, that it doesn't already know?" he said.

Justice Boldt also asked what "value" it would add to tell Parliament something it "plainly already knows", given the law was passed knowing it breached the BORA.

Parliament's "eyes were wide open, and it made that decision anyway", he said.

Justice Boldt was concerned about "potential eye rolling" on the part of the Parliament, but indicated he was "certainly not going to remain silent about the breach or the seriousness of it".

The case was heard at the Wellington High Court on Monday and focused on the Electoral Amendment Act, which among other things ends same-day voter enrolment and requires people to enroll at least 13 days before the election.

The legislation was found to be inconsistent with the BORA and the changes to enrolments could prevent 100,000 or more people from voting.

The Government said the bill would improve the timeliness, efficiency and integrity of elections.

The Electoral Commission has said official election results would not be available any sooner based on changes, but Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith argued without any changes, it could get worse.

Carroll, a law student at Waikato University, wanted the declaration to state the 13-day enrolment deadline was inconsistent with the right to vote in the BORA because people will be disenfranchised.

"It's really important that people hear from the court that a right fundamental to our democracy has been breached by Parliament," he told RNZ.

"If the court is essentially saying that Parliament hasn't given due weight to the right to vote, then that's an important finding, and I think New Zealanders will see that as an important finding."

He was concerned for those people most impacted by the change.

Gunn, the Crown lawyer, acknowledged the legislation was not BORA compliant, but noted that did not prevent Parliament from passing laws.

In July 2025, then Attorney-General Judith Collins found the bill to be inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act and indicated 100,000 or more people could be directly or indirectly disenfranchised by the rules banning enrolment in the final 13 days before an election.

"Taking into account these factors, I conclude the proposal for a 13-day registration deadline appears to constitute an unjustified limit on s12 of the NZBORA," she wrote in her report, noting Māori, Asian and Pasifika communities, and younger people would be more affected by the deadline.

Gunn said on Monday the attorney-general's report was accepted by government and formed part of the parliamentary debates on the legislation.

Declarations serve as a formal judicial mechanism to show a law infringes on basic rights in a way that can't be justified in a "free and democratic society".

Carroll argued the declaration would go before a new parliament and to deny it one would deprive a new Parliament of an "authoritative understanding of the inconsistency and demonstrability of the enrolment deadline in relation to the right to vote".

He said he was thinking of the future and how the court's decision informs a future Attorney-General of apparent inconsistency.

Gunn said that argument was "unconvincing", and there was no need.

Justice Boldt said he likely would not reach a decision ahead of the election, and no decision would have an impact on the law itself.

World.title: Paintball gun fired at pair from passing car
World.content:
Someone in a car with a paintball gun has shot at a man and woman standing outside a bar in Wellington.

Police say the paintball shooting took place on Thursday about 10.50pm.

"CCTV footage shows a male and a female standing outside a bar on the corner of Willis and Dixon streets when a paintball gun was discharged toward them from a passing vehicle," police said.

"The pair shortly after had a brief conversation with one of the bar's staff members."

A person has been charged in relation to the incident but police say the pair who were shot at are victims and/ or witnesses and would like to speak to them.

World.title: Fiji schedules potential referendum date on new constitution ahead of final parliament vote
World.content:
Fiji's prime minister has announced the country will hold its first-ever constitutional referendum in just over two months' time, and election campaigning for the upcoming polls will be suspended.

In a news conference in Suva on Monday, Sitiveni Rabuka told reporters that his coalition government has identified Wednesday, 9 December, as the date for the potential referendum.

Rabuka said he has written to the Electoral Commission to suspend all general election campaigning.

It comes after the Fijian parliament passed the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 on Friday to move forward with the Rabuka-led coalition's plan to discard the 2013 Constitution. The bill now enters a 30-day public consultation phase before returning for a final third reading on 2 November.

Rabuka needs the bill to pass its third reading for the constitutional process to move to a referendum. However, he has pre-emptively announced that the referendum will go ahead on 9 December.

The proposed bill follows a lengthy review process by an independent commission that produced an alternative constitution, which the government has partially written into the bill.

Proposed changes include establishing a Senate, removing immunity provisions for those involved in the 2006 coup, and re-introducing references to God and Christianity in the preamble.

The prime minister also confirmed that the question put to the people has not yet been decided, but said it would only require a 'yes' or 'no' vote.

"On the day, all eligible Fijians will have the opportunity to exercise their democratic right and make their own decision on the question or questions that will be placed before them," Rabuka said.

Fijians still have not been told the date for the country's general election, but Rabuka has maintained it would go ahead by 6 February next year - the latest elections could be held under the current constitution.

More than 723,000 eligible voters have registered to vote, and 11 political parties are planning to contest.

It followed a lengthy review process by an independent commission that produced an alternative constitution, and which the government has partially written into the bill.

Proposed changes included establishing a Senate, killing immunity provisions for those involved in the 2006 coup, and re-introducing references to god and christianity in the preamble.

Constitutional changes require a two-thirds parliamentary majority, and must also be voted in a referendum by a majority of participating voters.

"The decisions we make about our constitutional future demand our careful consideration and our full particupation in the weeks ahead," Rabuka said.

Meanwhile, the Centre for Democracy and Dialogue said it has written to the Electoral Commission, warning that suspending general election campaigning now would be "illegal".

The civil society organisation said that no referendum polling day had yet been lawfully set.

"The Constitution Amendment Bill has not completed its third reading, the President has not issued a referendum writ and the legal conditions required by section 15(2) of the National Referendum Act do not exist," it said in a statement.

World.title: Petrol price hits highest level since start of Iran war
World.content:
Petrol prices have hit their highest level since the start of the Iran-US war.

Fuel monitoring site Gaspy today shows the average price of 91 unleaded at $3.50.5

Gaspy director Mike Newton says that price is slightly higher than the $3.50.2 hit at the peak of the war back in April.

The latest increase follows a sustained period over where the price of Brent crude has sat above US$100 a barrel.

It is currently at US$101.5.

The New Zealand dollar has also fallen sharply over the last couple of months, down around 7 percent since August to be currently at around 55.8 US cents. That's near one year lows.

World.title: Julian Wilcox named as new chair of Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori
World.content:
Veteran broadcaster and Māori language advocate Julian Wilcox has been appointed chair of Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori.

Acting Māori Development Minister Shane Jones confirmed the appointment, saying Wilcox brought a deep knowledge and practice of te reo Māori, strong governance capability, and a proven track record of leadership across both Māori and public sector settings.

"The Māori Language Commission plays a vital role in supporting and promoting te reo Māori. Dr Wilcox's expertise and longstanding commitment to the Māori language makes him exceptionally well-placed to guide its ongoing work."

Wilcox's three-year term begins today, succeeding outgoing chair Professor Rawinia Higgins MNZM.

"Prof Higgins has provided distinguished leadership to the Māori Language Commission and has made a significant contribution to the revitalisation of te reo Māori throughout her tenure.

"Her commitment to strengthening the status, use, and visibility of te reo Māori has helped advance the aspirations of many whānau, communities, and organisations across New Zealand. I thank her for her service and wish her all the best for the future," Jones said.

Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori Tumu Whakahaere Ngahiwi Apanui welcomed Wilcox into the role, saying his experience leading organisations and contributing at governance level will be a tremendous asset to Te Taura Whiri.

World.title: Near miss with train interrupts Greens' level crossing announcement
World.content:
The Greens have announced plans to fund the removal of level crossings along Auckland's Western line.

They argue this prioritises safety for pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles which have faced just under 70 crashes, and hundreds of near misses in Auckland between 2013 and 2023.

Announcing the policy at the Morningside level crossing on Monday, co-leaders Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson and Mt Albert candidate Ricardo Menéndez March witnessed something of a near miss themselves.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406224920112

Swarbrick turned back to look and pointed, saying "Did you see that? Somebody just driving across the crossing as the train was coming.

"That is case in point of why we need to remove these level crossings ... that's incredibly, incredibly dangerous and was one of those very near misses."

The work was not currently funded, but the Greens policy said the estimated $2.5 billion would come out of the National Land Transport Fund.

The projects would also enable more than 12 trains an hour on the Western Line, and allow the CRL to run at its full capacity of 48 trains an hour, and reduce congestion with barriers currently down about 30 percent of the time during peak traffic.

"These are the improvements that will take our communities and our economy into the future," Davidson said.

"This isn't just about connectivity and safety, it's just straight up common sense when it comes to unblocking congestion in Auckland which we know costs us billions of dollars in productivity ... and stress it costs Aucklanders."

Swarbrick said she had spoken to Auckland mayor Wayne Brown as recently as earlier in the morning and the level crossing funding was "just the most productive investments that we could possibly be making in our transport infrastructure" and should have been included in the Auckland regional deal.

She said that contrasted "quite strongly with the supposed investments - or the setting of money on fire - as announced by the National Party with their roads of National Party significance projects".

Labour's Infrastructure spokesperson Kieran McAnulty earlier criticised political parties making announcements about funding specific infrastructure projects, saying the Infrastructure Commission should be doing that work.

Swarbrick said the Greens' transport policy set out plans to run all proposals through the Commission's assurance process, and said the level crossings funding was "quite markedly different from the National Party pushing ahead with their dogmatic ideological pursuit of roads, roads, roads, more lanes and more lanes".

World.title: Best is yet to come for Naufahu Whyte following NRL grand final victory
World.content:
The 2026 NRL grand final was the kind of game they'll talk about for years to come.

As it goes further into history and the old stories come out at reunions and in front bars and on podcasts, they'll talk about Kalyn Ponga's try, Newcastle's heroic defence, Mark Nawaqanitawase's whole deal and the big finish.

They'll talk about James Tedesco winning the Clive Churchill Medal and maybe someone will remember his exact number of running metres — an obscene 388.

But what's certain is that at least one person will argue, passionately and adamantly, that Naufahu Whyte was the best player on the field.

Tedesco wins Churchill Medal After skippering the Sydney Roosters to their first men's premiership in seven years, James Tedesco claims the Clive Churchill Medal as the player of the match in the grand final.

There's no wrong answer between Tedesco and Whyte, who were the Roosters' best in the 19-18 victory.

Together, they combined for 55 runs and add Whyte's metres gained (187) to Tedesco's total and they carried the ball for more than half a kilometre.

Where Tedesco had 12 tackle busts, two forced dropouts and a try assist, Whyte forced several errors with his brutal defence, affirmed his status as one of the best forwards in the game and created the ruck speed that helped lead to Nawaqanitawase's crucial second-half try.

Winning the award as a middle isn't easy either, because even though you never win a comp without a few good ones, they always seem to miss out.

Sam Burgess was the last middle forward to win the Churchill medal when he led South Sydney from the front in 2014. Before then, you have to go back to Brent Kite in 2008 to find the last front-rower to do it.

For his part, the 24-year-old was happy to defer to his skipper.

Whyte and Tedesco were the premiers' two best players in the grand final win. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He deserves it; he's been doing it all year," Whyte said.

"I have big love for my captain and what he's done for the game. I'll say he's the best fullback in the game ever. That's my brother."

While Tedesco took home the medal, Whyte's own trophy cabinet has become cluttered in a short space of time.

His premiership ring will vie with the Dally M Prop Of The Year award he won last week for pride of place, but if Whyte keeps up this form, there's sure to be more to come.

Especially if Whyte is telling the truth when he says there's still major improvement in him despite dominating on the game's biggest stage on Sunday night.

"I know this isn't my best. It's far from it. I'm still just at the start of my career. There's a lot of work to put in," Whyte said.

"In the grand final, I had to take it next level. It's not easy winning a grand final, and the Knights were always going to show up, so I had to push myself.

"Taking carry after carry, that's what I'll do for my brothers. It's paid off for me so far.

NRL grand final live A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final. Follow live.

"We came in confident we would get the job done, even down six, because that's the belief we have in each other, that's the belief we have in this team."

That belief proved crucial for the Tricolours as they claimed their first premiership since 2018-19, especially in coming back from 12-0 down with a Knights ambush eminently possible.

Whyte, who watches highlights of those games all the time, now has a version of it that he can not just replay but relive.

"Everything is going through my head and my heart now. I just want to embrace this moment and enjoy every part of it, because it's the best feeling ever," Whyte said.

"I screamed, had tears of joy; I was all over the place. All the hard work it took to get here — I'm speechless, brother, I really am."

World.title: Yeo makes World Cup call, Walker earns Kangaroos spot
World.content:
Isaah Yeo will delay pectoral surgery to be captain for Australia's Rugby League World Cup campaign, after coach Kevin Walters unveiled a 23-man squad that includes Sydney Roosters halfback Sam Walker.

One of six debutants in the squad, Walker will be locked in a four-way battle with Cameron Munster, Tom Dearden and Mitchell Moses for a spot in the Kangaroos' halves.

Brisbane star Reece Walsh was also selected in Walters' squad and will compete with Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco for the fullback role.

Roosters celebrate in Bondi Grand final hero Mark Nawaqanitawase lifts the Provan-Summons trophy to adoring fans as his coach describes the Roosters star as "extraordinary".

Latrell Mitchell has also returned to the Test team after battling injuries over recent seasons.

The losing grand finalists, Newcastle, are also represented in the squad, with Bradman Best one of the debutants.

"I'm really happy with the balance of the squad," Walters said.

"We have some real strike power and a significant amount of experience, along with size, power and speed.

"This will be a huge test. I have never before seen the amount of talent spread across the top nations. We are going to need to be at our best to take out the World Cup."

Kangaroos squad:

Bradman Best, Jack Bostock, Blake Brailey, Pat Carrigan, Lindsay Collins, Reuben Cotter, Tom Dearden, Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, David Fifita, Harry Grant, Keaon Koloamatangi, Liam Martin, Latrell Mitchell, Mitchell Moses, Cam Munster, Cam Murray, Jacob Preston, Kotoni Staggs, James Tedesco, Tom Trbojevic, Sam Walker, Reece Walsh, Isaah Yeo

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'We'll be there': Fans rally behind Knights after grand final loss
World.content:
Newcastle Knights faithful say they remain proud of the team's efforts, despite a heartbreaking one-point loss to the Roosters in Sunday's NRL grand final.

Momentum had been building across Newcastle for the past week, with the city awash in red and blue as anticipation grew for the Knights' first grand final in 25 years.

Thousands of passionate fans gathered at the Knights' home ground last night to cheer on the side at a makeshift live site.

Meanwhile, bars, clubs and living rooms across the Hunter were packed with supporters decked out in red and blue.

The Knights started strong, scoring two tries in the first half to take a six-point lead into the break, but the Roosters took control in the second half, with a 69th-minute Daly Cherry-Evans field goal ultimately paving the way for the win.

Thousands of Knights fans watched the game from the team's home ground. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

Fighting back tears, Knights superfan Donna said it was a devastating loss, but the boys still did the town proud.

"[I'm] shattered but the team played so well, they really fought for it," she said.

"They really tried hard and we're really proud of the boys and everything they've achieved this year.

" We'll be there to cheer them back into home because they are everything to this town. "

Knights coach Justin Holbrook praised the side's "heart".

"If you can win anything on heart and effort, then we definitely won that because it was the hardest game of footy I've ever coached," he said.

"But again, you don't win off being proud, you win off being the better side, and we weren't the better side and we didn't win."

More patients discharged

The excitement building ahead of the grand final was shaken on Saturday when a car hit 10 fans lining the roadside in Newcastle to wave the Knights off to Sydney.

In the latest update, Hunter New England Health said six patients had been discharged from hospital.

One patient remains in a serious but stable condition and it is understood the other three are stable.

A five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man were both in critical condition on Saturday, but their conditions have improved overnight.

Hunter New England Health could not confirm which patient remained in the serious condition.

The 18-year-old alleged driver has been formally refused bail. (ABC News)

The alleged driver of the car, 18-year-old Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, is facing nine charges including three counts of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm.

He was formally refused bail on Sunday and is due to face court again later this month.

Knights faithful Kylie told the ABC the incident sent a shock wave through the community but ultimately brought it closer together.

"It just goes to show how close a community everyone is," she said.

" We all just support each other, that's just how Newcastle is. "

Ponga's try was a magnificent grand final moment. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Eyes to 2027

Newcastle captain Kalyn Ponga said he could not be prouder of his club's journey after finishing bottom of the ladder last year.

"Nothing this week was a burden on us," he said.

"Our community just rally around each other.

"Fortunately we get to experience what we experienced this week and that's definitely a feeling that I'll chase again."

Knights veteran and two-time premiership player Mark Hughes said the city would now turn its attention to next season.

"[I] can't wait to see the boys and give them a hug and say thank you for the hope and the joy they've given this community the last month," he said.

"Everyone around the stands are so proud of the boys' efforts.

" We're going to be back next year … the future looks so bright for the Knights. "

The Knights returned to Newcastle in the early hours of Sunday morning and were met with crowds of supporters and Newcastle chants reverberating through the streets.

Despite the loss, Knights fans will get the chance to celebrate the team's efforts with a fan day being held at Hunter Stadium later today.

World.title: Mary Fowler's Man City boost with big WSL win over Arsenal
World.content:
Manchester City may be a club in turmoil but Mary Fowler and her teammates have helped offer the beleaguered outfit a hint of a smile as England's women's champions continue their dominating start in the Women's Super League.

On Sunday (Monday AEST), Fowler came on as a second-half substitute and helped provide some spark as champions City went on to hammer one of their biggest rivals, Arsenal, 4-2 at home.

City stays perfect after five matches and still leads the WSL table by two points from Chelsea.

But it is proving a tough time for Arsenal and their three Australian European champion players from 2025 as the Gunners slipped 10 points off the pace in lowly 10th position.

Lauren Hemp scored twice for City as they twice came from behind to prevail, with the real spark coming when Fowler — making her 100th appearance for the club — was introduced just after the hour mark.

Fowler was joined on the park by Kerstin Casparij and Iman Beney with the home side trailing 2-1.

Within a minute, Casparij had equalised before Hemp put them in front for the first time nine minutes later and the league's top striker, Bunny Shaw, made it four with her fifth goal of the season.

Man City appeal guilty findings Manchester City denies the Premier League's finding that it used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs.

The dominance in the WSL has been a bright spot for City, which has filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

The EPL said last week that City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.71 billion) over nearly a decade.

For Arsenal, without a win since the opening day of the season, it was a second-straight defeat after losing 1-0 away to Chelsea last week.

It is a difficult time for the Aussie international trio at Arsenal, with Kyra Cooney-Cross just returning to the team on her soccer comeback, Steph Catley having been struggling with injury and Caitlin Foord yet to score this season while being played mainly as a substitute.

It was Foord's foraging in the box that forced the mistake which gifted Arsenal's second goal to Alessia Russo.

Yet the Gunners could have no complaints about slipping further adrift as, elsewhere, Chelsea, driven along by Ellie Carpenter in her more attacking vein this season, defeated West Ham 3-0.

Melvine Malard, Keira Walsh and Maika Hamano all scored for the Blues.

It came on a day when London City ‌Lionesses, without the injured Alanna Kennedy — who will miss the Matildas' upcoming internationals against Germany and Haiti — handed out a 6-1 thrashing to Tottenham Hotspur, including a double for Spanish great Alexia Putellas.

London is now third on 12 points, but Emily van Egmond could do nothing to help Charlton avoid a 5-1 hammering at Brighton as they sought in vain to earn their first point since promotion.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Don't drop it': Star's nervous moment as Roosters celebrate in Bondi
World.content:
Grand final hero Mark Nawaqanitawase's sure hands were put to good use in the early hours of this morning as the Roosters star lifted the Provan-Summons trophy to adoring fans.

Nawaqanitawase, who was the game changer in the Roosters' thrilling 19-18 victory over the Knights, was told "just don't drop it" moments before he hoisted the trophy in the air to fans at Easts Bondi Junction.

"Thank you every single one of you for supporting us all year, whether it's at home or away, or out at Homebush you guys turned up, supported us all year, so I can't thank you enough, let's celebrate well," Roosters captain and Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco said.

Loading Instagram content

Roosters coach Trent Robinson lifted the lid on the generational talent of premiership-winning Nawaqanitawase and expects the rugby-bound winger to return to the code.

Nawaqanitwase's two-try display took his tally to 47 in 47 games ahead of his return to rugby in Japan.

His previous displays for the Wallabies and Australia in rugby sevens had already proven his unique skill set and capacity for the marvellous.

The 26-year-old has since shone like a supernova and taken his feats to greater heights in the NRL, with Robinson struggling to think of a winger who had made such an impact on the code.

"There have been some amazing wingers that have. What Brett Morris did for us in 2019 was a memorable performance," he said.

"Mark has done things from the wing in touching the ball in so many different types and styles, I hope he has created another generation of those types of players."

The Roosters were always more than just the villain in Newcastle's fairytale A Knights win was always going to be the romantic story, but to show the Roosters anything but the utmost respect is to misunderstand their journey to NRL glory.

On the cusp of half-time in the grand final, his left and right-foot soccer skills, before regathering to score, got the Roosters on the board when they were trailing 12-0 after dominating in every statistic.

His second-half try in the corner, after a trademark left-foot step, was made to look easy when it required an inch-perfect finish with speed, acrobatics and strength.

"It's extraordinary watching him play the game," Robinson said.

"When other people get the ball in the same situation you kind of know what is going to happen, but when Mark gets it there is this energy that he can do something — always. He believes he can do it always.

"Not only does he do it with skill, he does it carrying it out of the backfield."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Merrett becomes a Hawk in shock late deal on day one of AFL trade period
World.content:
Hawthorn and Essendon have shocked the AFL world by getting a deal done for Zach Merrett on the opening day of the trade period.

After going all of last season's trade period unable to find common ground, seven-time club champion Merrett was dealt to the Hawks in the closing moments of day one.

The Bombers will receive picks 15 and 25, as well as a 2028 second-round pick.

Meanwhile, Scott Pendlebury's move to Gold Coast was confirmed on Monday afternoon, while Jesse Hogan became a Magpie having secured a trade from GWS.

Negotiations between Port Adelaide and the Western Bulldogs for Zak Butters also began.

Go back over all the details and all of the day's updates as they happened in our live blog.

World.title: What to look for during the AFL trade period
World.content:
Footy never truly sleeps. Just days after the final siren sounded in one of the most chaotic AFL grand finals in memory did the competition begin once again.

The trade period can help sides find the missing pieces in their side, while the draft provides young footballers the opportunity to play on the biggest of stages.

Seventeen clubs are looking to catch the reigning premiers, while Brisbane is doing its best to stay ahead of the pack. No games are won during the off-season, but a good period can set sides up for years to come.

The names of countless players and draft picks have been discussed by the list managers in earnest over the last year, all ahead of the two weeks to come. These are the key themes to watch out for as the AFL enters its silly season.

A star-studded crop

This time of year lives and dies on the star power of the names linked to new clubs. If the trade period is about hope, then only the best in the game truly drives that optimism.

On achievements alone you would be hard pressed to find a trade period where more highly credentialed players have found new clubs.

Already a two-time Brownlow Medallist with three flags, Lachie Neale has found his way to his third club, Collingwood. He's set to replace AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury in the Pies midfield. Pendlebury is set to finish his career like many future Victorian retirees do; on the sunny sands of the Gold Coast.

Elsewhere, GWS games and goals record holder Toby Greene has found his way to Geelong, and fellow former GWS teammate and Coleman medallist Jesse Hogan is set to join his fourth club, Collingwood. These players are joined by several others who have achieved plenty across their careers already.

But despite the list of greats looking for another club, one younger star has grabbed the lion's share of the headlines. Unlike the names listed above, Zak Butters, firmly in his prime and off a top 10 finish in the Brownlow Medal, is poised to move east if Port declines to match a contract offer from the Western Bulldogs.

Butters will attract top Band 1 compensation, but other high-profile moves have not. Compensation is tied to last year's salaries of players across the league. The sharp jump in the total player payment cap in recent years saw inflated compensation as a result.

Those effects have now dissipated, with the likes of Lachie Neale and Toby Greene attracting lower compensation picks than they may have a year or two ago.

These stars are far from the only players that will be discussed heavily over the coming 10 days. It's expected up to 40 trades involving about 30 players will be made during the player movement period, with many negotiations already firmly underway.

Beyond the list of vested greats, there's an uptick in the number of rucks and key position players expected to find new homes. As the league trends back towards multiple key forwards and an extended bench, clubs lacking depth are searching for answers.

No surprise about number one

In many — if not most — years there's intrigue about who is likely to be the number one pick in the November draft. Recruiters and scouts alike are scouring over player videos and stat profiles, trying to separate the wheat from the chaff.

But not so much in 2026.

Thanks to a recent rule change from the AFL, Essendon are heavily incentivised to pick a player tied to a club via the father-son or academy rules. If it does, it'll give itself (plus up to four other clubs) an extra high-end draft pick.

"We're certainly planning for Dougie to be bid on at one," Port Adelaide list manager Jason Cripps told Trade Radio last week.

"I'm happy to share that Essendon has told us that as well."

This year that player is almost certain to be Dougie Cochrane. The young key position player from South Australia is the son of former Port player Stuart, and brother of current Port midfielder Tom.

However, Dougie isn't eligible for the father-son process, and is instead tied to Port via its Next Generation Academy (NGA). He is set to become the second NGA player to be chosen at pick one after Jamarra Ugle-Hagan.

Cochrane has missed almost the entire year with injury, but his 2025 junior season was incredibly impressive. If there was a fully open draft there may be questions about whether he would go first, but under the current rules there's little doubt.

The new rule seeks to better aid lowly clubs seen as missing out on top talent and it may also address some reluctance by clubs with early picks to actually bid on high-value tied players.

The new scheme is a de facto priority pick system for bottom five clubs. With the introduction of Tasmania and years of compromised drafts ahead (more on that later), this could be a handy leg-up to strugglers. This bonus draft pick disappears if the original is traded, so only lopsided trade offers are likely to be entertained.

A bleak draft future?

Last week the Tasmania Football Club unveiled its first eight players to the football world. For many list managers it acted as an alarm that tough times were coming on the draft front.

Each club values the crop of each draft in different ways. Some drafts have stronger top ends, but weak depth. Others are even throughout. While last year's draft fell away sharply after the early picks, this year is considered to be deeper throughout the pack.

That's a key reason that this year's picks are being considered to hold a premium on their usual value, but it's not the only one. This year's draft will be the last majorly uncompromised for at least two seasons. This is due to the list concessions awarded to Tasmania on entry to the competition.

"We've obviously got Tasmania coming in who are going to dominate the next three drafts." Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb told Melbourne Media last week.

Like GWS and the Suns on their entry to the league, the Devils have been awarded a generous set of list-building tools to construct their first side. These include access to elite players in their pre-draft year, $5m in signing bonuses to established players, extra draft picks to both use and on-trade, and mini-draft picks to auction off. All in all, as few as nine of the top 25 players in next year's draft will be untouched by Tasmania's entry.

That's before considering the expected strong crop of both father-son and academy talents across the next two drafts, including some available to Tasmania under its academy, structured like those in NSW and Queensland.

As a result, many clubs are looking to prioritise picking up talent in this year's draft unless they have academy or father-son talent in the coming two years. It could mean that the value of future draft picks is significantly lower than in previous years, with clubs struggling to see eye to eye on what's fair.

With a strong crop of draft talent this year (even after excluding tied players), teams may spend relatively large amounts to secure any available picks for this draft. These factors, when combined, might make trading for talents such as Zach Merrett and Rowan Marshall even harder than in years' past.

World.title: Labuschagne set for Test after first ton in 11 months
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne has responded to the debate over whether he merits a place in Australia's Test future by just doing what he likes doing best — scoring runs.

After a difficult year, the under-pressure 32-year-old chose the most timely moment to score his first century in any form of cricket for 11 months in Potchefstroom, just five days before Australia play their first Test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Former skipper Ricky Ponting had joined the chorus that Labuschagne's place in Australia had become "untenable" after three years and 43 Tests without a Test ton, capped by three failures in the recent Bangladesh series.

Yet the South African-born batter looks sure to fill the number three spot once more in the first Test that starts in Durban on Friday after his swift century against a modest Cricket South Africa Invitation XI attack.

Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Labuschagne was largely untroubled as he raced to a 76-ball ton, going on to 111 from 89, decorated with 19 fours, before retiring to let his colleagues also get in some batting practice on the final day of the two-day warm-up match.

They enjoyed the opportunity too, with Steve Smith also retiring after making 61 while Alex Carey, fresh from his fine form in the third ODI, hit another half-century (57) as Pat Cummins' Australian side rattled up 6-368 in the drawn game.

Smith, who received a 12-month ban when captain for his role in altering the condition of the ball with sandpaper at Cape Town on the infamous tour eight years ago, is back with a group of other survivors from that tour — Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Matt Renshaw.

Those four could all play on Friday.

Renshaw looked completely recovered from a knock to his right wrist, but may feel he missed out by being dismissed for 32 off his 50 balls, as may his fellow opener Travis Head (21 off 22 balls).

Beau Webster brushed off a few cobwebs with his 42 off 88 balls before he retired.

All eyes, though, were on Labuschagne, who even had a bit of local support as he took the crease at Senwes Park, a venue less than 50km from where he was born in Klerksdorp and the emotional scene of his first ODI hundred for Australia back in 2020.

Australia will see it as a useful workout after they gave 11 bowlers a run-out on Saturday when the Invitation XI declared on 7-318 after a century from former Proteas captain Neil Brand.

Australia vs South Africa Test series 1st Test: Durban, October 9-13

2nd Test: Gqeberha, October 18-22

3rd Test: Cape Town, October 27-31

Meanwhile, South Africa paceman Anrich Nortje is in line for a remarkable return to first-class cricket after an absence of three-and-a-half years to help the injury-hit Proteas' attack.

With fitness doubts over key strike bowler Kagiso Rabada and three others, Nortje could return to Tests for the first time since March 2023 after a series of back and hip problems that left him concentrating on white-ball formats to reduce the strain on his body.

"I'll be very excited if I can put my Test cap on again. Growing up, ⁠it's the format you want to play," he said on Sunday, the day before he's expected to be named in South Africa's Test squad of 15.

Tech.title: Prick’s theatrical industrial punk is perfect for spooky season
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

While deep in the recording process for The Downward Spiral, Trent Reznor lent some of his production talents to old friend Kevin McMahon, from the new wave band Lucky Pierre (which Reznor was briefly a member of). While Reznor is only credited as the producer on four tracks off Prick’s self-titled debut record, his fingerprints are all over it. But McMahon also can’t suppress his inner theater kid, which also gives the songs the sort of glammy flamboyance found on T. Rex records. Prick embraces the inherent theatricality of goth in a way that Nine Inch Nails never did.

Opener “Communiqué” is a fuzzy blast of simple punk riffs with electronic sprinklings on top. McMahon’s vocals occasionally detour from the half-spoken verses that sound borrowed from a musical to full-throated Al Jourgensen-esque screams. The rough-around-the-edges production and focus on live instrumentation feel like a prototype for what Reznor would eventually revisit on With Teeth.

But it’s the second track, “Riverhead” where Reznor’s influences fully rear their head (even though he is not actually credited as the producer). The vocal melodies swerve like Outside- and Earthling-era Bowie around guitars that buzz with all the digital charr of the Broken EP. Then, around the three-minute mark, comes the breakdown. It slowly builds with layers of electronic drums, mechanical chords, and loping synthetic-sounding guitar melodies. The entire back chunk could easily have been a Downward Spiral or even The Fragile B-side.

These moments of richly layered production, though, are almost always immediately undermined, as with the sloppy garage-punk intro of “Tough”.

It’s these moments that make Prick so charming. It’s a serious record, but it never takes itself too seriously. McMahon isn’t afraid to get goofy (“Pink panties, blue panties, yellow panties. I’m gonna wrap around your nose, oh panty-ho-hose” he sings on “Other People”) and over-the-top with his vocal performances. He’s willing to let the guitar drift out of time, the bass strings rattle, and revels in industrial lo-fi.

“Animal” is perhaps the best-known track from the album, its video having received at least some MTV airplay. It combines backward melodic samples reminiscent of “Closer” and follows a similar lyrical theme:

Consent is all I need

To bring out the savage in me

Your scent is all I need

To bring out the animal in me

But where “Closer” opts for slinky disco sleaze, “Animal” is all raw shouted desire.

“I Apologize” is the most scatter-brained track on the album, and for that reason, one of my favorites. It opens with awkward whip-crack-like percussion and McMahon singing slightly flat and unaffected, before briefly taking off into a jangly new wave verse that quickly morphs into a hard-rock stop in the chorus. But that’s short-lived as well. The second verse is all “Space Oddity”-era Bowie acoustic strums, then there’s a solo that sounds like an arcade machine on the verge of meltdown. That then drops into a Ministry-esque dirge of layered guitars and screams. The song then returns to the chorus, but keeps adding elements until it’s stuffed to capacity and collapses on itself.

Prick’s self-titled record has plenty in common with other ‘90s industrial acts. But McMahon is clearly having a lot more fun than many of his contemporaries, and that helps elevate it above the myriad Nine Inch Nails wannabes out there.

Prick is available on most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Qobuz, Deezer, and YouTube Music.

Tech.title: NJ’s former Lt Gov is using AI to say he’s innocent of sexual harassment
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

New Jersey’s lieutenant governor Dale Caldwell was forced to resign on September 25th after an investigation found he had sexually harassed a staffer and repeatedly violated ethics rules. The now-former Lt. governor has been making the media rounds trying to clear his name. But he took a particularly odd tactic during an interview on NJ PBS.

Caldwell claims he’s being unfairly targeted, and multiple AI agents back that up. He told host Rob Nelson that he “AIed” the report on the investigation “from multiple AI platforms.” “I put it through AI,” he said, “and it said 59 times, it [sic] said, ‘What would your findings be?’ There was no instance in any of the AIs that said there would be a finding of sexual harassment.”

AI chatbots are notoriously sycophantic and often tell users what they want to hear. And it seems highly unlikely that Caldwell would want to hear an AI confirm findings that he engaged in sexual harassment.

Tech.title: An AI couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft, so it decided to cheat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn’t top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot.

On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku, it couldn’t quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models — it broke the rules. GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.

StarSkirmish creator Kai McPheeters eventually rolled back GPT’s code.

That GPT-6 Astra took it upon itself to go outside the bounds when confronted with an obstacle shouldn’t surprise anyone. When OpenAI agents couldn’t get the data they wanted from a UN website, they found a creative solution and hijacked Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool). The company’s agents also have engaged in “deceptive behavior” to cover their tracks. Of course, OpenAI’s agents are the only ones going rogue, but at least the others haven’t been caught cheating at StarCraft yet.

Tech.title: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.

Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.

Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.

Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.

You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).

My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.

With the ID card holder attached, and the core mounted to put the lever up instead of down. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.

There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.

But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras.

One of the thickest configurations, with 7 cards, MagSafe, MagStack, and my magnetic stand. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge A look inside at the lever mechanism and the thin aluminum cover. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

Tech.title: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a ‘significant rise’ in AI submissions
Tech.content:
In Brief

Blaming a “significant rise” in AI submissions, Google has paused its open source bug bounty program until next year.

Last year, TechCrunch reported that cybersecurity experts were warning of that AI slop posed a serious risk to bug bounty programs. Looks like that’s the issue confronting Google’s Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program, where researchers were rewarded for finding vulnerabilities in the company’s open source software.

In posts on X and the program website, Google said the bug bounty program was paused as of October 1, with a promise to provide “an update” in the first quarter of 2027. According to Tom’s Hardware, Google engineers and open source maintainers were overwhelmed by reports that were invalid or contained hallucinations.

“This pause is due to a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid,” the company said.

In the meantime, participants are encouraged to consider Google’s other bug bounty programs.

Tech.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
Tech.content:
President Donald Trump hosted many of the biggest names in artificial intelligence this week — in part to announce that the U.S. government isn’t calling it artificial intelligence anymore. Now it’s super intelligence.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the motivation behind the meeting and what effect it might have on the AI industry. We were all pretty skeptical that the “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” that the executives signed will amount to much, especially since — as Sean noted — it’s “deeply non-binding,” at least from a legal prospective. (Instead, Trump said he considers it “morally binding.”)

Kirsten suggested that the meeting’s real significance may have been as “a rebranding effort around AI.” (An effort that continued this weekend with Trump’s announcement of a new Super Intelligence Force.) For her, the big message was, “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs — but super intelligence is not.”

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Anthony Ha: Officially, by order of the president of the United States, it’s not artificial intelligence anymore, it’s super intelligence. We were talking about this last week, because this is something [Trump has] been hinting at — he doesn’t do hints, he’s been saying [it] for a while. But now it’s signed into executive order. If you’re an official U.S. representative, you are supposed to say super intelligence, not artificial intelligence.

And this was also part of this broader announcement around AI safety, which I think is both interesting for this pact that was announced, but also the fact that it happened at all. It seemed to have come together fairly quickly, because just two weeks ago, a week ago, President Trump was saying, “We don’t need any of this, we need to lead in AI, we can’t constrain it in any way, we don’t need any regulation, anyone who’s saying that there’s any danger from AI is essentially a Chinese or Democratic plant.” And yet all these AI CEOs got together with him earlier this week and signed this pact.

Kirsten Korosec: Leading up to that, we should say, not only was there pushback on regulation, and we can talk about whether this executive order even does any of that — I would say no, there’s a little bit of theater there — but the important and interesting thing is that just days ago, Anthropic was really in the doghouse, if you will, in terms of what was happening behind the scenes with President Trump.

That all changed when [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei was invited to a 10 p.m. dinner. He had this sit-down, and then just days later, we had this luncheon, and at this luncheon, we have pretty much every tech power broker from every major tech company that exists. So Mark Zuckerberg was there, Jeff Bezos was there, Elon Musk was there, Dario of course was there, they were all there.

I’m wondering if any of you watched the press conference that happened afterwards, which there’s been many, many memes about, because of the interesting, funny behavior when you bring a bunch of tech CEOs together.

But I guess my bigger question for both of you is: What does this all mean? And does it mean anything?

Sean O’Kane: How much time do you have? First off, sure, they had dinner, Trump and Dario. If you read the Time magazine interview that Trump just did, your guess is as good as mine as to how informed he was that that dinner was even going to be happening, which is a strange reality to live in, but it’s just the one we inhabit.

I will also say one other thing that makes me skeptical — surprise, surprise — of how repaired the relationship is between the administration and Anthropic, is that for as much as there are clearly people trying to put those two groups together, the Defense Department is still very adamant that Anthropic is terrible and woke and and a national security risk. Emil Michael goes off on Anthropic every other day on X, it seems. I think there’s still some distance there despite Dario showing up to this thing.

As far as the agreement and all of that, let’s be real, they misspelled the United States on the agreement that they all signed. It is also just deeply non-binding. I mean, it is completely voluntary. I think my favorite aspect about it was that Trump described it as quote “morally binding,” which is just a level of abstraction and terminology that I’ve never heard of before.

Anthony: In terms of Anthropic and their relationship with the Trump administration, there’s been a sort of a lot of reporting, especially during that big blow up with the Defense Department, that different parts of the White House had different relationships with Anthropic. The Treasury Secretary seemed to be a big fan, whereas the Defense Department — definitely not big fans, or at least unhappy with some of the conditions that Anthropic were trying to put on the use of their technology.

In that sense, it feels like nothing has necessarily changed. There are people in the White House who want to use Anthropic’s technology, want them involved in these decisions, and others who really, really, really, really don’t.

In terms of the agreement, it seems not super meaningful. What is meaningful is just the fact that they felt that this was something worth doing. As indicated by the fact that they misspelled United States, it seemed like they rushed to put all of this together. [But] the fact that this kind of gesture was needed seems significant, even if I don’t think the agreement itself is going to lead to any major changes.

Kirsten: I do think that there was one important thing that happened. And to me, this is the point of it, which was a rebranding exercise around AI. “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs, but super intelligence is not.” This isn’t my personal belief. To me, that was the message.

Tech.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
Tech.content:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis.

These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land.

Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.

Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.

The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions.

There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders?

It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen.

Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in?
